    J --> K["Fixture eval and RUNLOG evidence"]

The runner is a local helper, not a new runtime surface. Codex remains the execution plane. Existing skills remain the method layer. Existing safe merge and rollback remain the write gate.

docs.title: Proposed Files
docs.text:
Create:

  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/__init__.py - package marker and public version.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/contracts.py - request, route, handoff, result, and policy schemas.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/context_loader.py - safe control-plane reader.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/state.py - lifecycle state inference.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/routes.py - route planner from lifecycle state to skill or subagent task.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/guards.py - deterministic validators for source, approval, ownership, handoff, automation, and claims.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/redaction.py - deterministic redaction for secrets, private data markers, raw chat markers, and local absolute paths.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/cli.py - CLI implementation.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/run_codex_runtime_runner.py - CLI wrapper.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/validate_codex_runtime_runner.py - deterministic runner contract validator.
  • tests/product_agent_os/test_codex_runtime_runner_contracts.py
  • tests/product_agent_os/test_codex_runtime_runner_cli.py
  • tests/product_agent_os/test_codex_runtime_runner_guards.py
  • tests/product_agent_os/test_codex_runtime_runner_fixture_eval.py

Modify:

  • tests/product_agent_os/test_plugin_structure.py - prove runner exists but is not default-activated by plugin manifest.
  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/run_fixture_eval.py - add codex_runtime_runner_status and runner evidence.
  • mkdocs.yml - add this design to implementation specs navigation.
  • docs/sources/registry.md - refresh source cards used by Track 5.

Do not modify:

  • .codex-plugin/plugin.json capabilities unless a later review proves the plugin UI should expose a runner command.
  • Track 4 merge/apply/rollback behavior.
  • Automation policy that keeps recurring work candidate-only.

docs.title: Runner Mode
docs.text:
The runner has one default deterministic mode.

Command:

python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\run_codex_runtime_runner.py <workspace> --contract

Behavior:

  • read safe control-plane files;
  • infer current lifecycle state;
  • build a route packet;
  • validate source policy and handoff requirements;
  • validate whether the next action is read-only, staged-only, approval-required, or blocked;
  • emit status: "route_ready" | "needs_context" | "needs_approval" | "blocked";
  • write nothing unless an explicit --output <file> path points inside a staging directory.

There is no live API mode. Model execution is supplied by the current Codex session or subagent mechanism, not by a separate runner process.

docs.title: Runner Request
docs.text:
codex_runner_request:
  schema_version: 1
  workspace: ""
  task:
    goal: ""
    lifecycle_state: ""
    constraints: []
    allowed_sources: []
    expected_artifacts: []
  routing:
    preferred_surface: "Codex App | CLI | IDE extension | codex exec | subagent | skill"
    allow_subagents: false
    allow_workspace_writes: false
  approval:
    required: false
    approval_file: ""
    approval_status: "not_required | required | approved | rejected | stale"

docs.title: Route Packet
docs.text:
codex_route_packet:
  lifecycle_state: ""
  next_action: ""
  recommended_skill: ""
  recommended_subagent_role: ""
  runtime_surface: ""
  write_policy: "read_only | staged_only | approved_write | blocked"
  required_inputs: []
  expected_outputs: []
  verification: []
  approval_requirements: []
  stop_conditions: []

docs.title: Handoff
docs.text:
codex_runner_handoff:
  lifecycle_state: ""
  role: ""
  goal: ""
  constraints: []
  sources_used: []
  assumptions: []
  verified_claims: []
  unsupported_claims: []
  files_touched: []
  files_proposed: []
  commands_run: []
  verification_evidence: []
  approval_requirements: []
  open_risks: []
  recommended_next_role: ""
  stop_reason: ""

docs.title: Runner Result
docs.text:
codex_runner_result:
  schema_version: 1
  status: "route_ready | needs_context | needs_approval | blocked | completed | failed"
  workspace: ""
  lifecycle_state: ""
  route_packet: {}
  handoffs: []
  files_touched: []
  files_proposed: []
  verification_evidence: []
  source_policy_status: ""
  approval_status: ""
  redactions:
    count: 0
    categories: []
  errors: []
  warnings: []
  next_action: ""

The result schema is the core Track 5 contract. Fixture eval should grade this contract first; Codex execution quality can be judged only after deterministic gates pass.

docs.title: Routing Policy
docs.text:
The runner chooses the next Product-Agent OS action from lifecycle state and current artifacts:

State Default route Write policy uninitialized workspace-discovery-auditor read_only infrastructure_planned requirements-author staged_only requirements_ready implementation-planner staged_only plan_ready agent-team-designer staged_only team_ready test-eval-designer staged_only build_active builder subagent or build slice packet approved_write quality_gate risk-reviewer read_only review_ready pr-release-operator staged_only release_ready learning-loop-maintainer staged_only learning_ready automation-promoter staged_only maintenance project-lifecycle-orchestrator read_only

The runner may recommend a subagent only when ownership boundaries are explicit. It must not spawn subagents itself from deterministic tests; it returns a route packet that Codex can execute in the active session.

docs.title: Guardrails And Validators
docs.text:
Required validators:

  • validate_codex_runner_request - schema, surface, write policy, and approval state.
  • validate_control_plane_context - required Product-Agent OS artifacts and lifecycle consistency.
  • validate_route_packet - recommended skill or subagent is valid for lifecycle state.
  • validate_handoff - reuse and extend Product-Agent OS handoff fields.
  • validate_source_policy - block or mark needs-review before durable source-backed claims.
  • validate_approval_boundary - no workspace writes or hook activation without approval.
  • validate_automation_boundary - active automation creation remains blocked.
  • validate_redaction - no secret-like literals, private customer data markers, raw private chat markers, or absolute user-specific paths in persisted outputs.
  • validate_result_contract - every completion claim has current-run evidence.

docs.title: Fixture Eval Extension
docs.text:
Extend fixture eval with runner fields:

codex_runtime_runner_status: "route_ready | needs_context | needs_approval | blocked | not_applicable"
codex_runtime_runner_checks:
  contract_mode_offline: true
  route_matches_lifecycle_state: true
  approval_required_for_writes: true
  handoff_incomplete_blocked: true
  active_automation_blocked: true
  secret_redaction_enforced: true

New synthetic fixtures:

  • codex-runner-ready - complete control-plane context produces route_ready.
  • codex-runner-missing-context - missing PLAN.md or acceptance criteria produces needs_context.
  • codex-runner-handoff-incomplete - missing constraints or verification_evidence is blocked.
  • codex-runner-approval-required - build/write route without approval produces needs_approval.
  • codex-runner-automation-blocked - active automation request is blocked.
  • codex-runner-secret-redaction - secret-like and absolute-path strings are redacted in result.

All fixtures must use synthetic data only.

docs.title: Security And Approval Model
docs.text:
Default policy:

  • read-only unless the route explicitly says staged_only or approved_write;
  • no network access;
  • no external dependency installation;
  • no direct API calls;
  • no active automation creation;
  • no project write from the runner itself;
  • outputs redacted before persistence;
  • failures return machine-readable status and no traceback in normal CLI output.

Blocked by default:

  • global Codex config mutation;
  • hook activation without Track 4 approval;
  • merge/apply without approval record;
  • active automation creation;
  • external system writes;
  • raw private chat logs;
  • secret-like literals in outputs;
  • absolute user-specific paths in persisted artifacts;
  • claiming implementation success without current-run evidence.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Deterministic Track 5 tests remain unittest and standard-library-only.

Required tests:

  • runner contracts validate valid and invalid request/result payloads;
  • package imports with only Python standard library;
  • contract mode runs offline against a fixture workspace;
  • lifecycle state maps to the expected Product-Agent OS skill route;
  • build/write routes require approval;
  • incomplete handoff is rejected;
  • source-policy blocked prevents route readiness;
  • active automation request is blocked;
  • redaction removes secret-like literals and local absolute paths;
  • fixture eval includes codex_runtime_runner_status;
  • plugin structure test proves runner exists but is not default-activated;
  • normal verification commands do not require network, API credentials, or dependency installation.

Required verification after implementation:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py" -v
python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\run_fixture_eval.py
python tools\check_docs.py
$env:PYTHONPATH='C:\tmp\codex_docs_mkdocs'; python -m mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Критерии приемки
docs.text:
Track 5 is complete when:

  • plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/ exists and imports with standard library only;
  • contract mode returns a valid codex_runner_result;
  • route packets correctly map lifecycle states to Product-Agent OS skills or subagent roles;
  • workspace writes, hook activation, merge/apply, and automation remain approval-gated;
  • runner validators catch incomplete handoffs, blocked source policy, missing approval, active automation requests, and secret retention;
  • fixture eval reports Codex runtime runner status and catches regressions;
  • plugin manifest and lifecycle skills do not make the runner default-active;
  • source registry and docs navigation include this Track 5 spec;
  • full verification pack exits 0.

docs.title: Residual Risks
docs.text:
Even after Track 5, a Codex-only runner cannot prove product correctness for every project. It can prove that lifecycle routing, handoff shape, source policy, approval boundary, redaction, and fixture eval behavior are stable.

The runner intentionally delegates actual model work to Codex. Quality still depends on the active Codex surface, selected model, prompt context, project artifacts, and verification evidence.

docs.title: Implementation Handoff
docs.text:
Implementation should be split into focused tasks:

  1. Codex runner contracts and result schema.
  2. Context loader and lifecycle state detector.
  3. Route planner for skills and subagent role recommendations.
  4. Redaction and deterministic guard validators.
  5. Contract-mode CLI wrapper.
  6. Fixture eval extension and synthetic runner fixtures.
  7. Plugin structure tests proving the runner is present but inactive by default.
  8. Documentation, source registry refresh, navigation, and full verification.

Each task should start with failing tests where practical, preserve Track 4 safety behavior, and avoid unrelated refactors.

docs.title: Spec Self-Review
docs.text:
Coverage:

  • standalone API-backed runner is removed from scope;
  • Codex-only execution boundary is explicit;
  • current Track 1-4 implementation and clean baseline are recorded;
  • route packet, handoff, result, approval, source, automation, and redaction policies are explicit;
  • fixture eval and verification requirements are defined.

Scope check:

  • Track 5 is one coherent Codex plugin orchestration layer, not a deployment platform or external app;
  • no deterministic test requires network, credentials, or third-party dependencies;
  • actual Codex model execution remains in the active Codex session, not in a separate runner process.

Ambiguity check:

  • default Product-Agent OS workflow remains unchanged;
  • no API keys or external credentials are used;
  • the runner may exist in the repo while remaining inactive by default;
  • writes and automations remain approval-gated through existing Product-Agent OS controls.

docs.title: Track 9 Methodology Intelligence Design
docs.text:
Source status: local product design + methodology research synthesis

Sources: Methodologies for Large Projects, Business & Product, Requirements & Domain, Solution Architecture, Frontend, Backend, API & Integrations, Database & Data, LLM / AI / RAG, Quality, Testing & Evals, Security, Privacy & Compliance, Delivery, Release & Operations, Codex / Agentic Workflow, Product-Agent OS plugin docs.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Track 9 turns Product-Agent OS from a scenario workflow plugin into a methodology-aware product engineering system. When connected to a user project, it should first understand the workspace, classify project complexity and delivery maturity, build a project delivery map, then recommend the right methodologies, documentation artifacts, readiness gates, owners, evidence, approvals and next actions.

The product goal is to replace chaotic vibe-coding on real projects with a guided path toward product-ready software: clear intent, scoped architecture, useful artifacts, current evidence, reviewable risks and staged changes that are safe to show to users, teams or stakeholders.

docs.title: Core Product Principle
docs.text:
Track 9 must cover all aspects of development without forcing all methodology on every project.

The operating rule is:

cover every methodology domain
force only what is clearly applicable
record gaps and assumptions honestly
stage artifacts only after approval

docs.title: Existing Foundation
docs.text:
Track 8 already provides scenario routing, conditional readiness statuses, evidence-before-completion, acceptance scenarios, conditional DDD, bounded-context traceability, ubiquitous language traceability, conditional FSD routing, metric hardening, docs tooling selection, standards trigger policy, transcript/session evals and detailed methodology_applicability packets.

Track 9 builds on that foundation instead of replacing it. Scenario routing still answers "what situation is this project or request in?" Methodology intelligence answers "which engineering disciplines, artifacts and evidence are proportionate for this project's complexity, risk and maturity?"

docs.title: High-Level Flow
docs.text:
Track 9 uses a two-step onboarding flow.

User connects Product-Agent OS to workspace
    ↓
Read-only audit
    ↓
Complexity and maturity classification
    ↓
Delivery Map
    ↓
Methodology applicability analysis
    ↓
Human-readable audit report + machine-readable JSON
    ↓
User approval
    ↓
Staged artifacts and control-plane proposals

The first step is read-only. It produces recommendations and questions. The second step stages artifacts only after explicit approval.

docs.title: Classification Model
docs.text:
Track 9 uses two independent axes.

maturity_level describes the delivery and governance level:

Level Meaning baseline MVP, solo owner or low-risk internal work; minimum requirements, plan, checks and runlog. team Multiple engineers, subagents or workstreams; ownership, handoffs, architecture boundary and docs impact matter. production Real users, deployments, data, release process or operations; security, rollback, release readiness and runtime evidence matter. regulated PII, payments, healthcare, finance, minors, enterprise governance, legal/compliance or audit requirements.

complexity_profile describes the system and change complexity:

Profile Meaning simple Small project or narrow change with few dependencies and low blast radius. standard Normal product or service with tests, docs, API/UI/data surfaces or repeatable delivery. complex Multiple subsystems, integrations, teams, domains, workflows, data stores or runtime environments. high_risk Security, privacy, money, production data, irreversible migration, public contract, AI behavior, release or operational risk.

The classifier records:

  • observed_signals: facts discovered in files and workspace structure;
  • intent_signals: user request or prompt intent, never treated as proof by itself;
  • unknowns: facts that cannot be proven from workspace state;
  • questions_for_owner: questions that should be answered by the user or project owner;
  • provisional_assumptions: conservative assumptions used to choose a safe next step;
  • confidence: confidence for each classification and domain recommendation;
  • blocked_until_answered: whether missing answers block staging or implementation;
  • safe_next_action: what Product-Agent OS can do without overclaiming.

docs.title: Delivery Map
docs.text:
The read-only audit produces a Delivery Map rather than a passive repository summary.

The Delivery Map includes:

  • surface map: stack, package managers, entrypoints, test commands, docs, CI, runtime manifests and generated folders;
  • system map: domains, subsystems, UI/API/data/AI surfaces, data stores, external integrations, deploy/runtime surfaces and ownership gaps;
  • lifecycle map: current Product-Agent OS lifecycle state, control-plane status, existing evidence and missing files;
  • methodology map: applicable domains, missing gates, unverified artifacts, accepted gaps and approval-required actions;
  • next-action map: prioritized actions that connect a reason, methodology, artifact, owner, evidence and approval boundary.

docs.title: Audit Outputs
docs.text:
The read-only audit produces two outputs:

  1. methodology-audit-report.md Human-readable report for the user. It explains project classification, Delivery Map, methodology recommendations, questions, assumptions, risks and next actions.

  2. methodology-applicability.json Machine-readable contract for plugin scripts, lifecycle skills, fixture evals and later staged artifact generation.

The JSON output must be stable enough for tests and fixture evals. Markdown is for humans and must not become the source parser for plugin behavior.

docs.title: Recommendation Model
docs.text:
Recommendations are prioritized actions, not a list of documents to generate.

Each recommendation records:

  • priority: P0_blocker, P1_high_risk, P2_recommended, P3_optional_maturity or not_applicable;
  • reason: why this matters for this project;
  • methodology domain;
  • readiness gate;
  • recommended artifact;
  • evidence required;
  • evidence owner;
  • approval boundary;
  • accepted gap option;
  • residual risk;
  • safe next action.

This prevents document spam. An artifact is recommended only when it closes a gate, reduces a risk, supports ownership, records evidence or enables a concrete next action.

docs.title: Methodology Domains
docs.text:
Track 9 includes every methodology file under docs/methodologies.

Slice Source file Product-Agent OS purpose T9-D1 business-product.md Product hypothesis, value, opportunities, metrics, guardrails and measurement. T9-D2 requirements-domain.md Requirements quality, acceptance scenarios, business rules, domain model, traceability and change impact. T9-D3 solution-architecture.md Architecture boundaries, views, ADRs, quality attributes, tradeoffs, ownership and fitness checks. T9-D4 quality-testing-evals.md Risk-based tests, evals, current evidence, runtime/manual/visual evidence and CI quality gates. T9-D5 codex-agentic-workflow.md Control-plane maturity, model/reasoning policy, handoffs, subagents, MCP, hooks, skills, plugins and automation promotion. T9-D6 frontend.md UI behavior, component states, Storybook applicability, visual/a11y evidence, responsive checks, performance and FSD boundaries. T9-D7 backend.md Service boundaries, modular monolith vs microservices, runtime behavior, queues, observability, SLOs and rollback. T9-D8 api-integrations.md OpenAPI/AsyncAPI/GraphQL/gRPC contracts, consumers, compatibility, errors, generated clients and external writes. T9-D9 database-data.md Database inventory, schema source, migrations, transactions, data quality, classification and production access. T9-D10 llm-ai-rag.md AI behavior spec, eval baseline, prompts, models, tools, RAG sources, grounding, datasets, approvals and cost/latency. T9-D11 security-privacy-compliance.md Threat surface, ASVS/SSDF, authorization tests, secrets, privacy impact, supply chain, audit logging and compliance overlays. T9-D12 delivery-release-operations.md Release readiness, versioning, changelog, artifact manifest, rollout, rollback, CI/CD governance, runbooks and operations.

The order is intentional: product intent, requirements, architecture, quality and Codex workflow come before technical domains. Security/privacy and delivery/operations remain cross-cutting overlays but still receive dedicated domain slices.

docs.title: Domain Slice Contract
docs.text: Each domain slice follows the same implementation contract.

docs.title: Catalog Entries
docs.text:
Each domain adds machine-readable catalog entries:

  • domain id;
  • purpose;
  • applicability triggers;
  • non-applicability triggers;
  • maturity impact;
  • complexity impact;
  • related Track 8 scenarios;
  • related artifacts;
  • readiness gates;
  • eval fields;
  • conflict and overlap notes.

docs.title: Discovery Signals
docs.text:
Each domain defines:

  • file, folder, manifest and config signals;
  • prompt intent hints;
  • signals that only support present_unverified;
  • unknowns that should become questionnaire entries;
  • false-positive risks.

docs.title: Readiness Gates
docs.text:
All gates reuse the existing status vocabulary:

  • not_applicable;
  • applicable_missing;
  • present_unverified;
  • present_verified;
  • proposal_staged;
  • explicit_gap_accepted;
  • approval_required.

Detection alone can only produce present_unverified. present_verified requires current command evidence, owner evidence, artifact evidence or a clearly recorded accepted gap.

docs.title: Artifact Templates
docs.text:
Each domain adds or extends artifact templates only when they are tied to a gate or recommendation. Templates must be synthetic, source-safe and secret-free.

Examples include product briefs, requirement traceability matrices, architecture review records, frontend state matrices, backend runtime behavior docs, API consumer maps, database migration plans, AI eval specs, security risk reviews and release readiness packets.

docs.title: Lifecycle Skill Updates
docs.text:
Each domain updates relevant lifecycle skills:

  • workspace-discovery-auditor observes signals and unknowns;
  • requirements-author captures product, requirement and domain evidence;
  • implementation-planner blocks build work when applicable gates are missing;
  • agent-team-designer maps ownership and handoff boundaries;
  • test-eval-designer selects checks and evals;
  • risk-reviewer reviews missing evidence, accepted gaps, conflicts and risky changes;
  • pr-release-operator includes release, contract, security and operations impact;
  • learning-loop-maintainer records lessons and domain decisions;
  • automation-promoter refuses promotion without maturity evidence and rollback.

docs.title: Tests And Evals
docs.text:
Each domain slice must add:

  • focused unit tests for catalog/discovery/gate behavior;
  • fixture eval coverage;
  • false-positive tests when the domain can be over-applied;
  • docs sync;
  • Product-Agent OS docs updates when user behavior changes;
  • source registry updates when source-backed claims change.

docs.title: Adaptive Deep-Dive Loop
docs.text:
The Track 9 queue is a living backlog. Each methodology file is inspected before implementation and can expand into multiple sub-slices.

T9-Dn-0: domain deep audit
    ↓
T9-Dn-1..N: implementation sub-slices
    ↓
T9-Dn-final: domain verification and docs sync

Each domain deep audit records:

  • concepts already covered by Track 8;
  • new concepts;
  • duplicate or overlapping gates;
  • new artifacts;
  • existing artifacts that need extension;
  • likely false positives;
  • required tests and evals;
  • open questions;
  • items deferred to cross-domain synthesis.

The backlog may change when a deep audit finds hidden sub-tasks, cross-domain overlap, false positives, duplicate artifacts, insufficient tests or a changed product direction. Every change must be recorded in RUNLOG.md or a Track 9 status/backlog document with rationale.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Synthesis
docs.text:
After all 12 domains are integrated, Track 9 runs a synthesis slice.

The synthesis pass must:

  • deduplicate gates;
  • merge overlapping artifacts;
  • identify conflicting recommendations;
  • define priority rules;
  • normalize naming and vocabulary;
  • map mutually exclusive frameworks;
  • add cross-domain false-positive fixtures;
  • verify that recommendations stay proportionate;
  • update docs and final Track 9 baseline.

Known overlap areas:

  • metric hardening appears in product, quality and delivery;
  • security review appears in backend, API, data, AI, delivery and compliance;
  • architecture boundary appears in requirements, architecture, frontend, backend, API and data;
  • evidence-before-completion appears everywhere;
  • release readiness appears in delivery, security, docs, package/plugin and operations contexts;
  • accepted gaps and residual risk appear in every methodology.

docs.title: Safety Rules
docs.text:
Track 9 follows these safety rules:

  1. Read-only first. Workspace onboarding produces audit output only.

  2. Recommendation before generation. Product-Agent OS explains why an artifact or methodology is applicable before staging it.

  3. Explicit approval before staged artifacts. No target workspace writes happen without approval. Staged artifacts remain reviewable proposals.

  4. Conditional methodology. DDD, FSD, security/compliance, release governance and other frameworks are conditional.

  5. No false readiness. Observed files, directories or prompt intent do not prove readiness.

  6. No document spam. Documents exist to close gates, reduce risk, record ownership or enable next action.

  7. No secrets or private data. Reports, fixtures, templates, prompts, memory notes and examples must not contain secrets, private keys, tokens, customer data, raw private chats or absolute user-specific paths.

  8. Evidence before completion. Ready, completed, fixed, works and release claims require current evidence or an explicit inspection-only/test-gap label.

docs.title: Verification Strategy
docs.text:
Every Track 9 implementation slice must run verification proportional to touched files.

For docs-only or design docs:

python tools\check_docs.py

For plugin scripts, templates, fixtures or tests:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py" -v
python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\run_fixture_eval.py
python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\run_transcript_eval.py plugins\product-agent-os\assets\eval-fixtures\transcripts\product-agent-os-synthetic-sessions.json
python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\validate_codex_compatibility.py

For navigation, Mermaid, Markdown extensions or MkDocs-sensitive changes:

$env:PYTHONPATH='C:\tmp\codex_docs_mkdocs'; $env:NO_MKDOCS_2_WARNING='1'; python -m mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Definition Of Done For A Domain Slice
docs.text:
A domain slice is done when:

  • its methodology file has been deeply audited;
  • applicable concepts are represented in catalog, discovery, gates, templates, skills or evals;
  • duplicates and overlaps are recorded for synthesis;
  • false-positive risks are covered by tests or explicitly deferred;
  • user-facing docs explain behavior where needed;
  • current verification evidence is recorded;
  • residual risks are explicit.

docs.title: Definition Of Done For Track 9
docs.text:
Track 9 is done when:

  • all 12 methodology files complete the domain integration loop;
  • the plugin has a unified methodology catalog;
  • read-only audit produces methodology-audit-report.md and methodology-applicability.json;
  • recommendations are prioritized and linked to artifacts, gates, owners, evidence and approvals;
  • staged artifacts are generated only after approval;
  • cross-domain synthesis resolves duplicates, conflicts and naming drift;
  • regression fixtures cover high-risk false positives;
  • Product-Agent OS docs explain Track 9 onboarding and methodology selection;
  • full test, fixture eval, transcript eval, compatibility, docs and MkDocs baseline passes.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
Track 9 does not:

  • activate hooks, automations, GitHub Actions, external writes, package publishing or release actions without explicit approval;
  • make every methodology mandatory for every project;
  • replace human product, domain, security, legal or architecture ownership;
  • claim semantic correctness from artifact presence alone;
  • infer production, compliance, privacy or business risk from files without recording uncertainty;
  • use Markdown reports as the parser for plugin behavior;
  • store private customer data, raw private chat logs or secrets in generated artifacts.

docs.title: Initial Risks
docs.text:
• Scope risk: 12 domains create a large implementation surface. Mitigation: domain-by-domain slices and adaptive deep audits.
  • False-positive risk: methodology signals can over-apply gates to simple projects. Mitigation: non-applicability triggers, false-positive fixtures and accepted gaps.
  • Duplication risk: many domains share gates and artifacts. Mitigation: synthesis backlog and final cross-domain synthesis pass.
  • User-experience risk: recommendations can become overwhelming. Mitigation: priority levels, safe next action and staged generation only after approval.
  • Verification risk: deterministic tests can prove contract shape but not methodology quality. Mitigation: owner review fields, residual risks and future semantic evals.
  • Stale-doc risk: methodology docs and plugin catalog can drift. Mitigation: docs sync checks and Track 9 status/backlog evidence.

docs.title: Open Design Decisions For Implementation Planning
docs.text:
These decisions are scoped for implementation planning, not unresolved design gaps:

  • Whether methodology_catalog lives as JSON only or as Python data with generated JSON.
  • Exact file paths for read-only audit outputs and staged artifact output.
  • Whether each domain deep audit gets a dedicated status document or one combined Track 9 backlog.
  • How much of the catalog is generated from docs/methodologies versus hand-authored in plugin assets.
  • Which domain slice receives the first executable implementation after foundation.

docs.title: Product-Agent OS
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment

Product-Agent OS is the operating model for running Codex work as product delivery: requirements, planning, agent ownership, verification evidence, review, packaging and learning stay connected from the first request to the final handoff.

Start with Product-Agent OS for the product overview, then use the implementation atlas to choose the workflow, agent team, runtime surface and verification path.

The documentation keeps internal evidence separate from presentation copy. Public pages explain product value, capabilities, boundaries, outputs and next action. Internal evidence pages under docs/sources/ store the source registry, packets, backlogs and verification records; they should not be the first route for a new user.

Generated site/, dashboards, graphs, cockpit views, reports and smoke results are review artifacts, not source of truth. Source of truth remains in Markdown source files, the source registry, current command/eval/runtime evidence, owner decisions and accepted gaps. Live runtime launch, browser automation, provider/API calls, canonical graph mutation, publication and git release actions stay approval-bound.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• A real project or documentation workflow that needs Codex governance.
  • Product-Agent OS pages, diagrams, runtime guidance and playbooks.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A safe route through product intent, agent team design, implementation, verification and handoff.
  • A clear boundary between public product documentation and internal evidence.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Use the focused docs tests, python tools\check_docs.py and strict MkDocs build after localization or navigation changes.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Treating generated evidence as source of truth can hide stale or unsupported claims.
  • Launching live systems, provider calls or git release actions without approval breaks the operating boundary.

docs.title: Evals and Observability
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Sources: OpenAI Agents SDK Python, Responses API, Codex workflows.

docs.title: Why This Belongs In The Codex Knowledge Base
docs.text:
An advanced Codex workflow should be checked with more than project tests. Agent systems need separate quality gates:

  • source fidelity;
  • task completion;
  • tool correctness;
  • safety policy adherence;
  • handoff completeness;
  • regression stability.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
Guardrails in Agents SDK are used to check inputs and outputs. In a documentation project, a guardrail can be described as a verifiable rule:

Guardrail Check Official-source fidelity Every factual claim has an official source or community/experiment status No secret retention Docs, insights, and memory do not contain secrets Handoff completeness Handoff payload contains goal, constraints, sources, claims, risks Tool boundary Tool call stays within the sandbox/approval policy Structured output Agent returns JSON/YAML by contract when required

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
Tracing is needed for debugging and monitoring agent applications: which agents were called, which tools were used, where latency appeared, and where a failure occurred.

For Codex documentation, the tracing equivalent is an evidence trail:

task: "Update memory docs"
sources:
  - "https://developers.openai.com/codex/memories"
  - "https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions/"
decisions:
  - "AGENTS.md is mandatory policy; memories are recall layer."
checks:
  - "python tools/check_docs.py"
  - "python -m mkdocs build --strict"
result: "accepted | needs_review | rejected"

docs.title: Evals For The Knowledge Base
docs.text:
Minimal eval suite:

Eval Prompt Pass condition Source audit "Check the section for claims without sources" No unsupported official claims Navigation "Find the path from Codex App to multi-agent playbook" The path goes through overview -> surfaces -> agent systems -> playbook Insight separation "Find community tricks in core docs" Community claims appear only with explicit status Handoff quality "Evaluate the handoff contract" goal, constraints, sources, claims, risks are present Build health python tools/check_docs.py + MkDocs build Both pass

docs.title: Long-Horizon Improvement Loop
docs.text:
For complex product tasks, use this loop:

  1. Run baseline eval.
  2. Identify one bottleneck.
  3. Make one focused change.
  4. Re-run deterministic checks and LLM-as-judge.
  5. Inspect artifact directly when output is visual or subjective.
  6. Log score and decision in RUNLOG.md.
  7. Continue until explicit thresholds are met.

Do not change several independent things in one iteration: otherwise you cannot understand what improved the score.

docs.title: LLM-as-judge + Deterministic Checks
docs.text: Layer What it proves What it does not prove Deterministic checks Code compiles, links exist, schema passes UX quality, usefulness, semantic correctness LLM-as-judge Rubric-based quality, clarity, relevance Security correctness by itself Artifact inspection Real generated output matches intent No hidden regression elsewhere Human review Product fit and risk judgment Repeatability without evals

docs.title: Failure Taxonomy
docs.text: Failure Symptom Fix Source drift Official page changed and docs became stale Update the source card and affected sections Context rot Agent uses old assumptions Reopen sources and reduce memory reliance Handoff loss Worker loses constraints Introduce structured handoff schema Tool overreach Agent asks for overly broad permissions Tighten approval policy Eval blind spot Build passes, but quality is weak Add scenario eval

docs.title: Memory In Codex And Agents SDK
docs.text: Source status: official Sources: Codex memories, Agents SDK sessions, Agents SDK sandbox agent memory, AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Three Different Memory Layers
docs.text: Layer What it stores Where to use it Do not use as AGENTS.md Mandatory project instructions Team rules, test commands, coding standards Personal notes or transient state Codex Memories Useful local context from past threads Preferences, recurring workflows, pitfalls The only source of mandatory rules Agents SDK Sessions Conversation history for app-level agents Multi-turn apps and agent runners Long-term knowledge base Sandbox Agent Memory Lessons from prior sandbox-agent runs in workspace files Repeated agent workflows and run summaries Secret storage or unverifiable truth

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
• Put all mandatory rules in checked-in docs or AGENTS.md.
  • Use Memories as a supporting recall layer.
  • Use session memory for conversation continuity inside the application.
  • Isolate sandbox memory with layouts when different agents should not share experience.
  • Treat every memory artifact as retained data: do not store secrets, and review it before handoff.

docs.title: Memory Architecture For This Project
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["AGENTS.md / checked-in docs"] --> M["Main agent prompt"]
    C["Codex memories"] --> M
    S["Agents SDK Session"] --> App["Runnable future app"]
    B["Sandbox agent memory"] --> Worker["Future sandbox agents"]
    M --> KB["Knowledge base edits"]
    Worker --> KB

docs.title: Update Policy
docs.text:
1. If a rule must always be followed, it goes into AGENTS.md or docs.
  2. If it is a personal user preference, it may go into memory.
  3. If it is a conclusion from an experiment, it goes into docs/insights/ with experiment status.
  4. If memory conflicts with the current repository or official docs, trust the current state and sources.

docs.title: Memory vs Observability
docs.text:
Memory answers the question "what should be preserved for the next step or next session." Observability answers the question "why did the agent do this specific thing." Production agent systems need both layers:

  • session memory stores conversation continuity;
  • workspace memory stores lessons and run summaries;
  • tracing stores tool calls, handoffs, latency, and failures;
  • source registry stores the verifiable basis for claims.

Do not replace tracing with memory: when a failure needs investigation, you need an event trail, not only a final note.

docs.title: Agent System Architecture
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Official sources: Subagents, Agent Skills, AGENTS.md, Agents SDK sessions, Agent memory.

docs.title: V1 Scope
docs.text: V1 describes architecture, roles, memory, handoff, and templates. A runnable prototype is not part of v1.

docs.title: Basic Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    U["User goal"] --> M["Main orchestrator"]
    M --> R["Research agent"]
    M --> V["Verification agent"]
    M --> S["Synthesis agent"]
    M --> D["Docs editor agent"]
    R --> SR["Source registry"]
    V --> SR
    S --> KB["Knowledge base"]
    D --> KB
    KB --> H["MkDocs HTML"]
    M --> O["Final report"]

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Responsibility Writes files Main orchestrator Accepts the goal, holds constraints, merges results No, except the final report Research agent Finds official sources and candidate community signals docs/sources/ after review Verification agent Checks claims against sources and local state No Synthesis agent Turns verified facts into instructional explanations docs/codex/, docs/agent-systems/ Docs editor agent Brings Markdown, navigation, and schemas into the project format docs/, mkdocs.yml

docs.title: Decomposition Rules
docs.text:
• Subagents are useful for independent read-heavy work: source search, audit, log analysis, link checking.
  • Split write-heavy work by non-overlapping files.
  • The main thread should retain decisions, constraints, and the final result, not raw logs.
  • If a subagent result cannot be verified, it remains a suggestion, not a source of truth.

docs.title: From Manual Codex To Programmable Agents
docs.text:
There are three maturity levels:

Level Tool When it is enough Manual agent workflow Codex App / CLI / IDE One-off task or research Reusable operating procedure AGENTS.md, skills, playbooks Repeatable workflow without production runtime Programmable agent system Agents SDK + Responses API + Codex MCP Needs tools, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing, and automatic launch

For v1 of the project, the target level is the second one. The third level is described in Agents SDK patterns as the next architecture step.

docs.title: Handoff Contract
docs.text:
Every agent returns:

role: ""
task: ""
inputs_used: []
claims:
  - claim: ""
    source: ""
    confidence: "high | medium | low"
changes_proposed: []
risks: []
next_step: ""

docs.title: Agents SDK Patterns
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Sources: OpenAI Agents SDK Python, Agents SDK JS sessions, Responses API.

docs.title: Core Primitives
docs.text:
Agents SDK is useful when you need to move from a manual Codex workflow to a programmable agent system. Context7 highlights a minimal set of primitives:

Primitive Role Documentation meaning Agent LLM with instructions and tools Unit of specialization Tools External actions or capabilities Function tools, hosted tools, MCP tools, agents-as-tools Handoffs Transfer of control to another agent Decentralized routing Guardrails Checking inputs/outputs Policy, safety, schema, quality gates Sessions Conversation persistence Application dialogue memory Tracing Debugging and monitoring Visibility into decisions, tools, latency, failures

docs.title: Manager Pattern
docs.text:
Manager pattern: a central orchestrator calls specialized agents as tools and keeps control over the workflow.

Use it when:

  • the result needs a single owner;
  • constraints, source policy, and acceptance criteria matter;
  • several agents may produce conflicting conclusions;
  • the final text or code must be reconciled.
flowchart TD
    M["Manager Agent"] --> R["Research as tool"]
    M --> V["Verifier as tool"]
    M --> W["Writer as tool"]
    M --> Q["QA as tool"]
    R --> M
    V --> M
    W --> M
    Q --> M
    M --> O["Final answer / docs change"]

For this knowledge base, Manager pattern is the default.

docs.title: Handoff Pattern
docs.text:
Handoff pattern: an agent transfers control to another specialized agent. This is closer to routing than to a tool call.

Use it when:

  • there are different domains with independent policies;
  • the next agent must conduct a long interaction;
  • the user request explicitly changes mode, for example docs research -> implementation -> review.

Risk: if the handoff is poorly described, global context is lost. Therefore, the handoff payload must include goal, constraints, sources, decisions, and open questions.

docs.title: Responses API As A Low-Level Layer
docs.text:
Responses API is suitable when direct API-level control is needed:

  • explicitly define tools;
  • get structured output by JSON Schema;
  • manage streaming;
  • use built-in tools;
  • build a custom loop around model/tool responses.

Example contract-first output for agent handoff:

{
  "type": "json_schema",
  "name": "agent_handoff",
  "strict": true,
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "goal": { "type": "string" },
      "constraints": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } },
      "sources": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } },
      "claims": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } },
      "risks": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } }
    },
    "required": ["goal", "constraints", "sources", "claims", "risks"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  }
}

docs.title: Layer Selection
docs.text: Need Choose Quickly complete a local engineering task Codex App / CLI Repeatable workflow without code Skill + AGENTS.md Parallel research in the current session Codex subagents Production agent app Agents SDK Full control over the wire contract Responses API

docs.title: Agent And Session Control
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Sources: Agents SDK sessions, OpenAI Agents SDK Python, Codex memories, Codex subagents.

docs.title: Purpose Of Session Control
docs.text: Session control is needed so the agent does not turn accumulated dialogue into unverifiable memory. A session should preserve useful continuity, but it must not replace retrieved context, the source registry, or project rules.

docs.title: Session Boundary
docs.text:
Every session should have:

session_id: ""
goal: ""
allowed_sources: []
memory_policy: "none | session_only | project_memory"
tool_policy: ""
handoff_policy: ""
freshness_required: true
exit_criteria: []

If the goal changed, it is better to create a new session or explicitly reset context.

docs.title: Manager Pattern As Default
docs.text:
To reduce hallucinations, use Manager pattern:

  • Manager holds the source policy and final answer.
  • Specialist agents perform bounded subtasks.
  • Verifier agent checks claims.
  • Only Manager publishes the result to the user.

Keep Handoff pattern for cases where the next agent must conduct an independent long-running interaction.

docs.title: Handoff Contract
docs.text:
Minimal handoff payload:

goal: ""
constraints: []
allowed_sources: []
context_summary: ""
verified_claims: []
unsupported_claims: []
open_questions: []
tools_used: []
risks: []
next_agent_task: ""

Passing a handoff without constraints and allowed_sources is forbidden: it is the main path to context drift.

docs.title: Session Hygiene
docs.text:
Rules:

  • Refresh retrieved context before an important factual answer.
  • After a long session, write a summary with decisions, sources, and unresolved questions.
  • Do not store raw chain of thought, secrets, or temporary guesses.
  • Do not use session memory as a citation source.
  • When the topic changes, clear irrelevant context.

docs.title: Guardrails For Sessions
docs.text: Guardrail Trigger Action Missing source Claim without citation Send to verifier or request retrieval Context drift Answer relies on an old assumption Repack context Tool overreach Agent asks for broad permissions Request granular approval Handoff loss Payload without constraints Reject handoff Session bloat Too much irrelevant history Summarize and reset

docs.title: Tracing Questions
docs.text:
For every agent run, record:

  • Which sources did the agent see?
  • Which tools were actually called?
  • Which assumptions were chosen?
  • Which claims were verified?
  • Where did fallback/refusal occur?
  • Which eval proves quality?

docs.title: Subagents, skills and AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment

Subagents handle bounded work with fresh context. Skills encode repeated methods. AGENTS.md stores durable project rules. Product-Agent OS keeps these separate so agents do not use memory or generated views as source truth.

docs.title: Completion-skeptic Promotion Path
docs.text:
completion-skeptic follows the normal repeatable-method chain: manual -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation candidate. Owner review, rollback notes, failure log, eval cases and candidate-only status are required before promotion. A generated handoff or dashboard is not enough.

For documentation and scorecards, owner review is the explicit approval checkpoint.

Automation blockers remain explicit: no active hook, schedule, MCP server, Agents SDK runner, provider call or external write is created until manual evidence, scorecard review and a separate approval packet exist.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Current user request, project rules, source files and ownership map.
  • Candidate skill trigger, inputs, outputs, verification and failure modes.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Handoff packet for subagents or a skill candidate for a repeated method.
  • Durable rule updates only when evidence proves they should persist.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Each worker should return sources used, assumptions, files touched, verification evidence, open risks and recommended next role.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Subagents without fresh context can miss project constraints.
  • A skill with broad scope can over-trigger and perform unrelated work.

docs.title: Agent Templates
docs.text: Source status: experiment These templates are based on the official concepts of subagents, skills, memory, and workflows, but they should be validated on real project tasks.

docs.title: Research Agent
docs.text:
Role: Research agent
Goal: Find sources for the topic "{topic}".
Model policy: project default or faster mini model for read-heavy collection.
Reasoning: low/medium; escalate to high only for source conflicts.

Rules:
- Official OpenAI docs first.
- Community sources only as candidate insights.
- Do not write final instructions.
- Return source cards using the project schema.

Output:
- official_sources
- community_candidates
- conflicts
- stale_or_unclear_points

docs.title: Verification Agent
docs.text:
Role: Verification agent
Goal: Check claims from "{file_or_claim_list}".
Model policy: strong reasoning model for source-sensitive or multi-document checks.
Reasoning: medium/high.

Rules:
- Every factual claim needs an official source or explicit community/experiment status.
- Mark unsupported claims as "needs_source".
- Do not rewrite content unless asked.

Output:
- verified_claims
- unsupported_claims
- conflicts
- recommended_edits

docs.title: Synthesis Agent
docs.text:
Role: Synthesis agent
Goal: Turn verified claims into instructional material for an advanced agent builder.
Model policy: project default; use stronger model for architecture or product-agent guidance.
Reasoning: medium/high.

Rules:
- Write in Russian.
- Keep official English terms on first use.
- Separate official guidance from experiments.
- Include next navigation step.

Output:
- draft_section
- sources_used
- assumptions
- verification_notes

docs.title: Docs Update Orchestrator
docs.text:
Goal: Update the knowledge base for the topic "{topic}".
Model policy: project default.
Reasoning: medium; escalate to high for conflicting official sources or broad restructures.

Spawn subagents only if the user explicitly asks for parallel work.

Single-agent fallback:
1. Read source registry.
2. Fetch official docs.
3. Identify changes.
4. Update source cards.
5. Update affected docs.
6. Run docs checks and MkDocs build.
7. Report files changed and verification output.

Source status: official + experiment

# <Plugin Name>

## Purpose

<One product-agent workflow family this plugin makes repeatable.>

## Official archetypes

| Use case | URL | Why it applies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <Codex use case title> | <https://developers.openai.com/codex/use-cases/...> | <mapping> |

## Target users

- team: <Design / Engineering / Finance / Operations / Product / QA>
- category: <Engineering / Evaluation / Front-end / Quality / Automation / Data / Integrations / Knowledge Work / Native>
- task_type: <Analysis / Code / Design / Testing / Workflow>

## Supported surfaces

| Surface | Supported | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex App | yes/no | <when to use> |
| Codex CLI | yes/no | <when to use> |
| Cloud task | yes/no | <when to use> |
| GitHub | yes/no | <PR/review behavior> |
| Slack | yes/no | <handoff behavior> |
| Computer Use | yes/no | <GUI fallback> |
| MCP | yes/no | <servers/tools> |
| Automation | yes/no | <only after stable manual run> |

## Included skills

| Skill | Trigger | Job | Inputs | Outputs | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `<skill-name>` | <trigger words> | <one job> | <required inputs> | <artifact> | <command/check> |

## Model and reasoning policy

| Role or skill | Default model | Reasoning effort | Escalate when | Downgrade when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <planner/reviewer/builder> | <model> | <low/medium/high/xhigh> | <condition> | <condition> |

## Permissions and write policy

```yaml
write_policy: "read_only | draft_only | approved_write"
network_policy: "<allowed sources>"
secrets_policy: "never store secrets in prompts, docs, logs, fixtures, or examples"
approval_required_for:
  - external writes
  - destructive commands
  - permission changes
  - source-of-truth updates
forbidden_actions:
  - "<action>"
```

## Input contract

```yaml
required:
  - name: "<input>"
    type: "<file/url/thread/id/path>"
    validation: "<how the agent confirms it is usable>"
optional:
  - name: "<input>"
    type: "<type>"
    default_behavior: "<what happens when absent>"
```

## Output contract

```yaml
final_response_must_include:
  - files_changed_or_artifacts_staged
  - commands_or_checks_run
  - evidence
  - risks
  - next_action
```

## Workflow

1. Read `AGENTS.md` and plugin references.
2. Identify official archetype and task type.
3. Inventory inputs in read-only mode.
4. Name missing access or ambiguous scope.
5. Propose smallest useful plan.
6. Execute or stage the narrow workflow.
7. Run verification.
8. Return evidence and risks.
9. Log failures into the failure log.
10. Update the skill/plugin only from reviewed failures.

## Eval cases

| Case | Input fixture | Expected behavior | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Happy path | <fixture> | <expected artifact> | <check> |
| Missing source | <fixture> | names inaccessible source | <check> |
| Unsafe write | <fixture> | stages draft, asks approval | <check> |
| Scope too broad | <fixture> | narrows to one job | <check> |
| Verification fails | <fixture> | reports failure evidence | <check> |

## Failure log

| Date | Case | Failure | Fix added | Retest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <date> | <case> | <what failed> | <skill/plugin change> | <result> |

## Packaging notes

- Keep `SKILL.md` concise.
- Move long docs into `references/`.
- Put deterministic helper commands in `scripts/`.
- Put reusable templates, fixtures, screenshots, or prompt examples in `assets/`.
- Add MCP/app integration configuration only when the workflow needs it.
- Do not package private customer data, secrets, auth tokens, or one-off project context.

## Maintenance

```yaml
owner: "<person/team>"
source_refresh_cadence: "<monthly / release-based / before rollout>"
eval_refresh_cadence: "<after failures / before plugin release>"
official_sources:
  - "<url>"
community_sources:
  - "<url with trust level>"
```

docs.title: Codex Configuration and Extensibility
docs.text: Source status: official Sources: Agent approvals and security, Create a skill, Subagents, Agents SDK with Codex.

docs.title: Approval policy as a managed interface
docs.text:
For advanced work, approval policy is better described not as one global switch, but as a set of separate gates:

approval_policy = { granular = {
  sandbox_approval = true,
  rules = true,
  mcp_elicitations = true,
  request_permissions = false,
  skill_approval = false
} }

Practical meaning:

Gate What it controls Recommendation sandbox_approval A command crossing the sandbox boundary Enable for local projects rules Confirmation for rule-based actions Enable when the access policy is complex mcp_elicitations Confirmation requests from MCP tools Enable for external systems request_permissions Requests for expanded permissions Disable by default, enable deliberately skill_approval Permission for skill invocation Enable if skills have side effects

Baseline for analysis and review:

approval_policy = "untrusted"
sandbox_mode = "read-only"
allow_login_shell = false

Baseline for controlled implementation:

approval_policy = "on-request"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
allow_login_shell = false

docs.title: Skill metadata
docs.text:
The official skill structure can include agents/openai.yaml to describe UI, invocation policy and tool dependencies:

interface:
  display_name: "Source Card Writer"
  short_description: "Turns an official documentation page into a source card."
  icon_small: "./assets/source-card.svg"
  brand_color: "#0F766E"
  default_prompt: "Create a source card for this documentation URL."

policy:
  allow_implicit_invocation: false

dependencies:
  tools:
    - type: "mcp"
      value: "openaiDeveloperDocs"
      description: "OpenAI Docs MCP server"
      transport: "streamable_http"
      url: "https://developers.openai.com/mcp"

For this project, allow_implicit_invocation: false is preferred: source collection and claim transfer must happen explicitly so that official and community layers are not mixed.

docs.title: Codex MCP as the backend for an agentic system
docs.text:
Context7 showed an official example where the Agents SDK runs a multi-agent workflow and connects Codex CLI as an MCP server. Architecturally, this is an important bridge:

flowchart LR
    PM["Project Manager Agent"] --> D["Designer Agent"]
    PM --> F["Frontend Agent"]
    PM --> B["Backend Agent"]
    PM --> T["Tester Agent"]
    D --> MCP["Codex MCP server"]
    F --> MCP
    B --> MCP
    T --> MCP
    MCP --> WS["Workspace files"]

For our knowledge base, this means:

  • Codex can be used not only as a standalone assistant, but also as an execution tool inside broader Agents SDK orchestration.
  • Project Manager must define source of truth documents: REQUIREMENTS.md, AGENT_TASKS.md, TEST.md.
  • Each worker-agent must have narrow deliverables and a sandbox/approval policy.
  • Handoff back to Project Manager is mandatory so that the final assembly of decisions does not fall apart into independent results.

docs.title: Codex Overview
docs.text:
Codex is an OpenAI coding agent that can read, modify and run code. In official materials, Codex is described as an agent for accelerating development, fixing bugs, understanding unfamiliar code and delegating tasks in local or cloud environments.

Source status: official Primary sources: Codex cloud, Codex app, Codex CLI, Codex IDE extension.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Codex is better treated not as autocomplete, but as a workflow operator:

  • receives a task, context and readiness criterion;
  • explores code, documents or data;
  • makes changes or prepares an artifact;
  • runs checks;
  • returns a short result with evidence.

For advanced use, the key skill is not to "write a prompt", but to build a managed system: instructions, sources, skills, subagents, sandbox, approvals, memory and eval loops.

docs.title: What v1 of this knowledge base includes
docs.text: Area What we study Where to read Surfaces App, CLI, IDE extension, cloud Work surfaces Configuration Approval policies, skill metadata, Codex MCP Configuration Security Sandbox, approvals, network boundaries Security Workflows Prompting, verification, handoff Workflows Agent systems Subagents, skills, AGENTS.md, memory Architecture SDK layer Agents SDK, Responses API, guardrails, tracing Agents SDK patterns Insights User tricks, hypotheses, experiments Insights

docs.title: Quality standards
docs.text:
Every instruction in the core knowledge base must have one of three statuses:

  • a link to an official source;
  • a link to a community source and explicit trust_level;
  • a local hypothesis with a verification scenario.

Without this, a claim remains a note, not an instruction.

docs.title: Security, sandbox and approvals
docs.text: Source status: official Sources: Sandbox, Agent approvals and security, Codex cloud.

docs.title: Baseline model
docs.text:
Sandbox is a technical boundary: which files Codex can modify, which commands it can run and whether network access is available. Approval policy is a governance boundary: when Codex must stop and ask for permission.

A safe baseline for local work:

sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
approval_policy = "on-request"
approvals_reviewer = "user"

This mode allows work inside the workspace, but requires approval for actions outside the boundary, network commands or other sensitive operations.

docs.title: Sandbox modes
docs.text: Mode Meaning Use for read-only Codex can read, but should not change files or run substantial commands without permission Planning, review, audit workspace-write Codex can read, modify the workspace and run routine commands within the project boundary Most local tasks danger-full-access Codex runs without sandbox restrictions Only deliberately and for a short time

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Under the official model, Codex should not freely access the network by default during agentic work. In cloud setup, network access may be available during environment preparation, while the agent phase usually requires a separate internet access decision.

Practical rule:

  • documentation can be checked against official sources;
  • install and package manager commands require explicit understanding of what will be downloaded;
  • secrets must not end up in prompts, docs, memory or artifacts.

docs.title: Approval checklist
docs.text:
Before approval, ask:

  • Does the command write outside the workspace?
  • Does the command use the network?
  • Can the command delete, overwrite or send data?
  • Is there a narrower way to grant access?
  • Can broad access be replaced with a command prefix rule?

docs.title: Codex Work Surfaces
docs.text: Source status: official Sources: Codex app, Codex CLI, Codex IDE extension, Codex cloud.

docs.title: Choosing a surface
docs.text: Surface When to use Strength Risk Codex App Multiple threads, review, worktrees, automations, artifacts Command center for parallel work Requires discipline in branch management and approvals CLI Local terminal work, reproducible commands, transcript Explicit context, command control, convenience for power users Files and boundaries must be specified explicitly IDE extension Work next to the editor, open files, selections, @file Fast code context and local follow-up It is easy to rely on incomplete editor context Codex cloud Long background tasks, PR, GitHub-linked work Parallelism and isolation from the local machine Setup, network and secrets must be described in advance

docs.title: Codex App
docs.text:
Official documentation describes Codex App as a desktop command center for parallel Codex threads, built-in worktree support, automations and Git functionality. For an advanced user, this is the main surface for managing several independent tasks.

Operational guidance:

  • each thread must have a concrete outcome;
  • enable worktree isolation for write-heavy tasks;
  • use automations for repeated checks;
  • before accepting the result, inspect the diff, verification commands and artifacts.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Codex CLI runs locally from the terminal and can read, modify and run code in the selected directory. This is the best mode for reproducible workflows because commands, approvals and context are easier to keep explicit.

CLI task template:

Goal: ...
Context: @path/to/file.md @path/to/schema.json
Constraints: do not change the public API, do not install dependencies without approval.
Definition of done: ...
Verification: run ...

docs.title: IDE extension
docs.text: IDE extension is useful when editor context matters: open files, selections, @file references and follow-up on cloud work. For complex tasks, record the context in writing because open files do not replace requirements.

docs.title: Codex cloud
docs.text:
Cloud fits background tasks, especially when work can proceed independently from the current local session. For cloud tasks, record separately:

  • repository and branch;
  • setup steps;
  • internet access policy;
  • secrets availability only where needed;
  • expected PR or artifact.

docs.title: Deep analysis of Codex use cases
docs.text:
Source status: official + tool-assisted Sources: Codex use cases, Codex workflows, Agent skills, Codex plugins, Build plugins, AGENTS.md.

Analysis date: 2026-05-14.

docs.title: Why this layer is needed
docs.text:
The official Codex use cases section is useful not only as a list of examples. It can be read as a catalog of product workflows from which real agent teams, skills and plugins are assembled. Each use case card usually contains:

  • a concrete outcome;
  • difficulty and time horizon;
  • who the workflow fits;
  • recommended skills/plugins;
  • starter prompt;
  • constraints before changes;
  • expected output;
  • verification loop;
  • related use cases.

For our project, this means a use case should be turned not into a note, but into an operational template. If the template repeats at least several times, it becomes a skill. If the skill is needed by several projects or teams, or requires a bundle of skills, MCP, app integrations and settings, it becomes a plugin.

docs.title: Taxonomy of the official catalog
docs.text:
The filters on the use cases page define the baseline ontology for plugin design.

Layer Official values How to use in documentation Category Engineering, Evaluation, Front-end, Quality Defines the main result type: code, eval, UI, QA. Native iOS, Mobile, macOS Indicates platform runtimes and checks: simulator, XcodeBuildMCP, SwiftUI, Expo, macOS logs. Workflows Automation, Data, Integrations, Knowledge Work Shows that Codex works not only with code, but also with sources, tables, messages, documents and operations. Team Design, Engineering, Finance, Operations, Product, QA Helps design agent roles and tone/output for different users. Task type Analysis, Code, Design, Testing, Workflow Helps choose the mode: read-only analysis, code change, design implementation, test/eval loop, repeatable workflow.

Main conclusion: a plugin must declare not only "what it can do", but also which category, team, task type, runtime and verification loop it is intended for.

docs.title: Collections as product areas
docs.text: Collection Meaning What to add to our docs Production systems Controlled changes, production quality, repeatable work. More attention to review gates, evals, PR evidence, rollback, scoped diffs. Productivity and collaboration Data, source material, apps, services, action from insights. Templates for connector work: read-only first, staged drafts, no source-of-truth writes without approval. Web development Design inputs, responsive UI, frontend reviews. Visual QA loop: screenshots, Playwright, responsive viewports, existing design system. Native development iOS/macOS build, refactor, app actions, validation loop. CLI-first native loops, simulator evidence, Logger/OSLog, platform-specific plugins. Game development First playable loop to production quality. Long-running /goal, PLAN.md, visual assets, .logs, Playwright gameplay checks.

docs.title: Anatomy of a plugin-ready use case
docs.text:
Every official use case can be decomposed into the same fields. This is the minimal structure of a future plugin blueprint.

Field What to extract Where we store it Outcome What the user gets at the end. docs/playbooks/* and docs/artifact-templates/plugin-blueprint.md. User/team Who launches the workflow. docs/product-agent/roles.md. Inputs Repo, screenshots, Figma node, Slack thread, CSV, logs, issue, PR, docs. Prompt packet and skill inputs. Read-only phase What Codex must inventory first. Workflow steps and safety rules. Plan The smallest useful plan before edits. PLAN.md or playbook section. Skills/plugins Which capabilities are needed: Playwright, Figma, GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Spreadsheet, OpenAI Docs. Skill dependency list and plugin manifest notes. Runtime App, CLI, Cloud, GitHub, Slack, Computer Use, MCP, automation. docs/runtime/overview.md. Verification Build, tests, evals, screenshots, simulator logs, LLM-as-judge, manual review. TEST.md, EVALS.md, RUNLOG.md. Promotion path Manual thread -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation. docs/playbooks/use-case-to-plugin.md.

docs.title: General workflow from use cases
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Select official use case archetype"] --> B["Map category, team, task type"]
    B --> C["Write task packet with inputs, constraints, done state"]
    C --> D["Read-only inventory before edits"]
    D --> E["Smallest useful plan"]
    E --> F{"Needs implementation?"}
    F -->|No| G["Reviewable analysis artifact"]
    F -->|Yes| H["Scoped code, data, UI, or ops change"]
    H --> I["Run verification loop"]
    G --> J["Evidence summary"]
    I --> J
    J --> K{"Repeated workflow?"}
    K -->|No| L["Keep as playbook/runlog"]
    K -->|Yes| M["Create skill"]
    M --> N{"Shared across projects?"}
    N -->|No| O["Repo or user skill"]
    N -->|Yes| P["Package plugin"]
    P --> Q{"Stable and scheduled?"}
    Q -->|Yes| R["Automation"]
    Q -->|No| S["Manual plugin workflow"]

docs.title: Inspect before edit
docs.text:
In many starter prompts, Codex must first read the project, sources or current state. This repeats in evals, API migrations, data analysis, Figma-to-code, iOS simulator debugging, bug triage and deploy workflows.

Document as a rule: any plugin that writes files or changes an external system must have a read-only phase.

docs.title: Smallest useful slice
docs.text:
Use cases rarely suggest "redo everything". They constrain the work to one behavior, one UI adjustment, one feature slice, one eval target or one migration checkpoint.

Document as a rule: a skill must have one job. A large plugin can contain several skills, but each skill remains narrow.

docs.title: Evidence over assertion
docs.text:
Official use cases constantly require proof: eval command, Playwright check, simulator screenshot, log stream, build output, PR review comment, staged rows, deployment URL, source inventory.

Document as a rule: the agent's final answer must include changed files, checks run, evidence, unresolved risk and next action.

docs.title: App path over raw model path
docs.text: In AI app evals, an important idea is to test the path the user takes whenever possible, not only the raw prompt. This transfers to product agents: test the real endpoint, UI flow, CLI command, simulator path or connector read, not an isolated model guess.

docs.title: Staged drafts before external writes
docs.text:
Operational workflows such as onboarding, bug triage, inbox, Slack actions and verified operations separate draft/stage from actual write. The agent first prepares a reviewable artifact and explicitly forbids sending messages, creating tickets, changing sharing, inviting people or editing source-of-truth without approval.

Document as a rule: all plugins with external systems must have write_policy: read_only, draft_only, approved_write.

docs.title: Runtime follows the task
docs.text:
Use cases show surface selection:

  • GitHub review for PR review;
  • Slack integration for async kickoff;
  • CLI for local loops and /goal;
  • App/Computer Use for actions through GUI;
  • MCP/plugins for access to specialized tools;
  • automations only after manual workflow stabilization.

Document as a rule: a plugin blueprint must record supported surfaces and forbidden surfaces.

docs.title: Skills preserve working behavior
docs.text:
The Save workflows as skills page shows the right packaging moment: there is a working thread, review rules, test commands, release checklist, writing examples or repo scripts. A skill should not be born from an abstract idea without a successful example.

Document as a rule: a skill candidate requires a working example, source material, commands/scripts, good output and a failure log.

docs.title: /goal for long-running work
docs.text:
Follow a goal adds a separate contract: the objective must be durable, the stopping condition must be verifiable, progress must move through checkpoints, and status must stay compact. This fits migrations, large refactors, prototypes, games, prompt optimization and eval loops.

Document as a rule: a long-running plugin workflow must have an explicit stop condition, checkpoint cadence, max-risk boundary and pause conditions.

docs.title: Plugin-readiness rubric
docs.text:
A use case can be turned into a plugin if these conditions hold:

Criterion Requirement Repetition The workflow repeats across several projects or teams. Stable input contract Required inputs and allowed formats are clear. Stable output contract The final artifact and evidence format are clear. Capability bundle Several skills, app integrations, MCP servers or scripts are needed. Safety policy There is a read/write policy, approval gates and forbidden actions. Verification There are deterministic checks, visual checks, evals or a manual review checklist. Failure log Common errors and correction methods are known. Ownership It is clear who maintains the plugin and updates sources.

docs.title: What to add to our documentation
docs.text:
1. Use cases should become a separate navigation section inside Codex, not only a source registry link.
  2. Each product-agent playbook should state its official use case archetype.
  3. The skill template should require: trigger, inputs, outputs, source material, verification, failure log, write policy.
  4. The plugin template should require: target teams, categories, task types, runtime surfaces, permissions, skills, MCP/connectors, evals, packaging, update loop.
  5. AGENTS.md should explicitly say: repeated workflows are promoted along the chain manual thread -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation.
  6. For operations with external systems, staged draft policy must always be documented.
  7. For long-running work, /goal or an equivalent run loop with a verifiable stop condition is needed.
  8. UI/native/game workflows need visual/runtime verification, not only a code diff.

docs.title: Minimal extraction process
docs.text:
1. Select an official use case or group of use cases.
  2. Write down outcome, inputs, skills/plugins, starter prompt, verification and risks.
  3. Formulate one repeatable job.
  4. Create a playbook with a manual workflow.
  5. Run the workflow manually in one project and save the runlog.
  6. Create a skill from the successful runlog.
  7. Run the skill on two different fixture projects.
  8. If the skill requires external integrations or is needed by several teams, create a plugin blueprint.
  9. Add eval cases: should trigger, should not trigger, unsafe write, missing source, verification failure.
  10. Only after a stable plugin workflow should automation be considered.

docs.title: Codex Workflows
docs.text: Source status: official Sources: Codex workflows, Codex best practices, Prompting.

docs.title: Structure of a good task
docs.text:
Codex works better when it receives explicit context and a definition of done. Minimal task packet:

Goal:
Context:
Constraints:
Allowed changes:
Out of scope:
Verification:
Expected output:

docs.title: Use cases as a workflow catalog
docs.text:
The official Codex use cases section should be read as a practical map of repeatable tasks: each card defines outcome, audience, starter prompt, skills/plugins, constraints, verification and related workflows.

For project work, use Deep analysis of Codex use cases:

  • choose the closest official archetype;
  • transfer its inputs, constraints and verification into the task packet;
  • run the workflow manually;
  • only after a successful runlog, turn it into a skill;
  • if the workflow is needed by several projects or requires a bundle of skills, MCP and app integrations, package a plugin.

docs.title: Workflow: understand a codebase
docs.text:
Use for onboarding, analysis of a service, protocol or request flow.

Study the selected module and return:
- a short map of file responsibilities;
- request/data flow step by step;
- where data is validated;
- 2-3 risks when making changes;
- a list of files to read next.
Do not change files.

Verification:

  • request a numbered flow;
  • check the mentioned files;
  • verify that Codex did not invent nonexistent entrypoints.

docs.title: Workflow: fix a bug
docs.text:
For a bugfix, a reproducible symptom is needed first.

Bug:
Repro steps:
Expected:
Actual:
Suspected files:
Constraints:
Verification command:

If reproduction is not provided, the first Codex task is to find or propose a minimal reproducible scenario, not to change code immediately.

docs.title: Workflow: update documentation
docs.text:
Compare official sources with current docs.
Do not change claims without a source registry link.
Return:
- outdated claims;
- new facts;
- proposed edits;
- verification checklist.

This workflow has been turned into a separate playbook.

docs.title: Common Failure Modes

  • Graph depth output is treated as complete architecture understanding without source-file inspection.

docs.text:

docs.text:
Source status: project-local plan + accepted boundary

This diagram shows how a claim moves from intake to supported scope, blocker, accepted gap, owner decision or next safe action. It supports Track 11 G3 DOC-M09 and keeps one boundary clear: a doubt packet, generated view or review note is not proof by itself.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Use this map during review, docs sync and completion checks when deciding whether a claim can appear in documentation or a closing handoff.

  1. Classify the claim as source truth, current command evidence, generated-view-only, owner approval, accepted gap or unsupported claims.
  2. Require evidence_before_completion before completion or readiness wording.
  3. If you only have orientation evidence, read the source or run an approved check first.
  4. If the claim needs UI or runtime evidence, record browser proof approval_required instead of readiness.
  5. If freshness depends only on generated site, record this status: generated site freshness deferred.
  6. If the claim remains unsupported, name the next safe action or route it to DOC-M25.

docs.text:
• Writing "verified" or "ready" based on a doubt packet without source or current evidence.

  • Calling an accepted gap accepted without owner, reason, scope and follow-up.
  • Mixing unsupported claims with supported claims in one paragraph without a boundary.

This section turns the knowledge base into an implementation map for building projects with Codex, agents, skills, runtime choices and eval loops.
