docs.text:
1. Start with Product-Agent Delivery Lifecycle to see the full path from idea to release.
  2. Use planning matrix architecture when work needs a task matrix, staged delivery or completion report.
  3. Use Agent Team And Skills to split roles, ownership and reusable methods.
  4. Use Runtime Decision Map to choose Codex App, CLI, Cloud, codex exec, MCP, GitHub Action or automation.
  5. Check Source And Generated Evidence Boundary when work depends on generated graph, cockpit HTML, reports or site/.
  6. Use First-Run Cockpit Architecture, Evidence And Risk Lifecycle and Architecture Intelligence Diagram Atlas when first-run outputs become documentation or handoff material.
  7. Check Skill Exposure And Invocation Boundary when a claim touches source bundle, installed cache or active session behavior.
  8. Check Skill Lifecycle before turning a playbook into a skill.
  9. Finish with Context, Memory, Verification to reduce unsupported claims and keep useful knowledge.

    B1 --> C["Agent team and skills"]
    C --> D["Runtime decision"]
    D --> E["Source/generated boundary"]
    E --> F["Architecture Intelligence maps"]
    F --> G["Implementation loop"]
    G --> H["Skill exposure boundary"]
    H --> I["Skill lifecycle"]
    G --> J["Context and verification"]
    I --> K["Reusable project methods"]
    J --> L["Product-ready output"]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Product goal, source context and project constraints.
  • Existing control-plane files, routes, skills and runtime options.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A practical route through the Product-Agent OS operating model.
  • Links to the next artifact for delivery, planning matrix architecture, team design, runtime selection, source/generated trust, Architecture Intelligence maps, skill exposure, skill promotion and verification.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Each atlas page should have a practical diagram, usage guidance, related artifacts and failure modes. Run python tools\check_docs.py and strict MkDocs after navigation or Mermaid changes.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Decorative diagrams can hide missing implementation decisions.
  • Skipping the atlas can lead to runtime or agent choices that are not aligned with approvals and evidence.
  • Treating generated views, browser proof gaps or installed skill cache as source truth can create unsupported completion claims.

docs.title: Product-Agent Delivery Lifecycle
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment

This diagram shows the end-to-end product delivery loop for Codex work, from idea to release notes and updated agent operating documentation.

flowchart TD
    A["Idea / user request"] --> B["REQUIREMENTS.md"]
    B --> C["Source review"]
    C --> D["PLAN.md"]
    D --> E["Agent team design"]
    E --> F["Candidate skills"]
    F --> G["Runtime choice"]
    G --> H["Focused implementation"]
    H --> I["TEST.md"]
    H --> J["EVALS.md"]
    I --> K{"Pass?"}
    J --> K
    K -->|No| L["Focused fix loop"]
    K -->|Yes| M["Review"]
    M --> N["Release packet"]
    N --> O["RUNLOG.md learning"]
    O --> P["Rules, skills or automation candidate"]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Product goal, users, constraints and success metric.
  • Source review, project rules and available runtime surface.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A reviewable sequence of requirements, plan, implementation, evidence, review and learning artifacts.
  • Candidate skills or automation only after repeated manual success.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Confirm that requirements, plan, tests, evals and run log are current before claiming a slice is ready.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Starting implementation before requirements and plan can create broad unowned changes.
  • Automating a workflow before evidence and failure handling can repeat mistakes.

docs.title: Runtime decision map
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment

Use this map to choose where Codex work should run: Codex App, CLI, codex exec, GitHub Action, MCP, Agents SDK or automation.

flowchart TD
    A["Work item"] --> B{"Ambiguous or needs steering?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Codex App / IDE extension"]
    B -->|No| D{"Stable command?"}
    D -->|Yes| E["CLI or codex exec"]
    D -->|No| F{"CI or PR event?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["GitHub Action with approval"]
    F -->|No| H{"Programmable orchestration?"}
    H -->|Yes| I["MCP or Agents SDK"]
    H -->|No| J["Manual playbook"]
    J --> K{"Repeated and stable?"}
    K -->|Yes| L["Automation candidate"]
    K -->|No| M["Keep manual"]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Uncertainty level, risk, required tools, approval boundary and expected evidence.
  • Existing project rules for sandbox, network, external writes and git actions.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A runtime choice with explicit evidence and rollback expectations.
  • A safe next action for manual work, skill promotion or automation candidate.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Runtime choice should be recorded with source context, allowed commands, forbidden actions and stop conditions.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Using automation or MCP to compensate for an unclear prompt contract can hide missing requirements.
  • A live or external runtime needs separate explicit approval and current evidence.

docs.title: Skill Exposure And Invocation Boundary
docs.text:
Source status: official + project evidence

This diagram shows how a Product-Agent OS skill moves from the source bundle to the installed cache and then to an active Codex session. A file in the source tree does not prove that the skill is available in the current session, and a cached skill does not prove implicit invocation policy.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Source bundle<br/>plugins/product-agent-os"] --> B["Packaged plugin artifact"]
    B --> C["Installed cache<br/>personal-product-agent-plugins"]
    C --> D["Fresh Codex session"]
    D --> E{"Skill visible in active instructions?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Invocation candidate"]
    E -->|No| G["Session exposure gap"]
    F --> H{"Implicit policy evidence?"}
    H -->|Current route/eval proof| I["Supported invocation claim"]
    H -->|No current proof| J["planned-only / unsupported claim"]
    G --> K["Next safe action:<br/>read-only session/cache check"]
    J --> K
    I --> L["Owner-reviewed docs or control-plane update"]

docs.title: How To Use
docs.text:
Use this page before claiming that a Product-Agent OS skill auto-engages:

  1. Check the source bundle: which skills, templates and scripts exist in the repository.
  2. Inspect the installed cache only through read-only checks, and do not run a cache refresh without separate approval.
  3. Check the fresh Codex session: whether the current session sees the skill and its trigger.
  4. Keep present_unverified separate from current route/eval proof.
  5. Mark auto-engagement as planned-only until fresh evidence exists for active session behavior.

docs.title: Related Artifacts
docs.text: Artifact Role Evidence Limit plugins/product-agent-os/ Source bundle for the plugin and skills. Source correctness, not installed exposure. Installed plugin cache Local copy that Codex may see. Cache presence, not active session invocation. Active session instructions What is actually loaded into the current context. Session exposure, not fixed auto-engagement without route/eval proof. RUNLOG.md Current-cycle decisions and evidence summaries. Handoff evidence, not runtime proof by itself. DOC-M25 Final generated site freshness route. Not part of skill invocation; only proves site/search/sitemap freshness after it runs.

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
• Treating a source file as installed skill exposure.
  • Treating installed cache as proof that the current session will invoke the skill automatically.
  • Treating a session summary as source truth.
  • Running a cache refresh without approval and rollback evidence.
  • Letting generated docs or a diagram page promise fixed auto-engagement without current route/eval proof.
  • Mixing browser proof approval_required or generated site freshness deferred with skill invocation proof.

docs.title: Safe Next Action
docs.text: If a claim touches auto-engagement, create a read-only packet first: source path, cache path, active session exposure, trigger wording, current invocation evidence, unsupported claims and owner decision. Until that packet exists, this page records only the architecture boundary, not fixed behavior.

docs.title: Skill lifecycle
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment

This diagram shows how a repeated workflow becomes a reusable skill and later an automation candidate only after evidence exists.

flowchart LR
    A["Manual workflow"] --> B["Playbook"]
    B --> C["Skill candidate"]
    C --> D["Trigger, inputs, outputs"]
    D --> E["Eval cases"]
    E --> F["Failure log"]
    F --> G{"Reliable?"}
    G -->|No| H["Refine manually"]
    G -->|Yes| I["Reusable skill"]
    I --> J{"Stable cadence?"}
    J -->|No| K["Assisted runs"]
    J -->|Yes| L["Automation candidate"]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• A successful manual workflow, playbook, source policy and failure examples.
  • Candidate trigger words, inputs, outputs and verification command.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A skill with one job, explicit boundaries, eval cases and failure modes.
  • A promotion decision for keeping the method manual, packaging it or proposing automation.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Run positive and negative eval cases before treating the skill as reusable. Automation still requires separate approval.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• A broad skill can hide unrelated behavior under one trigger.
  • Automation without stable inputs, outputs and rollback can create repeated unsafe actions.

docs.title: Source and Generated Evidence Boundary
docs.text:
Source status: project-local plan + accepted boundary

This diagram separates source truth, orientation evidence, generated-view-only outputs, current commands, owner approval and an accepted gap. It is a decision aid for Track 11 G3 DOC-M07, not proof of readiness by itself.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Source files"] --> B["source truth"]
    C["Requirements / PLAN / TEST / EVALS"] --> B
    D["Source registry"] --> B
    E["Current command evidence"] --> F["current command evidence"]
    G["Generated graph"] --> H["orientation evidence"]
    I["Cockpit HTML / generated reports"] --> J["generated-view-only"]
    K["Owner decision"] --> L["owner approval"]
    M["Recorded exception"] --> N["accepted gap"]

    B --> O{"Claim or next action?"}
    F --> O
    L --> O
    N --> O
    H --> P["Read source before claim"]
    J --> P
    P --> O

    O -->|Supported| Q["Document supported scope"]
    O -->|Missing command evidence| R["Run or record evidence_before_completion gap"]
    O -->|Needs runtime/browser| S["browser proof approval_required"]
    O -->|Generated site only| T["generated `site` freshness deferred"]
    O -->|Unsupported| U["unsupported claims stay out"]

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Use this map before moving statements from a generated graph, cockpit HTML, report or site/ build into user-facing documentation.

  1. Identify source truth: source file, source registry entry, planning marker or owner-reviewed artifact.
  2. Mark orientation evidence separately: generated graphs, cockpit HTML, summaries and dashboards help navigation but do not prove behavior.
  3. For done, ready, fixed or works claims, require current command evidence, owner approval or a recorded accepted gap.
  4. If the claim needs runtime or browser evidence, stop at browser proof approval_required.
  5. If the only freshness signal is generated site, keep this status: generated site freshness deferred.
  6. If evidence is missing, keep the statement under unsupported claims or leave it out.

docs.title: Related Artifacts
docs.text: Artifact Role docs/sources/registry.md Index for source-backed claims; not changed in this slice. .codex/workflows/control-plane-sync.md Decides whether root control-plane files need updates before closure. .codex/workflows/task-plan-lifecycle.md User-visible Task Brief and Completion Brief contract. DOC-M25 Follow-up source-doc item for additional evidence boundary routing. Generated graph / cockpit HTML orientation evidence or generated-view-only, not source truth.

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
• Treating generated graph, cockpit HTML or generated site output as proof without reading source files.
  • Hiding the approval boundary when runtime or browser proof is required.
  • Making readiness claims without evidence_before_completion.
  • Mixing owner approval and accepted gap: approval permits an action, while a gap records residual risk.
  • Moving unsupported claims from a report into core docs without a source boundary.

docs.title: Insights Layer
docs.text:
Source status: community | experiment

Insights are the unofficial layer: user tricks, observations, GitHub issues, Reddit patterns, blog posts, and local experiments. They are useful for improving work, but they are not a source of truth.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• An insight is not moved into the main guide without verification.
  • Every insight has verification_status.
  • If an insight conflicts with official documentation, it stays in insights with a conflict note.
  • If an insight is confirmed locally, add a reproduction or transcript summary.
  • If an insight becomes stale after a changelog update, mark it as stale.

docs.title: Verification Statuses
docs.text: Status Meaning unverified Found in community/source, not verified reproduced Verified locally once adopted Became part of the project workflow rejected Verification did not confirm it stale Was useful, but may have become outdated

docs.title: Adding An Insight
docs.text:
1. Copy the card template.
  2. Specify the source and date.
  3. Describe the risk.
  4. Define the verification.
  5. Move the conclusion into a playbook only after verification.

docs.title: Insight Card Template
docs.text:
Source status: community | experiment

claim: ""
source: ""
evidence: ""
works_for: ""
risks: ""
verification_status: "unverified | reproduced | adopted | rejected | stale"
checked_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
trust_level: "high | medium | low"

Minimal example:

claim: "Subagents should be launched only for independent read-heavy work."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/concepts/subagents"
evidence: "Official docs describe subagents as useful for parallel exploration, tests, log analysis, and warn about write-heavy coordination risk."
works_for: "Large review, source research, test triage."
risks: "Overuse increases token spend and can fragment context."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

docs.title: Initial Insights Backlog
docs.text:
Source status: official + community + experiment

These cards define the format of the insights layer. Some of them are based on official sources and can already be considered adopted; community-only claims should be added separately after verification.

claim: "For a multi-agent workflow, split read-heavy tasks first; write-heavy tasks require non-overlapping files and explicit ownership."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/concepts/subagents"
evidence: "Official guidance recommends subagents for exploration, tests, triage, summarization, and warns that parallel write-heavy work increases coordination overhead."
works_for: "Research, review, log analysis, documentation audit."
risks: "If several agents edit the same files, the risk of conflicts and lost decisions increases."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Rules that must always be followed should live in AGENTS.md or checked-in docs, not only in memory."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/memories"
evidence: "Official docs say to keep required team guidance in AGENTS.md or checked-in documentation and treat memories as helpful local recall."
works_for: "Team standards, test commands, documentation policy, source policy."
risks: "Memory can be local, disabled, unavailable, stale, or inappropriate for shared team rules."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "If a workflow repeats three or more times, a Skill candidate should have explicit inputs, outputs, and deterministic scripts only where needed."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills"
evidence: "Official skills guidance emphasizes focused jobs, imperative steps, explicit inputs/outputs, and scripts for deterministic behavior or external tooling."
works_for: "Source card creation, insight intake, docs refresh, claim verification."
risks: "An overly broad skill becomes hidden project policy and worsens predictability."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Community tips should be harvested as candidate claims, not copied into official guides."
source: "https://community.openai.com/"
evidence: "Community sources vary in version, platform, local config, and user assumptions."
works_for: "Insight backlog and experiment design."
risks: "Unverified tricks can conflict with current Codex behavior or security policy."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "medium"

claim: "For source-sensitive documentation workflows, Manager pattern is safer than Handoff pattern because one orchestrator retains source policy and acceptance criteria."
source: "https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python"
evidence: "Agents SDK documentation describes Manager pattern and Handoffs as distinct multi-agent design patterns."
works_for: "Research synthesis, documentation updates, claim verification."
risks: "Manager can become bottleneck if every task is serialized."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Structured outputs should be used for handoff payloads and verifier outputs when downstream automation depends on exact fields."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs"
evidence: "OpenAI API documentation describes JSON Schema-based structured outputs for constrained model responses."
works_for: "Source cards, insight cards, handoff contracts, eval outputs."
risks: "Overly rigid schemas can reject useful exploratory notes."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Granular approvals should be documented as part of agent architecture, not treated as a local runtime detail."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/agent-approvals-security"
evidence: "Codex documentation supports granular approval configuration for sandbox approvals, rules, MCP elicitations, permissions, and skill approval."
works_for: "Local implementation, Codex MCP workflows, skill design."
risks: "Too many approval prompts can slow iteration; too few increase blast radius."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Structured Outputs solve output-shape reliability, not factual reliability; factual tasks still need grounding, citations, and verification."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs"
evidence: "OpenAI documentation notes that structured outputs can still contain mistakes and require prompt adjustments, examples, or task decomposition."
works_for: "Handoff contracts, source-card generation, verifier outputs, eval result schemas."
risks: "Schema forcing can make a model fill required fields even when the input is unrelated unless fallback behavior is specified."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "For hallucination-sensitive workflows, design the eval before optimizing the prompt."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization"
evidence: "OpenAI model optimization guidance recommends establishing eval baselines and iterating prompts against representative test inputs."
works_for: "Prompt versioning, grounded answering, documentation QA, agent reliability."
risks: "A narrow eval can overfit prompts and miss real-world failure modes."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

claim: "Session memory should never be used as a citation source; retrieve authoritative context again for factual answers."
source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/memories"
evidence: "Codex memory guidance distinguishes helpful recall from required project guidance, and official docs remain source of truth."
works_for: "Long-running agent sessions, research loops, support assistants, documentation updates."
risks: "Over-retrieval can increase latency and cost; use targeted retrieval."
verification_status: "adopted"
checked_at: "2026-05-14"
trust_level: "high"

docs.title: API & Integrations
docs.text:
Source status: official + verified methodology + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Product-Agent OS behavior: detect API and integration work early, require a contract source of truth, route risky changes through consumer, security, compatibility and release gates, and produce reviewable artifacts before code changes reach public or semi-public contracts.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers HTTP APIs, message/event APIs, webhooks, GraphQL, gRPC, generated SDKs, external integrations, API security, error contracts, versioning, compatibility, documentation artifacts and Product-Agent OS candidates.

It does not choose a universal API style for every project. The project should select an API style based on consumers, latency, ownership, ecosystem, tooling and operational risk.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• OpenAPI Specification v3.2.0 is the current OpenAPI contract source checked for this research run. It describes HTTP APIs in a programming-language-agnostic format and includes operations, parameters, request bodies, responses, examples, security schemes and reusable components.
  • AsyncAPI Specification v3.1.0 is the current AsyncAPI contract source checked for this research run. It describes message-driven APIs in a machine-readable, protocol-agnostic format.
  • RFC 9110 defines HTTP semantics. HTTP API design should not invent local meanings for methods, status codes and content negotiation when standard semantics already exist.
  • RFC 9457 defines Problem Details for HTTP APIs and obsoletes RFC 7807. It should be considered the default candidate for machine-readable HTTP error payloads unless the project already has a stronger compatibility reason.
  • RFC 9700 is the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice as of January 2025. OAuth-based APIs should treat it as a security baseline source, not as optional prose.
  • OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 is the current OWASP API-specific risk catalog checked in this research run. It is useful for API threat modeling and security review gates.
  • JSON Schema current version is 2020-12 according to the official JSON Schema specification page. Projects using JSON payload schemas should state the dialect.
  • CloudEvents v1.0.2 and the CNCF CloudEvents project provide a standardized event metadata envelope option. It is useful when event interoperability across systems matters.
  • GraphQL has a latest release dated September 2025 and a working draft dated April 2026. A project should pin the GraphQL specification target it follows instead of saying only "GraphQL".
  • gRPC uses Protocol Buffers as the default Interface Definition Language and message interchange format; .proto files become the source contract for service methods and messages.
  • Pact documents consumer-driven contract testing as a contract-by-example approach. It complements schema contracts because it captures actual consumer expectations, not every theoretically possible schema state.
  • OpenAPI Generator can generate clients, server stubs and documentation from OpenAPI documents. Generated SDKs need a manifest, ownership, versioning and regeneration policy.
  • Stoplight Spectral is documented as a JSON/YAML linter with ready-to-use style guides for OpenAPI and AsyncAPI. It is a candidate for API lint gates when the project chooses that toolchain.
  • Google API Improvement Proposals are a vendor-specific but mature model for recording API design rules. The useful transferable idea is the local API style guide as a governed artifact.

docs.title: Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology When to apply Project-level behavior Contract-first development New public API, SDK, provider/consumer split Contract is written or changed before implementation; code and tests conform to it. Contract-aware development Existing code-first service Generated or maintained contract is updated in the same slice as behavior changes. Consumer-driven contract testing Multiple consumers, microservices, frontend/backend split Consumers express expectations through contract tests; providers verify before release. API lifecycle governance APIs move from draft to stable to deprecated Every endpoint/message has lifecycle state, owner, compatibility policy and deprecation path. Backward compatibility by default Public, partner, mobile, SDK or event contracts Changes are classified as breaking/non-breaking before implementation. Error-contract governance HTTP APIs expose machine consumers Error responses use a documented model, preferably Problem Details when compatible. Event-contract governance Async messaging, queues, streams, webhooks Event schema, idempotency, retry, ordering, correlation and dead-letter behavior are documented. Integration security by design Authenticated API, external provider, sensitive data Auth scheme, scopes, token claims, rate limits, object-level authorization and abuse cases are reviewed. Generated-client governance SDKs or typed clients are generated Generator, config, target languages, compatibility and release process are documented. API style-guide governance Large project or many teams Local API rules are versioned and lintable where possible. Two-stage review Public contract, migration, SDK, auth, event payload Stage 1 checks contract/security/compatibility; stage 2 checks implementation quality.

docs.title: Documentation artifacts and standards
docs.text: Artifact Purpose Candidate source/tool API inventory List APIs, owners, lifecycle states, consumers and source-of-truth files. Markdown/YAML table in repo. OpenAPI document HTTP API source of truth. OpenAPI v3.2.0 or project-pinned compatible version. AsyncAPI document Message/event API source of truth. AsyncAPI v3.1.0 or project-pinned compatible version. GraphQL schema GraphQL contract source. .graphql schema plus pinned GraphQL spec target. gRPC/protobuf IDL RPC contract source. .proto files and generator config. JSON Schema library Shared JSON payload contracts. JSON Schema 2020-12 unless project pins older dialect. Problem Details catalog Stable HTTP error types, status codes and extensions. RFC 9457. Auth and authorization matrix Schemes, scopes, roles, token claims, object-level rules. OpenAPI security schemes, OAuth BCP, OWASP API risks. Consumer map Human/system consumers, SDKs, generated clients, owners and approval path. api-consumer-map.md. Compatibility decision record Breaking/non-breaking classification and migration impact. ADR-style record or api-compatibility-record.md. Contract test matrix Provider verification, consumer tests, schema tests and negative cases. Pact, schema validators, stack-specific API tests. Generated SDK manifest Generator, version, config, target languages, owner and release process. OpenAPI Generator or stack-specific generator. Webhook/event delivery contract Retry, idempotency, ordering, signature verification, replay and dead-letter behavior. AsyncAPI, CloudEvents where applicable. External integration policy Read/write capability, sandbox credentials, approval and rollback path. Project control-plane artifact. API style guide Naming, pagination, filtering, versioning, status codes, errors and examples. Local rules inspired by selected API guidelines. Deprecation plan Timeline, compatibility mode, comms, release notes and removal criteria. Changelog/release packet.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the integration: internal HTTP API, public API, partner API, webhook, async event stream, GraphQL, gRPC, generated SDK, external provider or automation integration.
  2. Declare the contract source of truth. If there is no OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL schema or .proto, record the gap before implementation.
  3. Name provider, consumers, owners, generated clients and runtime environments.
  4. Classify the change as additive, behavior-compatible, potentially breaking or breaking.
  5. Update the contract before or alongside code. Do not let rendered docs or Swagger UI become the source of truth.
  6. Add examples for success, validation failure, auth failure and the most important domain failure.
  7. Document auth scheme, scopes, object-level authorization rules, rate limits and sensitive fields.
  8. Document the error model. For HTTP APIs, prefer RFC 9457 Problem Details when compatible with existing clients.
  9. For event/message changes, document schema, headers, correlation ID, idempotency key, retry policy, ordering guarantees and dead-letter behavior.
  10. For generated SDKs, update the generation manifest and record whether clients need a major, minor or patch release.
  11. Add or update contract tests: schema validation, provider verification and consumer-driven tests where consumer risk is high.
  12. For external writes, create a staged draft or approval artifact before the agent touches the external system.
  13. Add observability expectations: request IDs, correlation IDs, error counters, latency, rate-limit metrics and integration failure alerts.
  14. Record rollout, deprecation and rollback path in the release artifact.

docs.title: Discovery signals
docs.text:
• openapi.yaml, openapi.yml, openapi.json, swagger.yaml, swagger.json
  • asyncapi.yaml, asyncapi.yml, asyncapi.json
  • schema.graphql, *.graphql, *.proto
  • pact/, pacts/, contract-tests/, consumer-contracts/
  • api/, integrations/, webhooks/, sdk/, clients/
  • terms in requirements: API, endpoint, webhook, SDK, OAuth, scope, token, GraphQL, gRPC, protobuf, Kafka, queue, event, contract, deprecation, migration

docs.title: Readiness gates
docs.text: Gate Trigger Block condition api_contract_source_present Any API or integration change No named contract source or explicit gap record. api_consumer_map_present Public, partner, SDK, mobile or multi-team API Consumers, owners or generated clients are unknown. api_breaking_change_reviewed Breaking or potentially breaking contract change No migration plan, deprecation window or owner approval. api_security_reviewed Auth, scopes, token claims, sensitive data or external provider No auth matrix, threat notes or security reviewer route. api_error_contract_present HTTP API behavior or validation change Error response shape and examples are missing. event_delivery_contract_present Event, webhook, queue or stream change Retry, idempotency, ordering, correlation or dead-letter behavior is missing. generated_client_manifest_present SDK or generated client affected Generator/config/release impact is not documented. external_write_approval_present External system write or mutation No staged draft, approval record or rollback path.

docs.title: Candidate templates
docs.text:
• api-contract-review.md
  • api-consumer-map.md
  • api-compatibility-record.md
  • api-error-catalog.md
  • api-auth-authorization-matrix.md
  • api-style-guide.md
  • api-contract-test-matrix.md
  • generated-sdk-manifest.md
  • webhook-event-contract.md
  • external-integration-approval.md

docs.title: Candidate eval fields
docs.text:
• Contract source is named and linked.
  • Consumers and generated clients are named.
  • Breaking/non-breaking classification is present.
  • Migration/deprecation plan exists for breaking changes.
  • Auth scheme and authorization rules are documented.
  • Success and error examples are present.
  • Event delivery semantics are documented for async integrations.
  • Contract verification command or missing-tool gap is recorded.
  • External writes are staged and approval-bound.

docs.title: Tooling candidates
docs.text: Tooling area Candidate Notes HTTP API contract OpenAPI Default source for REST-like HTTP APIs. Pin spec version per project. Event API contract AsyncAPI Default source for message-driven APIs and webhooks when useful. Shared JSON schemas JSON Schema Declare dialect; avoid validator-default ambiguity. Error model RFC 9457 Problem Details Good default for machine-readable HTTP errors. API lint Spectral Useful when the project has an API style guide. Tool adoption requires stack check. Code/doc generation OpenAPI Generator Useful for SDKs/stubs/docs; generated output requires ownership and diff review. Consumer contracts Pact Useful when real consumer expectations matter more than schema completeness. Event metadata CloudEvents Useful for cross-system event interoperability; not mandatory for simple internal events. RPC gRPC/protobuf Useful for low-latency, typed, polyglot service-to-service APIs. Query API GraphQL Useful for client-shaped reads and schema-driven product APIs; requires governance for complexity, authorization and deprecation.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Treating rendered API docs as the source of truth instead of the machine-readable contract.
  • Shipping event payload changes without consumer compatibility review.
  • Assuming an internal API has no consumers.
  • Generating SDKs without a reproducible generator config.
  • Adding OAuth scopes or token claims without an authorization matrix.
  • Returning undocumented error payloads that clients cannot handle.
  • Treating GraphQL or gRPC as automatically superior to HTTP APIs without consumer and operational justification.
  • Letting contract tests duplicate only provider behavior instead of expressing consumer expectations.
  • Allowing an agent to write to external systems without staged artifact and approval.

docs.text:

  • Which schema compatibility rules should be encoded for JSON Schema, protobuf, GraphQL and AsyncAPI separately?
  • Should API security gates be based on OWASP API Top 10, ASVS, SSDF, or a combined project profile?
  • How should agentic API migrations handle generated clients across multiple repositories?
  • Which API test generators are mature enough for default recommendation by stack?

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
Source status: official + expert reference + vendor documentation + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Product-Agent OS behavior: detect backend work, force service boundary and runtime behavior clarity, route risky service changes through reliability/security/data/operations gates, and require evidence for tests, observability, rollback and production readiness before completion.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers backend services, modular monolith modules, workers, schedulers, queues, service boundaries, domain logic, background jobs, runtime configuration, resiliency, observability, SLOs, security, health checks, distributed consistency and operational documentation.

It does not mandate microservices, Kubernetes, a cloud provider or a specific framework. Those are conditional implementation choices, not default architecture rules.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App defines a methodology for service-style applications, including explicit dependencies, environment-based config, backing services as attached resources, build-release-run separation, stateless processes, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs as event streams and one-off admin processes.
  • OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral observability framework for traces, metrics and logs, with concepts for context propagation, baggage, semantic conventions, collectors and language instrumentation.
  • Google SRE guidance frames SLO work around user-relevant SLIs and recommends choosing a small number of indicators that represent what users care about.
  • NIST SSDF recommends secure software development practices that can be integrated into SDLC implementations.
  • OWASP ASVS provides a versioned basis for testing web application technical security controls and secure development requirements.
  • CNCF Cloud Native Definition characterizes cloud-native systems as loosely coupled, secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable and observable, supported by automation.
  • Kubernetes readiness, liveness and startup probes are distinct runtime health mechanisms. Readiness prevents traffic from reaching a service that is alive but not ready.
  • Hexagonal Architecture, also known as Ports and Adapters, separates application logic from UI, database and runtime adapters so the application can be tested and driven through multiple ports.
  • Martin Fowler's microservices guide defines microservices as independently deployable services built around business capabilities and highlights design-for-failure as a characteristic.
  • Microsoft Azure Architecture Center documents retry, circuit breaker, queue-based load leveling, health endpoint monitoring and saga patterns. These are vendor-specific docs, but the patterns are broadly useful as backend resilience and distributed workflow references.

docs.title: Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology When to apply Project-level behavior Modular monolith first Early or medium-size product, unclear service boundaries Keep deployable complexity low while enforcing module ownership and domain boundaries. Conditional microservices Independent scaling, team ownership or deployment autonomy is proven Services map to business capabilities, have independent deployability and explicit failure contracts. Hexagonal Architecture / Ports and Adapters Domain logic is important and adapters change Core use cases depend on ports/interfaces; database, HTTP, queue and vendor SDKs are adapters. Domain-Driven Design boundaries Complex business domain or ambiguous vocabulary Backend modules/services map to bounded contexts and ubiquitous language. TDD for domain logic Deterministic business rules and service logic Unit tests drive behavior before implementation. Integration-first backend testing Storage, queues, transactions, external adapters Tests exercise real or representative boundaries before release. Contract-aware service development Service exposes APIs/events or consumes external contracts OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Pact, .proto or provider contract changes are updated with code. Twelve-Factor service discipline SaaS/cloud-style backend Config, dependencies, runtime process model, logs and admin tasks are documented. SRE-inspired reliability Production service with users or downstream consumers SLO or explicit gap, user-relevant SLIs, runbooks and alert signals. Observability-driven development Debugging requires runtime evidence Traces, metrics, logs, correlation IDs and dashboard/alert expectations are captured. Resilience pattern design Remote dependencies, queues, load spikes or transient faults Timeouts, retry, backoff, circuit breaker, load leveling, backpressure and fallback are designed together. Secure SDLC Backend touches auth, sensitive data, money, secrets or privileged operations Security requirements, threat notes, abuse cases, audit logging and no-secrets evidence are required. Saga / compensating workflow Distributed business transaction cannot use a single ACID transaction Workflow state, idempotency, compensation, monitoring and failure recovery are documented. Runbook-driven operations Production service or scheduled job Operators get failure modes, dashboards, logs, restart/replay steps and escalation path.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the backend unit: module, monolith subsystem, service, worker, scheduler, consumer, API backend, integration adapter or migration runner.
  2. Name the service boundary: purpose, owner, inbound contracts, outbound dependencies, data ownership and deployment/runtime shape.
  3. If the domain is complex, map the boundary to bounded contexts and domain language.
  4. Decide whether Ports and Adapters is useful. Apply it when domain logic must stay independent from HTTP, database, queue or vendor SDK concerns.
  5. Document runtime behavior before implementing distributed behavior: retries, timeouts, idempotency, deduplication, backpressure, ordering, scheduling and replay.
  6. For every remote dependency, write a failure policy: timeout, retry, circuit breaker, fallback, alert and owner.
  7. For background jobs and queues, document payload contract, retry policy, dead-letter behavior, idempotency key and replay procedure.
  8. For distributed transactions, prefer a simple local transaction when possible. If not possible, document saga/compensation and monitoring explicitly.
  9. Define observability evidence: traces for request flow, metrics for service health, logs for decisions/errors and correlation IDs across boundaries.
  10. For production services, define SLO or record why it is not yet applicable.
  11. Treat health endpoints as contracts. Liveness, readiness and startup checks should not be vague aliases.
  12. Document config and secrets. Secrets must not appear in docs, prompts, fixtures, logs or examples.
  13. Route auth, sensitive data, money movement, privileged operations and irreversible side effects through security/risk review.
  14. Record rollback and recovery before claiming completion for risky backend changes.

docs.text:
• Directories: backend/, server/, services/, workers/, jobs/, queues/, cron/, schedulers/, consumers/, adapters/, repositories/, migrations/
  • Files: Dockerfile, Procfile, docker-compose.yml, k8s/*.yaml, helm/, serverless.yml, openapi.yaml, asyncapi.yaml, .proto
  • Terms: service, worker, queue, retry, timeout, idempotency, circuit breaker, background job, scheduler, migration, auth, token, secret, SLO, runbook, health check, readiness, liveness
  • Dependency signals: database clients, message broker clients, HTTP clients, payment/email/storage/search providers, cache clients

docs.text: Gate Trigger Block condition backend_service_boundary_present New service/module/worker or changed ownership Purpose, owner, dependencies or data stores are missing. backend_runtime_behavior_present Worker, queue, scheduler, remote dependency or background behavior Retry, timeout, idempotency, ordering, replay or failure mode is unspecified. backend_dependency_failure_matrix_present Remote service, DB, cache, queue or third-party dependency No timeout/retry/fallback/alert/owner policy. backend_observability_contract_present Production runtime behavior changes Logs/metrics/traces/correlation IDs or redaction notes are missing. backend_slo_or_gap_present User-facing or production service No SLO/SLI or explicit gap. backend_health_probe_contract_present Deployable service or worker with health checks Liveness/readiness/startup semantics are not documented. backend_security_reviewed Auth, secrets, sensitive data, money, privileged operations No security notes, threat/abuse cases or reviewer route. backend_data_consistency_strategy_present Multi-step data change, queue, outbox, saga or migration Transaction boundary, consistency model and recovery path are missing. backend_config_secrets_boundary_present Config/env/secrets change No config manifest or secret handling note. backend_rollback_plan_present Migration, irreversible side effect, external write or production behavior change No rollback, recovery or replay path.

docs.title: Candidate eval fields
docs.text:
• Service/module boundary, owner and purpose are present.
  • Dependencies and data stores are named.
  • Runtime behavior is documented for jobs, queues and remote calls.
  • Retry policy includes timeout, backoff, max attempts and idempotency.
  • Observability contract includes no-secrets logging and correlation IDs.
  • SLO/SLI exists or gap is explicit.
  • Health checks distinguish liveness, readiness and startup where applicable.
  • Security-sensitive behavior has a risk review route.
  • Data consistency and rollback plan exist for risky changes.
  • Verification commands include unit, integration, contract or runtime checks appropriate to the change.

docs.title: Tooling candidates
docs.text: Tooling area Candidate Notes Runtime service discipline Twelve-Factor Good default vocabulary for config, logs, processes and dev/prod parity. Observability OpenTelemetry Default cross-stack vocabulary for traces, metrics, logs, context propagation and collectors. Reliability SLO/SLI sheets Use user-relevant indicators, not every available metric. Service architecture C4, ADR, Ports and Adapters map Useful when service boundaries or adapters change. Runtime health Kubernetes probes or platform equivalent Use only when the deployment platform supports probe semantics. Resilience patterns Retry, circuit breaker, load leveling, health endpoint monitoring Vendor-specific docs are references; project implementation should be stack-native. Distributed workflow Saga/compensation docs Use only when local transaction/outbox is not enough. Security SSDF, ASVS, secret scanning, SAST/DAST where applicable Select by stack and risk profile.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Backend docs describe package structure but omit runtime behavior.
  • A retry is added without timeout, backoff, max attempts and idempotency.
  • Liveness and readiness endpoints are treated as the same thing.
  • Logs expose secrets, tokens, private data or full payloads.
  • A worker can process the same message twice but has no deduplication policy.
  • A queue has no dead-letter, replay or poison-message procedure.
  • A service boundary changes without owner review or ADR.
  • A distributed transaction is implemented without compensation or recovery evidence.
  • Microservices are chosen before module boundaries, deployment automation and observability are mature.
  • Completion is claimed after code inspection without integration/runtime verification.

  • Which resilience library examples are mature enough for stack-specific snippets?

docs.title: Business & Product
docs.text:
Source status: official + verified methodology + local implementation evidence + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Product-Agent OS behavior: require product intent, measurable user/business value, analytics or eval evidence, metric hardening and post-release learning before agents implement meaningful behavior changes or promote workflows into skills, plugins or automations.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers product hypothesis, value proposition, opportunity discovery, Lean MVP experiments, outcome-driven planning, HEART, North Star metrics, metric hardening, analytics taxonomy, qualitative feedback, AI product evals, release measurement and learning loops.

It does not mandate heavyweight product management for every code change, one universal North Star metric for all work, mandatory analytics instrumentation for internal-only mechanical changes or AI evals for non-AI behavior. The method is conditional: it becomes required when a change claims product value, user behavior change, business outcome, AI behavior quality, release impact or reusable workflow promotion.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• Google HEART describes a user-centered metrics framework and a Goals -> Signals -> Metrics process for mapping product goals to measurable signals.
  • Amplitude North Star guidance frames a primary value metric and supporting inputs around customer value and product/business outcomes.
  • Amplitude taxonomy guidance says product analytics starts with planned events, properties, naming conventions and key metrics; inconsistent event names or missing properties create data quality problems.
  • Amplitude implementation guidance assigns Data Governor ownership for tracking plan design, naming convention, taxonomy, data quality, privacy policy alignment and feature-success measurement challenge.
  • Product Talk Opportunity Solution Trees connect desired outcome, opportunity space, solution space and assumption tests. They also require a target customer/value proposition theory, a defined outcome and story-based customer interviews as useful inputs.
  • Product Talk distinguishes business outcomes, product outcomes and traction metrics; product outcomes are usually the right discovery scope because teams can influence them more directly.
  • The Lean Startup methodology frames product development as experiments that ask whether a product should be built, uses MVP to learn quickly, and uses Build-Measure-Learn, actionable metrics and pivot/persevere decisions.
  • Strategyzer Value Proposition Canvas identifies customer jobs, pains and gains, then maps product/service offering, pain relievers and gain creators against customer evidence.
  • OpenAI Codex AI-native engineering guidance says agents can handle mechanical build work, while engineers retain responsibility for product behavior clarity, architecture implications, domain alignment, guardrails and long-term quality.
  • OpenAI Codex verified operations guidance recommends structured inputs, approved scope, dry runs where possible, audit-ready outputs and reusable workflows only after a successful manual run.
  • OpenAI Codex AI app eval guidance recommends turning concrete user-visible AI behavior into repeatable eval suites before prompt, model, retrieval or agent changes merge.
  • OpenAI Evals/Promptfoo-style eval workflows are relevant for AI product behavior, but they do not replace product analytics, user research or post-release measurement.
  • The local Product-Agent OS implementation already has metric-spec.md, REQUIREMENTS.md, acceptance-scenarios.md, RUNLOG.md, metric_hardening_when_product_behavior_changes and release/operator checks for metric hardening.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• A behavior-changing slice should start from target user, opportunity/problem, expected outcome, non-goals, acceptance scenario and metric status before architecture or implementation tasks.
  • For internal refactors, dependency updates or mechanical docs changes, product metrics can be marked not_applicable when the reason is explicit.
  • A proxy metric is useful only when paired with counter-metric, guardrail, qualitative review and post-release review.
  • Product analytics events are project contracts. They require taxonomy, owner, property definitions, privacy classification and validation evidence.
  • AI product changes need both eval evidence for behavior and product evidence for value when they affect a user-facing promise.
  • Workflow promotion should follow the chain manual thread -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation only when value, verification, owner and safety boundary are explicit.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "A single metric proves product success." Metrics need context, guardrails, qualitative review and a decision horizon.
  • "More usage always means more value." Increased engagement can hide degraded trust, quality, latency, cost or support load.
  • "A feature request is an opportunity." Feature requests are possible solutions; opportunities describe unmet needs, pains or desires.
  • "North Star is mandatory for every slice." Small changes often need a local product outcome or explicit not_applicable metric status.
  • "Analytics data is reliable by default." Event/property drift, naming inconsistency and missing governance can invalidate decisions.
  • "Evals replace product metrics." Evals test AI behavior; product value needs user/business outcome evidence.
  • "Codex speed equals product value." Faster implementation is useful only when it advances the right outcome with current evidence.
  • "Automation follows any repeated workflow." Repetition alone is not enough; automation needs approved scope, rollback/disable path and audit evidence.

docs.title: Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology When to apply Product-Agent OS behavior Product hypothesis Any user/business behavior change Require target user, opportunity/problem, expected outcome, non-goals, assumptions and evidence gaps in REQUIREMENTS.md. Value Proposition Canvas New product, segment, capability or unclear value Record jobs, pains, gains, pain relievers, gain creators and evidence source. Opportunity Solution Tree Discovery, roadmap choice, multiple candidate solutions Trace desired outcome -> opportunities -> solutions -> assumptions -> tests -> decision. Lean Build-Measure-Learn MVP, risky assumption, uncertain demand/value Define smallest build, measure plan, actionable metric, learning threshold and pivot/persevere rule. HEART UX/user-centered product quality Choose relevant Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention or Task success metrics through Goals -> Signals -> Metrics. North Star / primary value metric Product-level value alignment Define primary value metric, input metrics, baseline, target, owner, window and guardrails. Metric hardening Product behavior change with measurement claim Require counter-metric, guardrails, proxy risk, qualitative review, privacy classification and post-release review. Analytics taxonomy/governance Usage data informs product decisions Define events, properties, naming convention, owner, validation workflow, privacy constraints and dashboard/report. Qualitative feedback loop Metrics are ambiguous or early Add interviews, support/sales/customer-success signals, review notes or accepted evidence gap. Outcome-driven planning Roadmap/large project decomposition Plan slices around measurable behavior/outcome, not only components or tasks. AI product evals Prompt/model/retrieval/tool/agent behavior changes Baseline first, one focused behavior, app-path eval where feasible, threshold, failure review and rerun before release claims. Release measurement Launch, rollout, beta, production change Define measurement window, dashboard/report, owner, rollback/decision rule and RUNLOG update.

docs.title: Product-Agent OS candidate rules
docs.text:
• requirements-author should output a product_hypothesis block for behavior-changing work.
  • requirements-author should mark metric_scope as required, not_applicable or accepted_gap; empty metric status should fail readiness.
  • implementation-planner should stop when a behavior-changing slice lacks user, opportunity/problem, expected outcome, non-goals, acceptance scenario or metric/gap.
  • test-eval-designer should map product behavior to deterministic tests, analytics validation, manual/exploratory evidence or AI evals.
  • pr-release-operator should block product success claims when only planned measurement exists.
  • learning-loop-maintainer should compare actual post-release signals with hypothesis and decide whether to continue, pivot, rollback or promote the workflow.
  • Promotion to skill/plugin/automation should require repeatable value, stable inputs/outputs, verification command/artifact, owner, safety boundary and failure mode.

docs.title: Candidate readiness gates
docs.text: Gate Required when Evidence product_hypothesis_present Behavior-changing work Target user, problem/opportunity, expected outcome, non-goals. target_user_segment_present User scope matters Primary, secondary and excluded users or accepted gap. value_proposition_evidence_present New segment/product/capability Jobs, pains, gains and evidence source/gap. opportunity_not_solution_present Discovery/roadmap work Opportunity statement has more than one possible solution. success_metric_present Product value claim Primary metric or explicit not_applicable reason. metric_hardening_when_product_behavior_changes Behavior change with metric claim Input metric, counter-metric, guardrail, proxy risk, qualitative review, owner. analytics_tracking_plan_present Usage data will be claimed Event/property taxonomy, naming convention, validation plan and privacy classification. qualitative_feedback_loop_present Early/ambiguous product signal Interviews, support/sales signal, review notes or accepted gap. ai_product_eval_when_ai_behavior_changes AI behavior changes Baseline eval, cases, assertions/graders, threshold and command or accepted gap. post_release_measurement_plan_present Release/rollout Window, dashboard/report, owner, decision rule and rollback/disable signal. release_measurement_evidence_present Success claim after release Actual metrics/eval/user feedback or explicit evidence gap in RUNLOG.md.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Solution bias: plan starts from implementation tasks and backfills product intent later.
  • Vanity metric: metric is easy to move but weakly connected to customer or business value.
  • Proxy optimization: team improves the metric while degrading quality, trust, cost, privacy or support load.
  • Data drift: events/properties change without taxonomy review and analytics dashboards become misleading.
  • Evidence gap hidden: release claim says "works" while measurement is planned but not yet observed.
  • Eval/product mismatch: AI eval improves while user outcome, support load or retention degrades.
  • Over-process: formal product artifacts are forced onto trivial mechanical changes instead of marking not_applicable.
  • Unsafe automation: repeated workflow is automated before ownership, verification, approvals and rollback are stable.

docs.title: Open questions for implementation
docs.text:
• Should product_hypothesis_present become a universal gate for every behavior-changing slice, or only for user-facing/product-labeled changes?
  • Should Product-Agent OS generate separate value-proposition.md and opportunity-tree.md, or keep them as optional sections inside REQUIREMENTS.md until the project grows?
  • What threshold should route a slice from simple metric-spec.md to a full analytics tracking-plan.md?
  • How should post-release measurement be represented when the project has no production telemetry yet?
  • Should workflow promotion into skill/plugin require a business/product metric, or is repeated engineering time saved enough when evidence is explicit?

docs.title: Codex / Agentic Workflow
docs.text:
Source status: official OpenAI + verified methodology + local implementation evidence + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Product-Agent OS behavior: operate Codex as an engineering system, not as a chat transcript. Durable rules, task state, handoffs, evidence, approvals and promotion decisions must live in repository artifacts. Chat remains a working surface; checked-in or staged artifacts remain the source of truth.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, AGENTS.md, skills, subagents, MCP, hooks, plugins, memories, sandbox, approvals, automations, Codex workflows/use cases, Agents SDK orchestration concepts, model/reasoning routing, context management, evidence-before-completion and Product-Agent OS lifecycle routing.

It does not create active hooks, MCP servers, automations, schedules, GitHub Actions or external writes. It does not replace official OpenAI documentation, and it does not treat community reports or memories as durable project rules.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• OpenAI Codex documentation describes customization as complementary layers: AGENTS.md for persistent project guidance, memories for useful local recall, skills for reusable workflows, MCP for external tools/context and subagents for delegated specialized work.
  • AGENTS.md is loaded before work starts and can be layered from global and project scopes. Files closer to the working directory override earlier guidance in the prompt chain.
  • Codex best practices recommend task prompts that include goal, context, constraints and done condition; complex work should plan before implementation.
  • Codex best practices describe AGENTS.md as the place to encode repo layout, commands, conventions, constraints and verification expectations.
  • Codex skills package instructions, resources and optional scripts. Skills use progressive disclosure: metadata is visible for discovery, while full instructions are loaded only when selected.
  • Codex plugins are the installable distribution unit. A plugin has .codex-plugin/plugin.json and can bundle skills, MCP configuration, hooks, apps/connectors and assets.
  • Codex MCP connects Codex to external tools and context providers through config.toml and supports stdio and streamable HTTP servers.
  • Codex hooks run deterministic lifecycle scripts and must be reviewed/trusted before non-managed command hooks execute.
  • Codex subagents can run specialized agents in parallel when explicitly requested. Subagents inherit sandbox and approval controls from the parent workflow, and parallel workflows consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs.
  • Codex approval and sandbox guidance treats sandbox mode and approval policy as key autonomy controls. Default workspace-write behavior can read/edit workspace files while requiring approval for writes outside the workspace or network access.
  • Codex memories can carry useful context across threads, but required team guidance belongs in AGENTS.md or checked-in documentation. Memories are a recall layer, not a rule source.
  • Codex automations schedule recurring tasks. Official guidance says to test automation prompts manually first, review early outputs and use skills to define maintainable recurring workflows.
  • Codex best practices summarize the promotion split: skills define the method, automations define the schedule.
  • Codex use cases show repeated patterns: structured inputs, constraints, verification, audit output, and promotion into skills or automation only after the manual workflow is stable.
  • Agents SDK guidance defines code-first agent applications where the application owns orchestration, tool execution, approvals and state. This is a different runtime layer from Codex App/CLI/IDE work, but it provides useful vocabulary for handoffs, tools, guardrails, sessions, tracing and evals.
  • Agents SDK orchestration guidance distinguishes handoffs, where a specialist owns the next response, from agents-as-tools, where a manager keeps ownership.
  • Agents SDK guardrails and human review guidance treats automatic validation and human approval as mechanisms that decide whether a run continues, pauses or stops.
  • OpenAI agent eval guidance recommends moving from traces to repeatable datasets and eval runs once "good" behavior is defined.
  • The local Product-Agent OS implementation already uses lifecycle skills, staged infrastructure rendering, candidate-only automations, fresh-context handoff artifacts, approval records, source-policy validation and evidence-before-completion checks.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• Product-Agent OS should treat Codex App/CLI/IDE extension as human-in-the-loop engineering surfaces and Agents SDK as a programmable app-orchestration layer.
  • Large project work should start with read-only discovery unless the requested task is trivial and already scoped.
  • The default promotion path should be: manual thread -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation.
  • Subagents should be used only when work is independent enough to split by files, subsystem or evidence output.
  • Parallel agents need fresh task packets, file ownership, forbidden files, expected evidence, stop conditions and handoff output schema.
  • MCP, hooks, plugins and automations should be capability surfaces with explicit permission, trust and rollback/disable boundaries.
  • Reasoning effort should be selected by task risk: lower for bounded read-only or mechanical work, stronger for architecture, debugging, security, eval judging, migrations and ambiguous multi-step work.
  • Memories can reduce repeated context, but the project should never depend on them for mandatory rules, source policy, secrets policy or completion criteria.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "More agents are always better." Subagents add token cost and coordination risk.
  • "Memory can replace documentation." Required team/project guidance belongs in AGENTS.md or checked-in docs.
  • "A repeated idea is ready for automation." Automation needs manual success evidence, stable inputs/outputs, owner, verification and disable path.
  • "MCP access means the agent may write external systems." MCP tools must follow source, approval, permission and side-effect boundaries.
  • "Hooks are harmless because they are local scripts." Hooks run inside lifecycle events and require trust review, provenance and failure handling.
  • "A plugin is just a folder of prompts." Plugins are installable packages with manifests, components, permissions, assets and update ownership.
  • "Agents SDK should replace Codex App/CLI for every workflow." Agents SDK is useful for code-owned agent apps; Codex App/CLI/IDE remain the product-agent work surfaces.
  • "Passing inspection proves completion." Completion claims need current evidence or explicit gaps.
  • "Subagents can share raw chat context instead of task packets." Fresh-context handoff should carry only the task contract, source constraints, ownership and expected evidence.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the task before starting: docs, web/front-end, backend, database, API, native/mobile, desktop, AI/eval, security, delivery/release, automation, plugin/skill, PR/review or long-running goal.
  2. Start read-only unless the task is trivial, already scoped and low-risk. Read AGENTS.md, relevant docs, target files, existing patterns, commands and sandbox/approval constraints.
  3. Write or update control-plane artifacts for long-running/product work. Use REQUIREMENTS.md, PLAN.md, TEST.md, EVALS.md and RUNLOG.md when the task spans multiple slices or has ambiguous acceptance criteria.
  4. Keep chat as an interaction surface, not the source of truth. Durable requirements, constraints, decisions and evidence must be written to project artifacts.
  5. Use AGENTS.md for stable project rules only. Do not put one-off instructions, private data, secrets, raw chat logs or speculative community tricks there.
  6. When a mistake repeats, add a concise durable rule or routing hint only after the failure is understood.
  7. Use skills when a workflow has a clear trigger, repeatable inputs, expected outputs, verification and failure modes.
  8. Create a skill from a proven manual workflow, not from an abstract idea. Log at least one successful run and one known failure/risk before treating it as reusable.
  9. Package a plugin only when the workflow must be shared, installed, bundled with MCP/hooks/apps/assets or maintained with a clear owner/update loop.
  10. Treat MCP as an external capability boundary. Document which tools/resources/prompts are exposed, what can mutate state, what needs approval and what data must not leave the workspace.
  11. Treat hooks as executable policy. Stage hook definitions, document event/matcher/command/failure behavior and require trust review before activation.
  12. Use subagents only for independent or specialist work. Every subagent needs a fresh task packet with sources, assumptions, owned files, forbidden files, expected evidence and stop condition.
  13. Avoid overlapping edits across subagents. If file ownership overlaps or the merge risk is high, use sequential execution with review checkpoints.
  14. Use worktrees or explicit ownership for parallel implementation. Do not let background work modify the same local checkout without a merge/rollback plan.
  15. Keep sandbox and approvals tight by default. External writes, CI/GitHub changes, publishing, production data, network-heavy actions, MCP side effects and hook activation need explicit approval.
  16. Select runtime by job: Codex App/IDE for ambiguity and steering, CLI for local engineering, codex exec for stable non-interactive jobs, GitHub Action for PR/CI, MCP for external tools, Agents SDK for code-owned agent apps, automation for stable recurring workflows.
  17. Set model/reasoning policy by risk. Use stronger reasoning for architecture, review, debugging, security, eval judging, migrations and ambiguous multi-step work; lower reasoning for bounded read-only collection or mechanical edits.
  18. Use memory only as recall. Required rules, source policy, acceptance criteria, secrets policy and verification commands must live in checked-in docs or current task artifacts.
  19. Require evidence-before-completion. A final claim must cite current commands, checks, artifacts, runtime output, traces/screenshots/evals or explicitly state what was not verified.
  20. Promote recurring workflows in order: manual thread -> playbook -> skill -> plugin -> automation. Automation is blocked until manual stability, owner, reviewable output, verification and disable/rollback path exist.

docs.title: Candidate eval fields
docs.text:
• The workflow starts from a classified use-case archetype and selected runtime surface.
  • The plan names source-of-truth artifacts and avoids relying on chat memory.
  • Read-only discovery includes current project docs, target files, commands and sandbox/approval context.
  • Subagent or specialist work includes fresh-context task packet, ownership, forbidden files, output schema and stop conditions.
  • Parallel work has explicit ownership or falls back to sequential execution.
  • Skills are promoted only from proven manual workflows with verification and failure modes.
  • Plugins include manifest, bundled component list, permissions, owner/update loop and eval cases.
  • MCP additions include capability, trust, data, secret and approval review.
  • Hook additions remain staged until trust review and failure behavior are documented.
  • Automations remain candidate-only until manual stability evidence exists.
  • Model/reasoning policy is explicit for durable agents or workflows.
  • Memory is used as recall only and never as mandatory source of truth.
  • Final claims cite current evidence or state gaps.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Chat contains the real requirements while project artifacts remain stale.
  • AGENTS.md accumulates vague preferences, obsolete rules or one-off instructions.
  • Subagents are spawned for overlapping edits without file ownership.
  • Handoffs omit source constraints, assumptions, expected evidence or stop conditions.
  • Skills are created from ideas without successful manual runs.
  • Plugins are packaged before permissions, evals and owner/update loop exist.
  • MCP tools are treated as safe because they are "just docs" even when they expose actions.
  • Hooks are enabled without trust review or failure-mode documentation.
  • Automations are scheduled before the prompt and tools are stable.
  • Memory stores context that should have been checked into docs, or contains private/secrets material.
  • Completion is claimed from inspection-only evidence.
  • Agents SDK concepts are copied into Codex runtime docs without distinguishing runtime layers.

docs.title: Database & Data
docs.text:
Source status: official + expert reference + vendor documentation + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Product-Agent OS behavior: detect database and data work early, require schema ownership, migration safety, privacy classification, backup/restore evidence, data quality gates, performance review and rollback/compensation evidence before production-impacting data changes.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers relational database schemas, migrations, constraints, indexes, query plans, backfills, data quality checks, analytical model contracts, privacy classification, retention, lineage, backup/restore and production data access.

It does not mandate PostgreSQL, Liquibase, Flyway, dbt, Great Expectations or OpenLineage for every project. These sources provide vocabulary and candidate artifacts; the actual stack must be selected from the project inventory.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL official documentation treats the current documentation as PostgreSQL 18 at the time of this research run. Its transaction isolation documentation describes Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable behavior, and explicitly notes serialization failure retry requirements for stronger isolation levels.
  • PostgreSQL constraints documentation defines integrity mechanisms such as check, not-null, unique, primary key, foreign key and exclusion constraints. Database integrity should not be documented only as application prose when database-level constraints are appropriate.
  • PostgreSQL indexes documentation and EXPLAIN documentation support performance review through index design and query plan evidence. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement, so write statements require transaction/rollback care during analysis.
  • PostgreSQL backup and restore documentation separates SQL dump and file-system-level backup approaches. Production database work needs backup/restore evidence rather than only a statement that backups exist.
  • Liquibase documents a changelog as an ordered list of changesets and tracks executed changesets in the DATABASECHANGELOG table. It also supports rollback definitions, preconditions, contexts and labels.
  • Flyway documents migrations as version-controlled SQL scripts for incremental schema/data changes, with versioned, repeatable, baseline and undo migration concepts. It also documents dry-run/deployment reports and schema history.
  • dbt data tests are SQL assertions that return failing rows; zero failing rows means the assertion passes. dbt also documents model contracts as a way to define and enforce model column names and data types for supported materializations.
  • Great Expectations defines Expectations as verifiable assertions about data, including completeness, schema, uniqueness, validity and volume checks, plus custom SQL expectations and multi-source comparisons.
  • OpenLineage defines an open standard for lineage metadata around dataset, job and run entities. It is useful when data products, analytics or AI/RAG pipelines need traceability.
  • NIST Privacy Framework 1.1 guidance supports privacy requirements, profiles, SDLC alignment and data-processing ecosystem risk management. Database methodology should treat sensitive data as a lifecycle and governance concern, not a late release checklist.
  • Fowler and Sadalage's Evolutionary Database Design describes putting migration scripts and application changes in version control, running them through CI/deployment pipelines and making database changes small. It also highlights transition phases for destructive changes.
  • The expand/contract pattern documents a multi-step migration approach: introduce new structures in parallel, update writes, backfill, validate, switch reads/writes, then remove old structures. This is vendor documentation from Prisma and should be treated as a practical pattern reference, not a universal standard.

docs.title: Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology When to apply Project-level behavior Evolutionary database design Product evolves continuously Schema/data changes are small, versioned, automated and tested with application changes. Migration-first planning Any schema, backfill or retention change database-migration-plan.md exists before execution. Expand/contract migration Live systems, shared DB, public consumers Add new structure in parallel, dual-write/backfill, switch reads/writes, then remove old structure. Database DevOps / migrations-as-code Team-owned database changes Migrations live in version control and run through repeatable tooling and CI/CD gates. Data integrity by constraint Relational data needs correctness guarantees Constraints and indexes are designed explicitly, not inferred only from ORM models. Transaction and concurrency design Multi-step writes, financial/accounting/state workflows Isolation level, locks, retry behavior and idempotency are documented. Data quality gates Business-critical, analytical or AI/RAG source data Executable tests/assertions validate uniqueness, nullability, accepted values, counts and drift. Data contracts Data models consumed by other teams/systems Column names, data types, semantics, owner and compatibility rules are explicit. Privacy-by-design PII, sensitive data, regulated data, retention changes Classification, minimization, retention, deletion and access controls are documented early. Backup/restore-first change management Production data, irreversible or high-risk migration Restore path is known and periodically tested before risky execution. Lineage-aware data operations Analytics, reporting, ML/RAG, cross-system movement Dataset/job/run lineage is captured or the gap is explicit. Performance-by-design New indexes, heavy queries, high-volume backfills Query plans, index impact, lock impact and runtime budgets are reviewed. Production data access control Any agent or developer touches prod data Approval, least privilege, audit trail and no-secrets/no-customer-data policy are enforced.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the work: schema change, data migration, backfill, retention/deletion, data quality, query/index performance, analytics model, lineage, backup/restore or production data access.
  2. Identify the database engine, environment, owner, data domain and source of truth for schema/migrations.
  3. Record whether the change affects production data, sensitive fields, external consumers, analytics, AI/RAG sources or public APIs.
  4. Create a migration plan before implementation for any schema, backfill or retention change.
  5. Prefer small, ordered, version-controlled migrations. Avoid hidden manual SQL as the only record of a change.
  6. For live/shared systems, use expand/contract or another compatibility-preserving strategy before destructive changes.
  7. Define transaction boundary, isolation assumptions, lock impact, retry policy and idempotency for multi-step writes or backfills.
  8. For constraints and indexes, document why they are needed, which queries or invariants they protect and what deployment impact they may have.
  9. For performance-sensitive changes, attach query-plan evidence and expected runtime/lock budget.
  10. For backfills, document batch size, resume key, throttling, validation counts, observability and abort behavior.
  11. Classify rollback as reversible, compensating or irreversible. Do not call a destructive migration rollback-safe without evidence.
  12. For production data, document backup/restore path and restore evidence before execution.
  13. Classify PII/sensitive fields before writing docs, fixtures, examples or prompts. Never copy production data into examples.
  14. Add data quality checks for primary keys, nullability, relationships, accepted values, counts and business-critical assertions.
  15. For analytical or AI/RAG pipelines, document data contracts and lineage or explicitly record the gap.
  16. Require approval and audit evidence before an agent or developer performs production data access or external data writes.
