• Secrets, tokens, private keys.
  • Full documents when one section is needed.
  • Old assumptions from memory without verification.
  • Community advice without a trust marker.
  • Raw subagent logs when a summary with sources is enough.

docs.title: Session vs memory vs retrieved context
docs.text:
Layer Purpose Risk Session Continuity of the current conversation Accumulates stale assumptions Memory Cross-session preferences and patterns Can be local and incomplete Retrieved context Verifiable facts for the answer Retrieval can miss the needed source Prompt instructions Policy and goal Can conflict with the user task

If facts matter, retrieve them again instead of relying on the session summary.

docs.title: Compression without distortion
docs.text:
When compressing context, preserve:

  • source IDs;
  • exact constraints;
  • decisions and rejected alternatives;
  • unresolved questions;
  • freshness dates.

Do not preserve:

  • rhetorical reasoning;
  • duplicate quotes;
  • unsupported conclusions as facts.

docs.title: Prompt & Context Engineering
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Sources: Prompting, Prompt engineering, Model optimization, Structured Outputs, OpenAI Cookbook.

docs.title: Separation of concepts
docs.text:
Prompt engineering is responsible for instructions: what the model should do, in what style, with what constraints and in what result format.

Context engineering is responsible for the working memory of a specific call: which facts, documents, citations, history, tool outputs and session state the model sees before answering.

To reduce hallucinations, the important part is not the "perfect phrase", but full control of the circuit:

flowchart LR
    Q["Question"] --> P["Prompt contract"]
    C["Retrieved context"] --> P
    M["Memory / session"] --> P
    P --> R["Model response"]
    R --> V["Verifier / guardrail"]
    V -->|Pass| O["Final answer"]
    V -->|Fail| E["Clarify / retrieve more / refuse"]

docs.title: Prompt as a contract
docs.text:
A good prompt should answer eight questions explicitly:

Question Prompt contract field Who answers? Role What counts as success? Goal What can it rely on? Context What is forbidden? Constraints What should happen with unknowns? Uncertainty policy Which tools can be used? Tools How should the result be returned? Output format How should the answer be checked? Verification

docs.title: Instruction hierarchy
docs.text:
For API and agentic systems, it is useful to separate levels:

  • System/developer instructions: stable policy, tone, safety, tool rules.
  • User task: concrete task, data, goal.
  • Retrieved context: facts, documents, tool outputs.
  • Examples: compact few-shot examples of the desired result.
  • Output schema: machine-checkable contract.

Do not put transient task details into the permanent system prompt. Do not put long-term policy into a user message if it must always be followed.

docs.title: Optimization cycle
docs.text:
OpenAI model optimization guidance describes a cycle: eval baseline, prompt/context, realistic test inputs, measurement, adjustment, repeat. For this knowledge base, this means:

  1. First define the eval: "the answer must cite source IDs", "it must not invent a source", "it must ask a clarification when data is missing".
  2. Then write the prompt.
  3. Check it on question sets similar to real ones.
  4. Version the prompt and record changes.

docs.title: Anti-hallucination baseline
docs.text:
Minimal baseline for factual tasks:

Answer only from the provided context.
If the context is insufficient, say what is missing.
Do not invent facts, citations, file paths, versions, prices, dates, or line numbers.
Separate verified facts from assumptions.
Return citations for every factual claim when sources are provided.

docs.title: Designing Questions for GPT Models
docs.text: Source status: official + experiment Sources: Prompting, Prompt engineering, OpenAI Cookbook.

docs.title: Formula for a good question
docs.text:
Bad question:

Tell me about agents.

Good question:

Goal: Design a multi-agent research workflow for updating Codex documentation.
Audience: Advanced agent builder.
Context: Use only the listed sources and the current docs structure.
Constraints: Do not mix official and community claims.
Output: Return architecture, roles, handoff contract, evals, risks.
Uncertainty: If a source is missing, mark the claim as needs_source.
Verification: State which docs/checks need to be updated.

docs.title: Prompt packet
docs.text:
Use this packet as the default:

# Role
You are ...

# Goal
...

# Context
<source id="S1">
...
</source>

# Constraints
- ...

# Unknowns and assumptions
- Ask a clarifying question if ...
- Otherwise assume ...

# Tools
- Use ... only when ...

# Output format
...

# Verification
...

docs.title: Specificity rules
docs.text: Instead of Write "Make it better" "Shorten to 800 words, preserve citations, add failure modes" "Analyze" "Find contradictions, unsupported claims, missing tests" "Explain in detail" "Give a mental model, workflow, examples, pitfalls" "Do not hallucinate" "If a claim is not supported by context, mark needs_source" "Answer JSON" "Return JSON by schema, use an empty array and missing_context when data is missing"

docs.title: When to ask a clarifying question
docs.text:
The model should clarify when:

  • the task has several incompatible interpretations;
  • critical input is missing;
  • the action may be dangerous or expensive;
  • the result depends on fresh facts and tools are unavailable;
  • user intent matters more than repo facts.

If ambiguity does not block the work, it is better to choose an explicit assumption:

Assumption: By "agents" I mean OpenAI Agents SDK, not general AI agents.

docs.title: Few-shot examples
docs.text:
Few-shot is needed when not only "what", but also "what a good answer looks like" matters. Keep examples short:

examples:
  - input: "Check claim: Codex launches subagents by itself."
    output:
      status: "rejected"
      reason: "Official docs require explicit user request for subagents."
      source: "https://developers.openai.com/codex/subagents"
  - input: "Check claim: Structured Outputs solve all hallucinations."
    output:
      status: "qualified"
      reason: "They constrain shape, but factual mistakes remain possible."
      source: "https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs"

docs.title: Checklist before sending
docs.text:
• Is there a concrete outcome?
  • Is there a list of allowed sources?
  • Is there a ban on unsupported facts?
  • Is there an output format?
  • Is there a rule for uncertainty?
  • Is there a verification criterion?

docs.title: Automations and GitHub
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment Sources: Codex automations, Codex workflows, Codex best practices.

Automation should come after a stable manual workflow or skill. GitHub workflows belong to CI/PR contexts when the repository owner has approved the trigger, permissions and rollback path.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Stable workflow, owner, cadence, expected evidence and failure handling.
  • GitHub or automation permissions, data policy and approval record.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Automation candidate, GitHub workflow proposal or approved recurring check.
  • Audit-ready evidence for what ran, where it wrote and how to disable it.

Good automation candidates include scheduled documentation freshness audit, system file hygiene audit for AGENTS.md, control-plane files, subagents, skills, workflows, hooks, evals and automation candidates, recurring security review, CI failure triage and release-note drafting.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Before activating automation, verify manual success evidence, input stability, output expectations and rollback/disable path.

System file hygiene automation should start as .codex/automation-candidates/system-file-hygiene-audit.md: weekly/monthly cadence, on-change trigger and size trigger are proposals, not an active schedule. Before approval, use only the read-only command:

python plugins\product-agent-os\scripts\validate_system_file_hygiene.py <workspace>

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• A scheduled workflow without stable inputs can repeat bad decisions.
  • GitHub permissions and external writes need least privilege and explicit approval.

docs.title: Non-interactive Codex and MCP
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment Sources: Codex CLI features, Codex with Agents SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK Python.

Non-interactive Codex runs are useful when the prompt contract is stable and verification is deterministic. MCP and Agents SDK orchestration are useful when the integration contract, permissions and audit evidence are explicit.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• A stable prompt, workspace path, sandbox policy and verification command.
  • MCP server or Agents SDK contract when orchestration is needed.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Deterministic command output, staged artifacts or an orchestration packet.
  • Evidence that the run stayed inside approved filesystem, network and tool boundaries.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Run non-interactive jobs with explicit commands and inspect output before making a completion claim.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Non-interactive mode is a poor fit for ambiguous first-run work.
  • MCP and Agents SDK tools can cross trust boundaries unless permissions and approvals are explicit.

docs.title: Runtime overview
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment Sources: Codex CLI features, Codex best practices, Codex automations, Codex with Agents SDK.

Product-Agent OS chooses runtime by uncertainty, risk and approval boundary. Codex App and IDE extension fit steering and review; CLI and codex exec fit deterministic local checks; GitHub Action, MCP, Agents SDK and automation require clearer contracts.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Work item, risk level, allowed commands and current approval policy.
  • Available surfaces: Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, GitHub, MCP, Agents SDK and automation.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• A runtime decision with expected evidence and forbidden actions.
  • A staged packet when live or external systems are proposed.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Record the chosen runtime, command evidence and stop condition. Do not claim runtime behavior from code inspection alone.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Live server launch, browser automation, provider calls and git release actions need explicit approval.
  • Automating before a workflow is stable can repeat unresolved failures.

docs.title: Worktrees, hooks and rules
docs.text:
Source status: official + experiment Sources: Codex best practices, Codex worktrees, Codex hooks, Codex rules, Agent approvals and security.

Worktrees isolate larger changes. Hooks and rules can guide or block unsafe actions, but they should remain explicit, reviewable and aligned with sandbox and approvals.

docs.title: Product-Agent OS lifecycle hooks
docs.text:
Product-Agent OS ships staged hooks through plugins/product-agent-os/assets/templates/hooks/ and render_infrastructure.py --stage. For an end project they land under .codex/hooks/ as proposed/staged assets, not as silently activated automation.

The lifecycle guard works as follows:

  • SessionStart reports control-plane and lifecycle file presence;
  • PreToolUse allows read-only discovery through a fast path that does not read the marker, but blocks mutating or non-read-only commands without .codex/product-agent-os/lifecycle-state.json;
  • the marker must be written only after a user-visible full field-list start brief and must contain task_start_brief_shown, task_id, scope, updated_at, approval_boundary, brief_schema_version: task_start_brief_v1, brief_format: field_list, brief_digest, and brief_fields_present with every required start brief field;
  • the per-write PostToolUse comment-sufficiency advisory checks only paths from the current patch instead of rescanning the entire dirty worktree;
  • after all writes, checks, and control-plane sync, the marker moves to ready_for_completion_brief and further mutations are denied;
  • Stop accepts one complete terminal Completion Brief without continuation, and requests at most one corrective continuation for an incomplete brief. No tool calls are allowed after a valid brief.

The marker is not a transcript store: do not put raw chat, secrets, private source bodies, private customer data, or credentials in it. Hook activation remains a separate approval boundary.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Change scope, branch/worktree policy, file ownership and approval boundary.
  • Hook or rule proposal with trigger, allowed action and failure handling.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Isolated workspace plan, hook proposal or durable rule update.
  • Clear guidance on what requires explicit owner approval.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Check that worktrees do not hide conflicting edits and hooks do not activate without approval.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Creating branches or worktrees without owner approval can conflict with project rules.
  • Hooks can block valid work or mutate state unexpectedly if they are too broad.

docs.title: ADD, DDD, TDD And FSD In LLM-Assisted Development
docs.text:
Source status: mixed source-backed draft Status: incoming research document. Before moving claims into core guidance, verify primary sources and explicitly separate Data-Driven Development from Domain-Driven Design.

Terminology boundary: this draft uses DDD as an incoming shorthand for Data-Driven Development. Product-Agent OS core methodology reserves DDD for Domain-Driven Design: domain language, bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, business rules, invariants and domain-to-architecture traceability. When this draft is referenced from Product-Agent OS docs or search results, treat Data-Driven Development as product/metric discipline and spell it out unless the local team explicitly defines the abbreviation.

docs.title: Table Of Contents
docs.text:
1. Short summary
  2. Terms
  3. ADD - Agentic-Driven Development
  4. DDD - Data-Driven Development (draft term; Product-Agent OS core DDD = Domain-Driven Design)
  5. TDD - Test-Driven Development
  6. FSD - Feature-Sliced Design / Development
  7. Key differences
  8. Strengths and limitations
  9. How the approaches fit together
  10. Use with LLM agents
  11. Web, mobile and desktop use
  12. Practical workflow
  13. Example: search across chat conversations
  14. Final recommendation
  15. Sources and useful links

docs.title: Short Summary
docs.text:
These approaches answer different engineering questions:

Data-driven development -> what to build and why it matters to users
FSD -> where code lives and how the app is structured
TDD -> how to prove behavior works correctly
ADD -> how to implement faster with LLM agents under human control

For modern LLM-assisted work, the useful sequence is:

Product hypothesis
  -> Feature boundary
    -> Acceptance tests
      -> Agentic implementation
        -> Human review
          -> Post-release metrics

For AI apps, semantic search, RAG, local indexing and user-data workflows, the high-value combination is TDD plus evaluation-driven testing, FSD for UI boundaries, controlled ADD and data-informed metrics.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Abbreviation Meaning Practical Use ADD Agentic-Driven Development / Agentic Coding Driven Development LLM agents help plan, code, test, repair and document work. DDD (draft term here) Data-Driven Development Product and engineering decisions use data, metrics and feedback. Product-Agent OS core DDD means Domain-Driven Design; spell out Data-Driven Development in public guidance unless the local team explicitly defines the abbreviation. TDD Test-Driven Development Write a failing test first, then implementation, then refactor. FSD Feature-Sliced Design / Feature-Sliced Development Frontend/UI architecture organized by layers, features and business entities.

Important: in established frontend practice, FSD almost always means Feature-Sliced Design. If a team uses another phrase such as "Future Sliced Development", clarify it because it is not the common standard term.

docs.title: ADD - Agentic-Driven Development
docs.text:
ADD treats the LLM agent as an active implementation participant, not just a code generator. A useful agent can inspect the repository, plan changes, write code, run tests, read failures, repair implementation, prepare a diff or PR, write documentation and suggest architecture improvements.

The human remains accountable for architecture, quality, security and final decisions.

Typical loop:

1. Goal / intent
2. Specification / acceptance criteria
3. Agent planning
4. Implementation loop
5. Test run
6. Error repair
7. Human review
8. CI / merge
9. Monitoring / feedback

ADD is especially useful when the task has clear boundaries, runnable checks, enough repository context and a review path. It is risky when the prompt is vague, tests are missing, secrets can leak, or the agent can perform external writes without approval.

docs.title: DDD - Data-Driven Development (Draft Term)
docs.text:
In this draft, DDD means Data-Driven Development. Product-Agent OS core guidance should not use that abbreviation without disambiguation because its canonical DDD is Domain-Driven Design. Product decisions start with a hypothesis, select metrics, instrument behavior, collect data, analyze results and decide whether to keep, change or remove the feature.

Useful loop:

hypothesis -> metric -> instrumentation -> data -> analysis -> decision

Data-driven work is strongest for product iteration, funnel changes, search relevance, onboarding, monetization, retention, AI quality thresholds and post-release learning. It is weakest when the metric is a proxy for user value, privacy is unclear, data is too small, or the team treats one number as proof without qualitative review.

Product-Agent OS should express this through a metric spec with primary value metric, input metrics, guardrails, counter-metrics, privacy classification, retention, owner signoff and post-release review.

docs.title: TDD - Test-Driven Development
docs.text:
TDD is the Red-Green-Refactor loop:

1. Write a failing test for the intended behavior.
2. Write the smallest implementation that makes it pass.
3. Refactor while tests stay green.

TDD is strongest for business rules, parsers, transformations, shared libraries, bug fixes, API contracts and regressions. It is weaker for visual polish, exploratory prototypes and ambiguous product discovery unless paired with acceptance scenarios or evals.

For LLM/RAG systems, unit tests are not enough. Use eval-driven checks for retrieval quality, factuality, grounding, citation quality, refusal behavior, tool selection and regression prevention.

docs.title: FSD - Feature-Sliced Design / Development
docs.text:
Feature-Sliced Design organizes frontend code around layers, slices and segments. A common structure is:

app/
pages/
widgets/
features/
entities/
shared/

The dependency rule is that higher layers can depend on lower layers, while lower layers should not import higher layers. Public APIs on slices make imports explicit and reduce accidental coupling.

FSD is useful for growing UI products, multi-team frontends, business-domain UI flows and apps with many reusable entities/features. It is excessive for tiny prototypes, backend-only work, simple scripts and teams that do not yet have a meaningful UI domain boundary.

docs.title: Key Differences
docs.text: Approach Primary Question Main Artifact Main Risk ADD How can agents safely implement this work? Plan, task packet, test evidence, review packet Autonomous changes without enough verification or approval Data-driven development Why should this feature exist or change? Hypothesis, metrics, experiment/review result Goodhart effects and privacy issues TDD How do we prove behavior works? Failing/passing tests and refactor evidence Writing tests for the wrong behavior FSD Where should UI code live? Layer/slice/segment structure and import rules Forcing UI architecture onto non-UI or small work

docs.title: How The Approaches Fit Together
docs.text:
The practical order for feature work:

  1. State a product hypothesis and success/guardrail metrics.
  2. Define the feature boundary and target user flow.
  3. Choose architecture placement, such as FSD slice for frontend work.
  4. Write acceptance scenarios and tests/evals first.
  5. Let an LLM agent implement inside the scoped boundary.
  6. Run tests/evals and inspect the diff.
  7. Record review evidence and release notes.
  8. Measure post-release behavior and iterate.

docs.title: ADD + LLM
docs.text:
Good LLM-agent tasks:

  • implement a narrow feature slice;
  • add tests and repair failures;
  • update docs and examples;
  • refactor inside a known boundary;
  • prepare a reviewable patch.

Unsafe delegation without more control:

  • irreversible migrations;
  • production data access;
  • external messages or tickets;
  • security-sensitive changes without review;
  • broad architecture rewrites without a plan.

docs.title: Data-Driven Development + LLM
docs.text: LLM agents can draft metric specs, instrumentation plans, experiment notes and post-release review packets. They should not invent user data, treat generated numbers as facts or bypass privacy review.

docs.title: TDD + LLM
docs.text: LLM agents are useful for writing a regression test, running it, implementing the fix and proving the red -> green transition. The human should still inspect whether the test captures the real behavior.

docs.title: FSD + LLM
docs.text: FSD helps agents place code predictably. The task packet can name the target layer/slice/segment, public API boundary, allowed imports and forbidden cross-layer shortcuts.

docs.title: Web, Mobile And Desktop Use
docs.text: Platform Useful Combination Notes Web apps FSD + TDD/evals + ADD + metrics Strong fit for feature slices, UI states, Storybook and product metrics. Mobile apps TDD/evals + ADD + platform build/simulator evidence FSD may apply for shared React Native/Flutter architecture but should not be forced onto native code. Desktop apps TDD/evals + ADD + OS-specific runtime checks Local filesystem, permissions, signing/update and GUI behavior need explicit evidence.

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text:
Recommended loop:

  1. Product hypothesis.
  2. Metrics definition.
  3. Feature boundary.
  4. Test/eval design.
  5. Agentic implementation.
  6. Human review.
  7. CI/evals.
  8. Release.
  9. Measurement.
  10. Iteration.

docs.title: Example: Search Across Chat Conversations
docs.text:
Feature: "Find commitments in chat exports."

  • Data-driven hypothesis: users need to find decisions and commitments faster than manual chat review.
  • Metrics: search success rate, time to answer, false positive rate, privacy incidents and qualitative review.
  • FSD boundary: UI feature slice for search, entity model for conversations/messages, shared UI for result list.
  • TDD/evals: parser tests, date normalization tests, search ranking eval, privacy/no-secret fixture.
  • ADD task: implement within the named files, run tests, update docs and produce a review packet.
  • Post-release review: compare user success and false positives against guardrails.

docs.title: When To Use Which Approach
docs.text: Situation Best Default Unclear product value Data-driven development and product discovery first Complex UI architecture FSD or another explicit frontend boundary Bug fix or shared behavior TDD with regression evidence AI/RAG behavior change Eval-driven tests plus TDD where deterministic Well-scoped implementation ADD with explicit plan, tests and review High-risk/security/data change Human review, approval boundary and rollback evidence before agent execution

docs.title: Final Recommendation
docs.text:
Do not treat ADD, data-driven development, TDD and FSD as competing methodologies. Use them as complementary controls:

  • data-driven development decides why a change matters;
  • FSD or another architecture method decides where code belongs;
  • TDD/evals prove behavior;
  • ADD accelerates implementation while keeping human ownership and verification.

Product-Agent OS should encode this as behavior-level contracts: inputs, outputs, ownership, verification, risks and the next artifact produced.

docs.title: Context7 Analysis
docs.text:
Source status: official + tool-assisted

Analysis date: 2026-05-14. Analysis channel: Context7 documentation retrieval.

docs.title: Context7 Libraries Used
docs.text: Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /websites/developers_openai_codex Official Codex documentation Subagent prompting, skill metadata, granular approvals and Codex MCP multi-agent example /openai/openai-agents-python OpenAI Agents SDK for Python Core primitives: Agent, tools, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing and multi-agent patterns /websites/developers_openai_api OpenAI API documentation Responses API, tool definitions, Structured Outputs, built-in tools, multimodal and stateful patterns /websites/developers_openai OpenAI Developers documentation Prompt structure, prompt objects, prompt versioning, context sections and eval-linked iteration /openai/openai-cookbook OpenAI Cookbook Hallucination guardrails, LLM-as-judge validation, RAG grounding and citation discipline

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
• Approval policy should be described through granular config: sandbox_approval, rules, mcp_elicitations, request_permissions and skill_approval.
  • A skill can extend agents/openai.yaml with UI metadata, invocation policy and dependencies, including MCP tools.
  • Official subagent prompting pattern: ask Codex to create one agent per item, wait for all results and then produce a consolidated summary.
  • Codex MCP can be used as an execution backend inside an Agents SDK multi-agent system where specialized agents call Codex for workspace work.
  • Custom agents can define their own model, model_reasoning_effort, sandbox_mode, MCP servers and skill config; unspecified fields inherit from the parent session.
  • Subagents inherit sandbox/approval controls from the parent workflow, while current-turn runtime overrides also apply to child agents.
  • Model guidance can start with a strong default for most tasks and use cheaper models for fast, bounded subtasks.

docs.title: Agents SDK
docs.text:
• Agents SDK is organized around a small set of primitives: agents, tools, guardrails, handoffs, sessions and tracing.
  • Two common multi-agent orchestration schemes are Manager pattern and Handoff pattern.
  • Tools can be function tools, hosted tools, MCP tools or agents-as-tools.
  • Sessions handle conversation persistence; tracing supports debugging, monitoring and workflow analysis.
  • Production workflows should set model choice explicitly at agent, run-level default or process fallback level.
  • Per-agent model selection is useful when a specialist consistently needs a different quality, latency or cost profile.

docs.title: Responses API
docs.text:
• Responses API is a low-level unified interface for agent-like applications.
  • Tools are described as function tools, MCP tools, image generation and other built-in tool types.
  • Structured Outputs through text.format with JSON Schema are useful for contracts between agents.
  • Built-in tools and multi-turn state complement Agents SDK when direct API-level control is needed.

docs.title: Prompt And Context Engineering
docs.text:
• A prompt should behave like a contract: role, goal, context, constraints, uncertainty policy, tools, output format and verification.
  • OpenAI prompting guidance supports versioned prompt objects, variables and eval-linked prompt iteration.
  • Hallucination reduction needs a system: grounded context, structured output, verifier/guardrail, evals and fallback behavior.
  • Structured Outputs reduce format failures, but still need fallback rules for incompatible user input.
  • Cookbook patterns are useful as practical layers for hallucination detection, LLM-as-judge scoring, factual accuracy, relevance, policy compliance and contextual coherence.

docs.title: Product-Agent Workflows
docs.text:
• Codex product work needs control-plane artifacts: requirements, plan, tests, evals, run log and PR evidence.
  • OpenAI Codex best practices emphasize Ask Mode before Code Mode, AGENTS.md for durable context, worktrees for parallel live work, and automations only after manual workflow stability.
  • Skills are the method layer; automations are the schedule layer; plugins are the distribution layer.
  • Long-horizon tasks need scored loops: baseline, one focused change, rerun eval, inspect artifact, log result and continue until explicit thresholds.
  • Production agents need model/tool/instruction foundations, guardrails, human intervention and incremental orchestration rather than immediate over-automation.
  • Reasoning level should match risk: low for fast scoped tasks, medium/high for complex changes and debugging, xhigh for long reasoning-heavy agentic work.
  • Use-case pages show a repeated production pattern: structured inputs, explicit approval, smallest useful plan, runnable checks/evals, audit artifact, then skill or automation only after the workflow is stable.

docs.title: Codex Use Cases And Plugin Extraction
docs.text:
• The use-case index provides a taxonomy for plugin design: category, native platform, workflow family, team and task type.
  • Most use-case cards can be reduced to one contract: outcome, best fit, inputs, skills/plugins, starter prompt, constraints, verification and related workflows.
  • A plugin should be a bundle of narrow skills, app integrations, MCP/CLI tools, write policy, eval cases and update loop, not a list of generic capabilities.
  • The Save workflows as skills and Create a CLI Codex can use pages show the promotion path: a working thread or command surface first becomes a skill, then can be packaged as a plugin.
  • Follow a goal adds a durable long-running contract: objective, verifiable stop condition, checkpoints, progress log, status inspection, pause/resume/clear.
  • UI, native and game use cases require runtime evidence such as Playwright, simulator screenshots, logs, build output, deployment URL or gameplay checks.
  • Operations and collaboration use cases require staged drafts: the agent prepares a reviewable artifact first and does not write to external systems without approval.

docs.title: How To Use These Results
docs.text:
• Claims from Context7 are treated as official only when the underlying source is developers.openai.com, github.com/openai/... or openai.github.io/....
  • Recipe-like fragments and architecture examples can move into playbooks as official + experiment because local integration still needs verification.
  • If Context7 and the current official page disagree, verify the official page directly before changing core instructions.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-23: Engineering Standards Layer
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /feature-sliced/documentation Feature-Sliced Design Layer import rule, public API rule on slices, controlled cross-slice exports /storybookjs/storybook Storybook autodocs tag, MDX Doc Blocks, component documentation pattern /oai/openapi-specification/3.1.1 OpenAPI Specification Security Scheme Object and supported scheme types

Findings:

  • FSD guidance should be used in Product-Agent OS only as a UI/default architecture boundary, not as a universal backend standard.
  • Storybook supports docs-as-code for UI states, while accessibility and visual checks remain project-specific gates.
  • OpenAPI findings support machine-readable API contracts and security scheme documentation, but source-of-truth status requires a direct OpenAPI Specification or OpenAPI Initiative link.
  • Direct web verification on 2026-05-23 found the latest published OpenAPI Specification was v3.2.0. The v3.1.1 Context7 query remains a compatibility/security-scheme reference, while core guidance should cite v3.2.0 as the current source.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-23: Documentation Tooling Research
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /websites/docusaurus_io Docusaurus Static documentation site generator, React/MDX orientation, versioned docs structure, versioning cost warning /mkdocs/mkdocs MkDocs Markdown source, YAML config, static HTML build, dev server/live reload, themes/plugins/Markdown extensions /storybookjs/storybook Storybook Autodocs through tags: ['autodocs'], MDX Doc Blocks, a11y parameters and component documentation pattern

Findings:

  • Docusaurus fits React/MDX-heavy product docs, public docs, i18n and versioned documentation, but versioning increases maintenance cost and should not be enabled automatically.
  • MkDocs remains a strong default for small and medium repos: Markdown plus one YAML config and strict static build map well to Product-Agent OS docs-as-code gates.
  • Storybook is both component documentation and a verification surface: stories define component states, Autodocs generates baseline docs, and a11y checks can become CI proposals.
  • Context7 tooling findings do not replace primary documentation links in docs/sources/registry.md; the registry must store official URLs and checked_at.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-24: Large-Project Methodology Section Research
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /feature-sliced/documentation Feature-Sliced Design Layer import rule, slices as business-domain partitions, public API rule and controlled cross-slice exports /storybookjs/storybook Storybook tags: ['autodocs'], !autodocs, MDX documentation templates and Doc Blocks /websites/spec_openapis_oas_v3_2_0 OpenAPI Specification 3.2.0 Components Object, reusable schemas/responses/parameters/examples/security schemes and security scheme examples

Findings:

  • FSD should remain frontend-specific and conditional: useful for growing UI architecture, but not forced onto backend, database, API, LLM or simple MVP work.
  • Storybook should be documented as component documentation and verification surface.
  • OpenAPI 3.2.0 should be the current HTTP API contract source for new API documentation guidance, while project tooling can still require compatibility notes for older versions.
  • Context7 was used as a retrieval layer only. The docs/methodologies/ pages cite primary sources directly and keep source-backed claims in docs/sources/registry.md.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-24: API Integrations Methodology Research
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /websites/spec_openapis_oas_v3_2_0 OpenAPI Specification 3.2.0 Operation Object, Components Object, reusable schemas/responses/parameters/examples/security schemes, operation-level security and deprecation fields /asyncapi/spec AsyncAPI Specification Channels, operations, messages, payload schemas, headers, correlation IDs, examples, reusable components and security schemes /websites/pact_io Pact Consumer-driven contract testing, provider verification, contract-by-example and how Pact complements OpenAPI/AsyncAPI schema contracts

Findings:

  • OpenAPI should be treated as the HTTP API source of truth when an HTTP API has human or machine consumers; generated docs render the contract, not replace it.
  • AsyncAPI should be used or explicitly considered for message-driven APIs, events and webhooks when channel/message semantics matter.
  • Pact complements OpenAPI and AsyncAPI: schema contracts define possible shapes, while consumer-driven contracts capture expectations actually used by consumers.
  • API & Integrations methodology needs gates for contract source, consumer map, compatibility classification, auth/security review, error examples, event delivery semantics, generated client manifest and external write approval.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-24: Backend Methodology Research
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /websites/12factor_net The Twelve-Factor App Codebase, dependencies, config, backing services, build-release-run, stateless processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs and admin processes /websites/opentelemetry_io OpenTelemetry Traces, metrics, logs, baggage, context propagation, instrumentation, collector and telemetry pipeline concepts /websites/kubernetes_io Kubernetes Liveness, readiness and startup probes, including the distinction between process liveness and traffic readiness

Findings:

  • Backend methodology should require runtime behavior documentation, not only module/code structure.
  • Twelve-Factor gives compact default vocabulary for config, dependencies, backing services, process model, logs, disposability and dev/prod parity.
  • OpenTelemetry should be the default cross-stack vocabulary for backend observability contracts.
  • Kubernetes probe semantics are useful as a production-readiness model even outside Kubernetes.
  • Backend readiness gates should cover service boundary, runtime behavior, dependency failure matrix, observability, SLO/gap, health probes, security review, data consistency, config/secrets and rollback.

docs.title: Addendum 2026-05-24: Database Methodology Research
docs.text:
Library ID Purpose Extracted Signal /websites/postgresql PostgreSQL official documentation Transaction isolation, constraints, indexes, EXPLAIN, backup/restore and official documentation scope

Finding:

  • Database methodology needs explicit migration, rollback, restore, indexing, data quality and privacy gates. Generated schema documentation is useful, but it must never expose secrets or production connection details.

docs.title: Project And Code Documentation For A New Engineering Team
docs.text: Source status: mixed source-backed draft Status: incoming deep-research report. Claims are useful for Product-Agent OS design only after primary-source verification and stable source entries in docs/sources/registry.md.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Good documentation is not a folder of files. It is a working knowledge system for the product: what it does, why it is structured that way, how to use its interfaces, how to change code without breaking the system, and how to keep that knowledge current.

Technical documentation guidance converges on a few principles: documentation should be correct, current, understandable, relevant, maintainable, linkable and version-controlled. The more a team can automate generation and checks, the lower the risk of documentation decay.

For a new team, the practical approach is to split documentation into layers:

  • architecture documentation explains system boundaries, component roles and decisions;
  • frontend documentation explains UI components, states, accessibility and design-system boundaries;
  • backend/API documentation explains runtime behavior, API contracts, errors, auth and operational behavior;
  • database documentation explains tables, columns, relationships, migrations and data rules;
  • release documentation explains what changed and how to roll back.

Architecture work benefits from ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 concepts, C4, arc42 and ADR. C4 provides context, container, component and optional code views. arc42 provides a ready structure for architecture communication. ADRs preserve one important decision, its context and consequences.

docs.title: Assumptions And Default Approach
docs.text:
The original request did not specify backend language, frontend framework, repository shape, public API status, team size or whether public docs are required. The default recommended setup is therefore:

Situation Starting Point Best Fit Small product or internal service MkDocs + Markdown + Mermaid + GitHub Pages-like hosting Simple setup, fast start and low infrastructure cost JS/TS product with rich UI Docusaurus + Storybook + TypeDoc/JSDoc + OpenAPI Product docs close to frontend components and MDX Python-heavy backend Sphinx + autodoc + Read the Docs or internal CI publishing Docstrings, generated API reference and cross-links Multirepo or enterprise documentation Antora + AsciiDoc + ADR + C4/Structurizr Documentation assembled from multiple repos and versions Database-heavy system DBML/dbdocs or SchemaSpy + migration tooling Frequently changing schema and a need for readable relation maps

Repository-local Markdown is a good baseline. If the organization needs a single portal over several repositories, the portal should aggregate source-controlled docs rather than become a parallel source of truth.

docs.title: Documentation Taxonomy
docs.text: Documentation Type Purpose Audience Update Trigger Typical Formats And Tools Project README Fast entry: what this is, how to run it, where to find more New developers, reviewers, DevOps Startup flow, structure or link changes Root Markdown Architecture overview System boundaries, external dependencies, containers and constraints Whole team, tech leads, architects, QA Architecture, integration or NFR changes arc42, C4, Mermaid, PlantUML, Structurizr ADR One meaningful decision and its consequences Developers, architects, future maintainers Architecturally significant decisions Markdown ADR, MADR UI component docs Purpose, props, states, accessibility and examples Frontend, QA, designers Component or design-system changes Storybook, MDX, JSDoc, TypeDoc HTTP API contract Resources, operations, schemas, auth and errors Backend, frontend, integrators, QA Every API change OpenAPI, Swagger UI, Redoc/Redocly Event/message contract Channels, messages, payload and producer/consumer roles Backend, integrations, platform team Every event contract change AsyncAPI Code reference Module/class/function interface and constraints Developers, sometimes SDK consumers Public interface changes JSDoc, TypeDoc, Sphinx, pydoc, Javadoc, C# XML docs Database docs Table, column, relation, migration and constraint meaning Backend, data/BI, DBA, analysts Schema changes DBML, dbdocs, SchemaSpy, SQL comments Changelog User-visible changes by version Users, support, team Every release Keep a Changelog + SemVer

docs.title: Architecture Documentation
docs.text:
Architecture documentation should answer three questions:

  1. Who are the stakeholders?
  2. What concerns do they have?
  3. Which views of the system answer those concerns?

For a new team, keep the first version small:

  • one overview page;
  • one C4 System Context diagram;
  • one C4 Container diagram;
  • a list of integrations;
  • an ADR index;
  • a short page for quality attributes and risks.

Recommended workflow:

  1. Create docs/architecture/overview.md.
  2. State the business purpose, primary users and external systems.
  3. Draw a System Context diagram.
  4. Draw a Container diagram for frontend, backend services, queue, database, cache, file storage and communication channels.
  5. Add three to five lines per container: responsibility, technology, inputs/outputs and constraints.
  6. Create an ADR for hard-to-reverse decisions such as database choice, queue, API standard, auth model, monorepo/multirepo or migration strategy.
  7. Add quality-attributes.md for performance, availability, security, observability, localization, accessibility and data requirements.
  8. Require architecture docs updates when a PR changes boundaries, integrations or critical NFRs.

Minimal architecture page template:

# Architecture Overview

## System Purpose
Short description of the business problem.

## Users And External Systems
- User A
- Operator B
- Payment provider
- Email provider

## Containers
| Container | Responsibility | Technology | Stores Data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Web app | UI and client logic | React/Vue/... | No |
| API service | Business logic | Node/Python/Java/... | No |
| Database | Persistent data | PostgreSQL/... | Yes |

## Key Constraints
- SLA
- Security or privacy constraints
- Performance constraints
- Deployment constraints

## Related ADRs
- ADR-0001 ...

docs.title: ADR Example
docs.text:
# ADR-0003 Choose OpenAPI As The REST API Contract

## Context
Frontend, backend and QA need one machine-readable source for operations, schemas, auth and errors.

## Decision
Use OpenAPI as the source contract for HTTP API changes.

## Consequences

### Pros
- Enables generated docs and contract checks.
- Gives frontend and QA a stable reference.
- Makes breaking changes easier to identify.

### Cons
- Requires regular maintenance.
- Can drift from implementation if not checked.

docs.title: Frontend Documentation
docs.text:
Frontend documentation should explain components and user-visible states, not just list files. Storybook is a strong default when a team has reusable components or design-system work. MDX and Doc Blocks can add narrative where automatic docs are insufficient.

Minimum component card:

# Button

## Purpose
Primary command trigger used in forms and toolbars.

## Use
- Primary action on a page or modal.
- Secondary action inside dense UI.

## Do Not Use
- As a navigation link when a link is semantically correct.

## Props
| Prop | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| variant | primary/secondary/danger | Visual intent |
| disabled | boolean | Prevents interaction |

## States
- default
- hover/focus
- disabled
- loading

## Accessibility
Keyboard focus visible, accessible name required.

## Related Code
`src/shared/ui/button`

For product UI, docs should include route/page, user flow, component variants, empty/loading/error states, accessibility notes, responsive behavior and Storybook links when available.

docs.title: Backend And API Documentation
docs.text:
Backend docs should cover runtime behavior, not only code structure:

  • service boundary and responsibility;
  • dependencies and failure modes;
  • API contract and error model;
  • auth and permission model;
  • configuration and secrets boundary;
  • observability: logs, metrics, traces, health checks;
  • rollback and recovery;
  • operational runbook.

HTTP APIs should use OpenAPI when humans or machines consume them. Event-driven APIs should use or explicitly consider AsyncAPI. Consumer-driven contract tests such as Pact can complement schema contracts when consumer expectations matter.

Minimal API docs should include:

# API Contract

Source contract: `openapi.yaml`

## Auth
...

## Error Model
...

## Compatibility Policy
...

## Verification
- Contract lint command
- Consumer/provider test command

docs.title: Database Documentation
docs.text:
Database docs should explain meaning, not only schema shape:

  • table purpose;
  • primary keys and foreign keys;
  • important columns;
  • business rules;
  • indexes and query assumptions;
  • migration history;
  • data retention and privacy notes;
  • backup/restore expectations.

Example:

# orders

## Purpose
Stores customer purchase records.

## Keys And Relations
- `id`: primary key
- `customer_id`: references `customers.id`

## Important Fields
- `status`: draft, paid, cancelled, refunded
- `created_at`: order creation time

## Business Rules
- Paid orders cannot be deleted.
- Refunds require an audit record.

## Change History
- 2026-05-01: added refund status.

DBML/dbdocs and SchemaSpy can generate useful views, but generated database docs must not expose secrets, connection strings or private production data.

docs.title: Documentation Process
docs.text:
Documentation should move through the same control loop as code:

  1. Identify the change type.
  2. Determine affected docs.
  3. Update source docs, not generated output first.
  4. Run docs checks/builds.
  5. Record evidence in TEST/RUNLOG.
  6. Keep generated HTML as review output, not source of truth.

For Product-Agent OS, every workflow should name:

  • inputs;
  • outputs;
  • owner;
  • verification;
  • risks;
  • next artifact.

docs.title: Tooling Recommendations
docs.text: Need Recommended Tooling Small internal docs portal MkDocs Product docs with MDX/React Docusaurus Python reference docs Sphinx + autodoc UI component docs Storybook HTTP API contract OpenAPI Event/message contract AsyncAPI Database schema docs DBML/dbdocs or SchemaSpy Architecture diagrams Mermaid for simple docs, Structurizr for C4-as-code, PlantUML for UML-heavy teams Release notes Keep a Changelog + SemVer Prose/style lint Vale when team style rules exist Markdown structure lint markdownlint or project-specific docs checks

docs.title: Multi-Agent Documentation Workflow
docs.text:
For a multi-agent system, split ownership by artifact type:

Role Ownership Output Product Manager Requirements, user journey, metrics REQUIREMENTS.md, metric spec Architect Boundaries, ADRs, diagrams architecture overview, ADRs Builder Code and local docs updates implementation diff Tester Tests/evals and evidence TEST.md, EVALS.md, run output Docs Maintainer IA, source status, links, localization docs pages, registry updates Release Operator Release notes and rollback release packet, RUNLOG

Each handoff should return sources used, assumptions, files touched, verification evidence, open risks and the recommended next role.

docs.title: Product-Agent OS Implications
docs.text:
Product-Agent OS should:

  • prefer behavior-level documentation over tool hype;
  • route docs tooling by project stack and maturity;
  • keep external hosting, CI activation and DB introspection approval-bound;
  • treat generated docs and dashboards as review surfaces, not source of truth;
  • keep source-backed claims in docs/sources/registry.md;
  • require Source status: on non-index docs pages;
  • preserve official OpenAI terms such as Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, subagents, skills, AGENTS.md, memory, sandbox, approvals, MCP and Agents SDK.

docs.title: Checklist For A New Team
docs.text:
1. Create README and architecture overview.
  2. Add C4 context/container diagrams.
  3. Start ADR index.
  4. Define API contracts with OpenAPI/AsyncAPI when applicable.
  5. Document core UI components and states.
  6. Add database dictionary for persistent data.
  7. Define docs build/check command.
  8. Add ownership and review rules.
  9. Keep generated output separate from source docs.
  10. Record verification evidence after each meaningful docs slice.

docs.title: Source Families Used
docs.text:
• C4 model and arc42 for architecture views.
  • ADR/MADR for decisions.
  • OpenAPI and AsyncAPI for contracts.
  • Storybook, TypeDoc, JSDoc, Sphinx, Javadoc and C# XML docs for component/code reference docs.
  • DBML/dbdocs and SchemaSpy for database docs.
  • MkDocs, Docusaurus, Antora and Read the Docs for docs portals.
  • GitHub Actions, CODEOWNERS, Vale, markdownlint, Keep a Changelog and SemVer for process and governance.

docs.title: Research Method
docs.text:
Use the same protocol for each methodology or tool:

  1. Find a primary or official source.
  2. Extract five to ten verifiable claims without promoting community summaries to rules.
  3. Label each claim as official, methodology, tool convention, community or experiment.
  4. Map applicability to web/front-end, native/mobile, desktop, backend/API, data, AI/evals, docs and operations.
  5. Connect the claim to a Product-Agent OS template, workflow, skill, eval, discovery signal, docs page or staged CI proposal.
  6. Record failure modes: where the method is harmful, excessive or requires a human decision.
  7. Add a verification surface: test, eval gate, docs check, contract check, browser/runtime check or review checklist.

docs.title: Development Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology Short Description Primary Sources Product-Agent OS Signal Agentic / AI-native development SDLC work where Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, subagents and skills help plan, build, test, review and document changes while a human keeps ownership of architecture, product and quality. Codex build plugins, Agent Skills, Building an AI-Native Engineering Team, Codex AI app evals Require scoped inputs, ownership, tests/evals, source policy, approval policy, run evidence and the promotion path manual workflow -> skill -> plugin -> automation. Data-informed development Product decisions made through goals, signals, metrics, guardrails and post-release learning. Google HEART paper, Amplitude North Star Use metric specs, guardrail metrics, privacy notes and anti-Goodhart protection. Do not confuse it with Domain-Driven Design. Domain-Driven Design Modeling complex business logic around a domain model, ubiquitous language and bounded contexts. Martin Fowler: Domain-Driven Design, Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Domain Language Apply only when domain complexity justifies it. Require a glossary, bounded contexts, aggregate/event choices only when useful, and explicit mapping to architecture boundaries. TDD Red-Green-Refactor loop: write a failing test, implement the smallest code that passes, then refactor with tests green. Agile Alliance TDD Require red -> green -> refactor evidence in RUNLOG or an explicit gap, especially for bug fixes and shared behavior. ATDD Acceptance tests written before implementation with product/customer, development and testing perspectives. Agile Alliance ATDD Connect REQUIREMENTS.md and TEST.md through acceptance scenarios before code changes. BDD Behavior scenarios and business outcomes expressed in a shared language for domain experts, testers and developers. Agile Alliance BDD Use for user behavior and business rules. It complements, but does not replace, unit/integration/contract tests. Feature-Sliced Design Frontend architecture methodology using layers, slices, segments, public API and import rules. Feature-Sliced Design documentation Treat as a strong default for growing UI apps, but do not force it onto backend/native/simple MVP work. Eval-driven AI development Repeatable eval suites for prompt/model/tool/RAG/agent behavior before changing production behavior. Codex AI app evals, OpenAI eval best practices Require a baseline, target path, no-secrets fixtures, assertions, run command and threshold. Docs-as-code Documentation lives with code, changes through review, and is built/checked as part of engineering workflow. GitLab documentation architecture, GitHub Actions workflows, GitHub protected branches Stage docs CI/CODEOWNERS proposals, but never enable external workflows without approval.

docs.title: Initial Gaps For Product-Agent OS
docs.text: Gap Why It Matters Research Action Conditional DDD, bounded context, ubiquitous language, FSD, metrics, evidence-before-completion, docs tooling and readiness statuses are now represented, but semantic sufficiency still needs owner review. Artifacts prove shape and traceability, not the correctness of domain terms, UI boundaries, metrics or evidence interpretation. Continue routing semantic sufficiency to owner review and accepted-gap records. ATDD/BDD need durable acceptance-scenario quality. Scenarios connect product requirements to test/eval-first work better than a generic checklist. Keep acceptance-scenarios.md and require product/development/testing review for important behavior. Docs tooling decisions need stack-aware routing. MkDocs, Docusaurus, Sphinx, Antora, Storybook, OpenAPI, DBML, Mermaid, PlantUML and Structurizr have different maintenance costs. Keep docs-tooling-decision.md and record present_unverified until commands run. Metrics need privacy and anti-Goodhart guardrails. One metric can distort behavior and telemetry can create privacy risk. Keep counter-metric, guardrail, qualitative review, retention and owner signoff fields. CI/CODEOWNERS/docs lint stay proposal-only. This preserves approval boundaries for external workflows and governance changes. Use explicit proposed_not_enabled or equivalent status in CI/governance templates.

docs.title: B34-I18N-M24 Architecture Decision
docs.text:
Decision: use mkdocs-static-i18n with suffix structure.

Rationale:

  • Material for MkDocs supports a header language selector through alternate language links.
  • mkdocs-static-i18n supports default language output at the site root and localized output under each locale path.
  • The suffix structure keeps the current RU page as the canonical base file and stores EN equivalents as *.en.md siblings.
  • fallback_to_default: false prevents untranslated RU pages from being copied into the EN output and avoids duplicate fallback pollution in search.

Configuration contract:

i18n_architecture:
  plugin: mkdocs-static-i18n
  docs_structure: suffix
  ru_default_at_site_root: true
  en_under: /en/
  fallback_to_default: false
  reconfigure_material: true
  reconfigure_search: false

Status terms for verification after the full-site B34E M47 correction: RU default at site root, EN under /en/, fallback_to_default: false, reconfigure_material: true, reconfigure_search: false.

docs.title: B34-I18N-M25 Build And Switcher

  • locale: ru as the default build at /;
  • locale: en as the English build at /en/;
  • Material language switcher links for RU and EN;
  • localized EN navigation over the public-ready page set;
  • localized site_name and site_description values;
  • search configuration with fallback protection through fallback_to_default: false and full-site page parity through reconfigure_search: false.

The language switcher is a documentation UI affordance only. It is not runtime automation and does not imply publication.

RU pages remain the canonical base pages. The RU localization policy is:

EN pages must be complete product-facing equivalents, not fallback placeholders. They keep matching structure, links and product claims, while avoiding Cyrillic text and internal implementation ledger terms.

docs.text:

docs.title: Common Approval Fields
docs.text:
Every Batch 35 action must define:

docs.title: Product-Agent OS: final pre-development review
docs.text:
Source status: implementation planning + critical review

Date: 2026-05-23. Based on the Track 8 detailed backlog, the gap matrix, Track 6/7 implementation notes and scenario review of Product-Agent OS.

docs.title: Final critical review
docs.text:
The Product-Agent OS idea is strong: the plugin turns Codex from a local task executor into a governed engineering operating layer. Its main value is not that the plugin knows OpenAPI, Docusaurus, DBML or Storybook, but that it can understand project context, choose applicable standards, create staged artifacts, connect work to tests/evals/docs and avoid dangerous external actions without approval.

Strengths of the current backlog:

  • Clear separation of concerns: methodologies, standards/specs, documentation tooling, discovery, readiness gates, lifecycle skills and verification.
  • A staged-first safety model: the plugin proposes artifacts and checks, but does not silently enable CI, hooks, hosted docs, DB introspection or automations.
  • Applicability statuses instead of a primitive present/missing model, so Docusaurus, PlantUML, DBML, Storybook and similar tools do not become dogma.
  • Scenario workflows for three important entry points: bug rescue, greenfield idea and complex system acceleration.
  • A test-first implementation plan: new behavior changes must start with failing tests.

Critical risks before implementation:

Risk Why it is dangerous How to close it in the backlog Artifact explosion The user may receive too many files and lose momentum. Introduce a per-mode minimum artifact set and progressive disclosure: minimum first, then advanced proposals. False confidence A template can look like quality even when runtime verification has not run. Distinguish present_unverified from present_verified everywhere; final responses must require command evidence. Over-governance The plugin may start requiring enterprise artifacts for a small MVP. Use applicability statuses, lightweight mode and not_applicable with a reason. Mode ambiguity One project can be bug rescue, complex system and security-sensitive at the same time. Introduce usage_mode.primary, usage_mode.secondary, confidence and routing reasons. Tool detection false positives A domain/ folder, .stories.* files or docs/ do not prove mature methodology. Discovery must distinguish signal presence, maturity evidence and verification command. Secrets/data exposure DB docs, integrations, env examples and logs may contain secrets or customer data. Use secrets-safe inspection rules, redaction fields and approval gates for DB/external systems. Weak user experience If the plugin dumps every gate in the first response, the user will leave. Use a scenario-specific first response and a short mode summary: what I found, what I need, next smallest step. Missing plugin success metrics There is no way to know whether the plugin makes work materially faster or better. Add a metric spec for the plugin itself: time-to-first-useful-artifact, false positive gate rate and rescue resolution rate. Runtime diversity Web/API are covered better than mobile, desktop, CI, security, release and legacy onboarding. Add 10 additional usage scenarios and fixture coverage. Apply path ambiguity Staging exists, but the user needs a clear path from proposal to approved apply. Explicitly state the approval/apply/rollback boundary in every scenario workflow.

Final conclusion: Track 8 is ready for implementation only after the scenario matrix is expanded. Methodologies and tooling are already organized well, but the plugin must be tested against typical real-life situations, not only against a list of standards.

docs.title: Addendum: behavioral evals and Codex-only scope
docs.text:
After comparative analysis of obra/superpowers, the backlog needs behavioral workflow evals inside the Codex-only scope, not multi-harness adapters. Product-Agent OS must verify correct plugin behavior in Codex App, CLI, IDE extension and .codex-plugin: route selection, first response, shortcut resistance, root-cause bug rescue, no-placeholder plans, two-stage review, fresh-context handoffs and finish options.

Constraint: ideas from Superpowers are used as community/opensource intake, not as a source of truth. Product-Agent OS must not add mandatory Claude/Cursor/OpenCode/Gemini adapters, aggressive always-on hooks or unconditional skill triggers. Any session-start/bootstrap logic remains a staged, approval-bound Codex hook proposal.

docs.title: 1. PR review before merge
docs.text:
Context: a developer opened a PR and wants to quickly check risks before review.

Plugin:

  1. Audits the diff/changed files.
  2. Classifies the mode as pr_review.
  3. Builds a risk map: behavior, API, DB, UI, security, docs, release impact.
  4. Checks acceptance scenarios and tests/evals coverage.
  5. If an API is touched, requires an OpenAPI/AsyncAPI update or explicit gap.
  6. If a public contract exists, requires changelog/SemVer impact.
  7. Returns a review packet: findings, missing checks, commands to run, docs impact, release risk.

docs.title: 2. Legacy repo onboarding and documentation debt
docs.text:
Context: a team received an old repository with no current documentation.

Plugin:

  1. Performs a read-only inventory.
  2. Classifies the mode as legacy_onboarding.
  3. Builds a system map: entry points, services, scripts, tests, config, docs, known risks.
  4. Does not try to rewrite code immediately.
  5. Creates a staged onboarding-map.md: how to run, where architecture boundaries are, where the source of truth is missing.
  6. Proposes a minimum docs set: README, architecture overview, runbook, docs tooling decision.
  7. Marks claims as present_unverified until commands have been run.

docs.title: 3. API contract migration
docs.text:
Context: an HTTP API must be changed or versioned.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as api_migration.
  2. Finds OpenAPI/Swagger tooling, generated clients, consumers and integration tests.
  3. Creates a migration plan: backward compatibility, breaking changes, deprecation, examples, auth/errors.
  4. Updates the API contract proposal before code.
  5. Requires contract tests and client impact review.
  6. Adds release/version impact and a changelog section.

docs.title: 4. AI/RAG quality regression
docs.text:
Context: an AI feature started answering worse, retrieval is wrong or hallucination risk increased.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as ai_eval_regression.
  2. Does not edit the prompt blindly.
  3. Creates/updates ai-eval-spec.md: dataset, baseline, rubric, thresholds, no-secrets policy.
  4. Runs or proposes an eval command.
  5. Changes only one factor per cycle: prompt, retrieval, reranker, chunking, model or tool.
  6. Compares baseline vs new result and logs residual risk.

docs.title: 5. Mobile/native feature with permissions and offline states
docs.text:
Context: a feature must be added to an iOS/Android/native app.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as native_mobile_feature.
  2. Checks platform build commands, simulator/emulator assumptions, permissions, offline states and screenshots/logs.
  3. Creates acceptance scenarios for flows and permission states.
  4. Requires runtime verification beyond code inspection.
  5. The docs tooling selector does not force web tooling unless shared docs exist.

docs.title: 6. Desktop/local-first app with filesystem and background jobs
docs.text:
Context: a desktop app works with a local DB, filesystem, indexer or background tasks.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as desktop_local_first.
  2. Builds a risk map: filesystem permissions, local DB migration, indexing, privacy, long-running work, app logs.
  3. Creates architecture boundary and data protection notes.
  4. Requires a runtime check: app launch, logs, sample file path, rollback of local data migration.
  5. Documentation records user data handling and recovery path.

docs.title: 7. Database migration and data model change
docs.text:
Context: schema, migration, retention, backfill or a critical query changes.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as data_migration.
  2. Requires a migration plan before implementation.
  3. Updates the database dictionary/DBML proposal.
  4. Checks PII/sensitive fields, retention, backfill, rollback and data quality checks.
  5. Does not run DB introspection or production DB commands without approval.

docs.title: 8. Security/auth/payment-sensitive change
docs.text:
Context: auth, permissions, payments, secrets, personal data or external writes are affected.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as security_sensitive_change.
  2. Strengthens the reasoning/review path and stop conditions.
  3. Creates a security risk review: threat surface, authz/authn, sensitive fields, abuse controls, rollback.
  4. Requires explicit approval for external writes and secret-sensitive operations.
  5. Does not store secrets in artifacts.

docs.title: 9. CI stabilization and flaky tests
docs.text:
Context: CI fails intermittently, tests are flaky or the build pipeline is unreliable.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as ci_stabilization.
  2. Collects failure evidence: job, command, logs, timing, environment.
  3. Separates deterministic failures from flaky symptoms.
  4. Proposes the smallest isolation plan: reproduce locally, narrow the test, stabilize dependency/time/network assumptions.
  5. Does not change GitHub Actions settings without approval.

docs.title: 10. Package, SDK, plugin or open-source release
docs.text:
Context: a public release artifact must be prepared.

Plugin:

  1. Classifies the mode as release_packaging.
  2. Checks public API, SemVer impact, changelog, docs, examples, package metadata and license/security notes.
  3. Requires tests/build/docs evidence.
  4. Prepares a release packet and rollback notes.
  5. Does not publish a package/release/tag without explicit approval.

docs.text: Category Additions Usage modes pr_review, legacy_onboarding, api_migration, ai_eval_regression, native_mobile_feature, desktop_local_first, data_migration, security_sensitive_change, ci_stabilization, release_packaging. Readiness gates PR risk review, migration plan, security review, native/desktop runtime verification, CI evidence, release readiness, plugin success metrics. docs.title: Track 8 goal
docs.text:
Make Product-Agent OS capable not only of generating control-plane artifacts, but also of selecting and verifying engineering methodologies, standards and documentation tooling based on project context:

  • methodologies: Agentic / AI-native development, TDD, ATDD, BDD, DDD, FSD, data-informed development, eval-driven AI development, docs-as-code;

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Do not install external tools automatically.
  • Do not turn Product-Agent OS into a multi-harness adapter. Track 8 checks only Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, .codex-plugin, bundled skills, Context7 MCP config and staged hook templates.
  • Do not enable CI, hooks, CODEOWNERS, hosted docs, GitHub Actions or automations without explicit approval.
  • Do not enable aggressive always-on skill triggers or session-start hooks without a staged proposal and explicit approval.
  • Do not make Docusaurus, PlantUML, DBML, Storybook or any other tool mandatory for every project.
  • Do not replace the runtime verification checklist with mere document presence.
  • Do not move community claims into core guidance without source status and verification status.
  • Do not start broad bug fixing without reproduction evidence, ownership boundary and rollback notes.
  • Do not scaffold an empty project before explicit approval of the chosen product/architecture direction.
  • Do not access external integrations, production DB, hosted docs, CI settings or secret-bearing configs without explicit approval.
  • Do not publish packages, releases, tags, docs sites, GitHub changes or external tickets without explicit approval.
  • Do not treat discovered logs, folders, package scripts or docs evidence as verified without a command, exit code and owner/reviewer evidence.

docs.title: Applicability model
docs.text:
Every methodology, standard or tool should receive one of these statuses instead of a boolean present/missing:

Status Meaning not_applicable Not needed for the current stack, scale or change. applicable_missing Needed but not found; requires a staged proposal or explicit gap. present_unverified Found, but the verification command is unknown or has not run. present_verified Found and backed by current verification/artifact evidence. proposal_staged A proposal is prepared but not applied to the project. approval_required Requires approval: external write, CI activation, hosted docs, DB access, secrets-sensitive operation. explicit_gap_accepted The gap is recorded and accepted by the owner as a temporary decision.

docs.title: Usage mode model
docs.text:
usage_mode should be composite because real tasks often intersect multiple scenarios: for example, bug rescue inside a complex system or a security-sensitive API migration.

Field Meaning primary Main mode that determines the first response and minimum artifacts. secondary Additional modes that add gates without changing the primary workflow. confidence low, medium, high; at low confidence the plugin should ask a short clarifying question or choose a safe fallback. reasons 2-5 facts from the workspace/user prompt explaining why the mode was selected. fallback Safe mode when classification is disputed, usually standard_feature or maintenance. first_response_contract What the plugin says or asks on the first turn: selected mode, evidence gap, approval boundary and next smallest action. minimum_artifacts Minimum staged artifact set for the mode; advanced proposals appear only when needed or approved. behavioral_eval_cases Prompt/session fixtures proving correct route, stop condition and absence of forbidden behavior.

Minimum initial modes:

bug_rescue
greenfield_idea
complex_system_acceleration
pr_review
legacy_onboarding
api_migration
ai_eval_regression
native_mobile_feature
desktop_local_first
data_migration
security_sensitive_change
ci_stabilization
release_packaging
standard_feature
docs_only
maintenance
