docs.title: Quality, Testing & Evals Methodology Research
docs.text:
Source status: official + expert reference + vendor documentation + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Target methodology page: ../../methodologies/quality-testing-evals.md

Target Product-Agent OS behavior: route every meaningful change through the smallest useful verification path, require current evidence before completion claims, separate deterministic tests from subjective evals, and block risky work when traceability, runtime evidence, contract checks or residual-risk records are missing.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers deterministic tests, acceptance scenarios, contract tests, integration/runtime tests, browser/mobile/native evidence, documentation checks, AI and subjective evals, CI quality gates, flaky test management, coverage, mutation/property-based testing, manual QA evidence and evidence-before-completion.

It does not mandate one test runner, 100 percent coverage, universal TDD, universal E2E testing or mandatory AI evals for every project. The method selects checks by product risk, architecture surface, user-visible behavior, data sensitivity and release impact.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• Agile Alliance defines Test-Driven Development (TDD) as a cycle where tests are written before programming and coding, unit testing and refactoring are intertwined.
  • Agile Alliance defines Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD) as expressing acceptance tests before implementation through customer, developer and tester perspectives.
  • Agile Alliance describes Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) as using executable scenarios and shared behavior language to improve communication across business, testing and development.
  • The practical Test Pyramid guidance emphasizes a balanced portfolio with tests at different granularity, many fast lower-level tests and fewer high-level tests.
  • Modern frontend guidance such as the Testing Trophy emphasizes static checks and integration tests for browser-oriented applications, but it is an expert heuristic, not a universal standard.
  • ISTQB Foundation Level guidance separates confirmation testing from regression testing, recommends impact analysis for regression scope and treats automated regression tests as a good fit for CI.
  • pytest documentation states that pytest supports small readable tests, assertion introspection, auto-discovery, modular fixtures, parametrization, CI guidance and flaky-test guidance.
  • Vitest documentation describes watch mode for development, run mode in CI, projects, snapshots, coverage through V8 or Istanbul, browser mode and isolation tradeoffs.
  • Playwright Test supports retries, classifies tests as passed, flaky or failed, and can capture traces on retry. Trace Viewer, screenshots and visual comparisons provide browser runtime evidence.
  • Playwright visual comparison guidance requires stable environments for reliable screenshot baselines.
  • Pact documents consumer-driven contract testing and provider verification for HTTP and message integrations.
  • Stryker mutation testing changes code under test and checks whether the test suite detects the mutants; mutation score is a signal about test effectiveness, not product correctness by itself.
  • Hypothesis is a property-based testing library for Python that generates examples from stated properties and can reveal edge cases missed by example-based tests.
  • GitHub Actions workflow syntax defines CI jobs, events, permissions, environments, matrix runs and reusable workflow structures. GITHUB_TOKEN permissions should be scoped deliberately.
  • Code coverage measures executed code, but coverage alone does not prove requirements, critical paths, contracts or user-visible behavior.
  • OpenAI evaluation guidance treats evals as systematic tests for AI applications and agent workflows, with datasets, graders, thresholds and regression loops.
  • Codex AI app eval guidance recommends adding a runnable eval suite before prompt, model, retrieval or agent changes merge.
  • Promptfoo provides declarative LLM app evaluation and red-team workflows with assertions, CI usage and metrics.
  • Ragas documents RAG and agent metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall and tool call accuracy.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• Product-Agent OS should generate framework-neutral quality artifacts first, then specialize to pytest, Vitest, Playwright, JUnit, Promptfoo, Ragas or other stack tools when detected.
  • Completion evidence should live in RUNLOG.md or a slice-specific evidence packet, while durable strategy belongs in TEST.md and EVALS.md.
  • CI is a verification surface, not an approval surface. Creating or changing external CI workflows should remain staged until explicitly approved.
  • Coverage thresholds are useful only when paired with requirement, critical-path and regression coverage.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "More tests always means better quality." The useful signal is risk coverage, fast feedback and failure usefulness.
  • "100 percent line coverage proves correctness." It does not prove assertions, behavior, contracts or user outcomes.
  • "E2E tests are the most realistic, so they should dominate." High-level tests are valuable but slower and more brittle.
  • "Manual QA is not evidence." Manual QA can be evidence when it has a charter, criteria, environment and captured result.
  • "AI evals are optional for AI behavior changes." For AI-facing behavior, prompt/model/retrieval/tool changes need baseline or explicit baseline gap.

docs.title: Methodologies
docs.text: Methodology When to apply Project-level behavior TDD / Red-Green-Refactor Deterministic logic, bugfixes, parser/validator/business rules Write failing test, run failure, implement minimal fix, rerun pass, refactor with tests green. ATDD / BDD Product behavior, workflow, business rules Acceptance scenario maps requirement to executable check or explicit manual/eval evidence. Test portfolio design Any non-trivial project Select static, unit, integration, contract, E2E, manual and eval checks by risk and feedback speed. Risk-based testing Time, CI budget or risk is constrained Prioritize checks by user impact, change risk, data/security exposure and historical failure rate. Confirmation and regression testing Bugfixes, migrations, refactors, dependency changes Reproduce original failure, prove fix, then check impacted unchanged behavior. Contract testing APIs, events, generated clients, external consumers Validate provider/consumer expectations and compatibility before integration or release claims. Integration testing Behavior depends on database, filesystem, queue, network or service boundary Exercise real or high-fidelity dependencies with reset strategy and failure evidence. E2E/runtime testing User-visible workflow or platform-specific behavior Browser/simulator/API/runtime path evidence with logs, screenshots, traces or reports. Visual and accessibility testing UI layout, design system or custom widget behavior Stable screenshots, component states, keyboard/focus/a11y checks and accepted diffs. Property-based testing Invariants, parsers, serializers, permissions, math, state transitions Generate many inputs from declared properties and keep shrinking/failing examples. Mutation testing Tests pass but assertion quality is uncertain Mutate source behavior and inspect surviving mutants for weak assertions or missing cases. Flaky test management Intermittent failures, timing, network, parallelism, browser tests Classify source, isolate, quarantine only with owner and expiry, keep flaky evidence visible. CI quality gates Shared branches, PRs, releases, packages Run deterministic checks with scoped permissions, artifacts, exact commands and exit codes. Eval-driven quality AI, docs, UX, search relevance, subjective outputs Dataset, rubric, grader, threshold, baseline/current run and failure review. Exploratory testing New workflows, unknown risk, usability, edge discovery Time-boxed charter, environment, notes, findings and follow-up checks. Evidence-before-completion Every meaningful slice Current command/eval/runtime/manual evidence or explicit inspection-only gap before success claims.

docs.title: Documentation artifacts and standards
docs.text: Artifact Purpose Candidate location Test strategy Quality model, test portfolio, risk tiers, ownership and CI gates. TEST.md Test/eval matrix Requirement to scenario to check to evidence owner mapping. test-eval-matrix.md Acceptance scenarios Business/user behavior expressed as examples with expected and forbidden outcomes. acceptance-scenarios.md Red-Green-Refactor log Bug or deterministic behavior proof with failing and passing command evidence. RUNLOG.md, red-green-refactor-log.md Bug reproduction record Original failure, reproduction steps, environment, fixture and fixed evidence. bug-reproduction.md Risk-based test plan Risk areas, impact, likelihood, selected checks and accepted gaps. risk-based-test-plan.md Regression impact map Changed files/contracts/data and impacted behavior to rerun. regression-impact-map.md Contract test map API/event/schema contracts, consumers, providers and verification command. contract-test-map.md Runtime evidence packet Browser/API/native/desktop/server command, environment, logs, screenshots and traces. runtime-evidence.md Visual/a11y evidence packet Viewports, component states, screenshots, accepted diffs, keyboard/focus/a11y result. visual-a11y-evidence.md Coverage policy Coverage type, threshold, excluded files, critical-path mapping and non-goals. coverage-policy.md Mutation test report Scope, mutation score, surviving mutants, ignored mutants and follow-up tests. mutation-test-report.md Property test spec Invariants, input generators, shrink/failure examples and seed handling. property-test-spec.md Flaky test ledger Test, symptom, suspected source, owner, quarantine expiry and rerun evidence. flaky-test-ledger.md CI quality gate proposal Jobs, permissions, triggers, artifacts, cache, matrix and rollback. ci-quality-gates.md Eval spec Objective, dataset, grader, rubric, threshold, command and owner. EVALS.md, ai-eval-spec.md Eval run report Baseline/current score, passing/failing cases, regressions and residual risk. eval-run-report.md Manual QA charter Scope, environment, checklist, notes, findings and reviewer. manual-qa-charter.md Completion evidence packet Commands run, exit codes, outputs, artifacts, accepted gaps and residual risks. RUNLOG.md, evidence-packet.md

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Start each slice by naming the user-visible behavior or technical contract that needs evidence.
  2. Choose the smallest useful verification path. A pure parser may need unit/property tests; a checkout flow may need integration/E2E; an AI answer may need evals.
  3. Map every acceptance criterion to a deterministic check, contract check, runtime check, eval, manual charter or explicit gap.
  4. For bugfixes, capture reproduction evidence first when feasible. If reproduction is impossible, record the gap and risk before changing code.
  5. Use TDD when behavior is deterministic and the failure can be expressed cheaply. Do not force TDD for exploratory UI, visual design or ambiguous product discovery.
  6. Keep test layers purposeful. Unit tests check local rules, integration tests check collaboration, contract tests check compatibility, E2E tests check user/runtime path.
  7. For API or event changes, require contract source and consumer/provider verification or an explicit compatibility gap.
  8. For UI changes, capture runtime evidence for layout, responsive states, interaction, keyboard/focus and accessibility when relevant.
  9. For native/mobile/desktop changes, use platform build/run/log/screenshot evidence rather than code inspection only.
  10. For AI, search, ranking, docs quality or subjective behavior, use eval datasets, rubrics, graders and thresholds.
  11. Use coverage as a gap-finding tool, not as the only quality target. Pair coverage with requirement and critical-path coverage.
  12. Use mutation/property-based testing when ordinary examples are likely to miss edge cases or weak assertions.
  13. Treat flaky tests as product-quality debt. Retries may collect evidence, but they do not remove the need to classify and fix the cause.
  14. CI changes should specify triggers, permissions, artifacts, cache, matrix, failure behavior and rollback. External CI mutation requires explicit approval.
  15. Manual QA must name charter, environment, evidence and reviewer. "Manual review" alone is not enough.
  16. Do not claim "works", "tested", "verified", "ready" or "quality improved" without current evidence from this run or an explicit inspection-only gap.
  17. Record residual risk in RUNLOG.md, EVALS.md or release packet so the next role does not inherit hidden assumptions.

docs.title: Candidate eval fields
docs.text:
• Every acceptance criterion maps to a check, eval, manual charter or accepted gap.
  • Bugfix includes reproduction evidence or explicit reproduction gap.
  • Deterministic behavior change uses Red-Green-Refactor where feasible.
  • Contract changes include source contract and compatibility verification.
  • Regression scope follows impact analysis.
  • Runtime claims include current runtime evidence.
  • UI claims include visual/a11y evidence where relevant.
  • AI or subjective quality claims include eval spec and rerun evidence.
  • Coverage threshold is paired with critical-path coverage.
  • Flaky tests are classified and not hidden by retries.
  • CI gates list commands, triggers, artifacts and permissions.
  • Manual QA evidence includes charter, environment, reviewer and findings.
  • Test fixtures, eval datasets, traces and screenshots are free of secrets/private data.
  • Final claims include current command/eval/runtime/manual evidence or explicit gap.

docs.title: Tooling candidates
docs.text: Tooling area Candidate Notes Python tests pytest, unittest, coverage.py, tox/nox pytest is a strong default when already present; preserve existing runner. Java/Kotlin tests JUnit, Gradle/Maven test tasks Use project build tool as source of truth. JS/TS tests Vitest, Jest, Node test runner Choose by existing stack; Vitest fits Vite-native projects. Browser/runtime tests Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO Playwright gives traces, screenshots, retries and cross-browser evidence. Component tests Storybook, Testing Library, Vitest Browser Mode Prefer user-observable behavior and documented component states. API contracts OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Pact, schema validators Contracts should be source-of-truth, generated docs are derived. Property-based tests Hypothesis, fast-check, jqwik Use for invariants, parsers, serializers, permissions and state machines. Mutation testing Stryker, mutmut, PIT Use selectively on critical logic to reveal weak assertions. Coverage reporting coverage.py, Istanbul/V8, Codecov Coverage is a signal, not proof of behavior. AI evals OpenAI Evals, Promptfoo, Ragas, custom app-backed evals Choose by privacy, CI fit, rubric type and stack. CI GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, Azure Pipelines Keep permissions scoped and evidence artifacts accessible. Reports JUnit XML, HTML reports, Allure, Playwright report Store enough evidence to debug failures without rerunning immediately.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• A plan lists tests after implementation but never proves failure or behavior.
  • Unit tests mock away the real risk while integration/contract behavior is untested.
  • E2E tests dominate the suite and become slow, flaky and ignored.
  • Coverage threshold becomes the goal and weak assertions still pass.
  • Contract compatibility is inferred from generated clients without provider/consumer checks.
  • Regression scope is selected by habit, not impact analysis.
  • Browser visual tests run in unstable environments and produce noisy diffs.
  • Retries hide intermittent failures without owner, classification or expiry.
  • CI is treated as green based on an old run.
  • Manual QA has no charter, criteria, environment or reviewer.
  • AI evals have no baseline, threshold, rerun command or failed-case analysis.
  • Test fixtures, traces or eval datasets contain secrets or private customer data.
  • Final response claims "works" from inspection only while runtime verification was available.

docs.title: Open questions for deeper research
docs.text:
• Should Product-Agent OS generate a framework-neutral test-eval-matrix.md first, then stack-specific runner files later?
  • Which changes should require Red-Green-Refactor as a blocker rather than a recommendation?
  • Should mutation/property-based testing be a conditional gate only for critical deterministic logic?
  • How should flaky test quarantine be represented in generated TEST.md and RUNLOG.md?
  • What minimum AI eval threshold policy should apply before model/prompt/retrieval migrations?
  • Should CI workflow proposals include least-privilege permissions by default, even when the target repo already has broader permissions?
  • How should manual QA evidence be normalized across web, desktop, native, backend and docs workflows?

docs.title: Requirements & Domain Methodology Research
docs.text:
Source status: official + verified methodology + local implementation evidence + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Target methodology page: ../../methodologies/requirements-domain.md

Target Product-Agent OS behavior: convert business intent into testable behavior contracts, domain language, domain boundaries and traceable implementation evidence before agents or engineers start building behavior-changing slices.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers requirements engineering, business analysis, user stories, ATDD, BDD, Gherkin, Example Mapping, Domain-Driven Design, EventStorming, Domain Storytelling, bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, domain invariants, domain events, context maps and traceability into architecture, API, UI, database, tests, evals and release evidence.

It does not force formal DDD, Gherkin, EventStorming, BABOK or ISO processes onto every project. These practices are conditional: they become required when domain complexity, stakeholder risk, compliance, team count, service count, user-facing behavior or AI/agent ambiguity makes informal requirements unsafe.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• Agile Alliance describes ATDD as a collaboration between customer, development and testing perspectives to write acceptance tests before implementing the corresponding functionality.
  • Agile Alliance describes BDD as a refinement of TDD and ATDD that connects proposed user stories to business outcomes, works outside-in and describes behavior in a notation accessible to domain experts, testers and developers.
  • Agile Alliance also warns that BDD is a conceptual approach and should not be reduced to a specific tool or programming language.
  • Agile Alliance user-story guidance treats user stories as user-goal-oriented work items whose acceptance criteria should be expressible in terms usable for automated acceptance tests.
  • Cucumber Gherkin reference defines executable specification structure with Feature, Rule, Scenario/Example, Given, When, Then, And, But, Background, Scenario Outline and Examples.
  • Cucumber guidance says Given describes initial context, When describes an event or action and Then describes an expected observable outcome.
  • Cucumber guidance says implementation details should be hidden in step definitions and expected outcomes should be observable to the user or external system instead of deeply buried implementation state.
  • Cucumber Example Mapping uses story, rules, examples and questions to clarify acceptance criteria before a story is pulled into development.
  • ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 is a requirements engineering standard for systems and software life-cycle processes and can be used regardless of project scope, product, methodology, size or complexity.
  • IEEE's public description of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 says it covers requirements engineering processes and products, defines the construct of a good requirement, gives attributes and characteristics of requirements and discusses iterative requirements processes.
  • IIBA describes BABOK as a globally recognized standard for business analysis practice, covering skills, deliverables and techniques across six knowledge areas.
  • Martin Fowler describes Domain-Driven Design as software development centered on a domain model with rich understanding of domain processes and rules, especially suited to complex domains.
  • Fowler describes Bounded Context as a central DDD strategic design pattern that divides large models and teams into explicit model boundaries with explicit relationships.
  • Fowler describes Ubiquitous Language as a rigorous shared language between developers and users, based on the domain model and evolved as understanding grows.
  • Domain Language is Eric Evans' DDD site and primary background source for DDD resources and terminology.
  • EventStorming describes itself as a collaborative workshop format for exploring complex business domains, cross-discipline conversations, service dynamics and event-driven software behavior.
  • Domain Storytelling positions domain stories as a way to learn domain language, reach shared understanding and derive requirements or backlog items from domain stories.
  • The C4 model defines architecture diagrams through hierarchical abstractions: software systems, containers, components and code, with system context, container, component and code diagrams plus supporting views.
  • OpenAPI 3.2.0 defines API operation and reusable component structures that can become downstream traceability artifacts for requirements, acceptance scenarios, domain terms and public contracts.
  • The local Product-Agent OS implementation already includes acceptance-scenarios.md, domain-modeling.md, domain_model_when_complex_domain, bounded_context_architecture_boundary_trace and ubiquitous_language_traceability gates.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• For Product-Agent OS, a behavior-changing slice should not start from folder structure or implementation tasks. It should start from requirement, owner, acceptance scenario, non-goals and observable evidence.
  • User stories are useful planning artifacts, but a story title alone is not a sufficient requirement. It needs acceptance criteria, business rules, examples, edge cases and open questions.
  • Gherkin is one acceptable scenario format, but not the only acceptable format. Product-Agent OS should accept equivalent behavior formats when they preserve actor, context, trigger, observable outcome and evidence mapping.
  • DDD should be conditional. It is required for complex domains, workflow-heavy systems, multi-service boundaries, enterprise vocabulary conflicts, data-heavy workflows and AI/agent systems that make domain decisions. It should not be forced onto trivial CRUD unless a human owner asks for it.
  • Ubiquitous language should be more than a glossary. A project term should trace to requirement, API/event/schema, UI label, code module or domain owner.
  • A bounded context should map to an architecture boundary or carry an accepted gap. Otherwise it remains a workshop artifact rather than an implementation control.
  • Domain expert review is required when requirements contain business rules, policy, financial/legal/compliance meaning or AI-generated domain claims.
  • Accepted gaps are valid only when explicit: owner, reason, scope, expiry/review date and downstream risk must be recorded.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "BDD replaces testing." BDD clarifies behavior and can generate executable scenarios, but it does not replace unit, integration, contract, exploratory, performance, security or eval checks.
  • "Gherkin is mandatory for BDD." BDD is a conceptual practice; Gherkin is one useful executable notation.
  • "A user story template is a complete requirement." A template without acceptance criteria, examples, business rules, constraints and evidence owner is incomplete.
  • "A glossary is ubiquitous language." Ubiquitous language must be used in conversations, models, code/API/UI and owner review.
  • "DDD is the right default for every project." DDD has coordination and modeling cost and is most useful for complex domains.
  • "Bounded Context equals folder or microservice." A bounded context is a model boundary; implementation boundaries should be traced, not assumed.
  • "OpenAPI is the requirements source of truth." OpenAPI is a contract artifact. It can trace requirements, but it does not replace business intent and acceptance scenarios.
  • "AI can infer domain rules from chat memory." Domain rules need source, owner confirmation or explicit accepted-gap status.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the work before implementation: new requirement, behavior change, bug, refactor with behavior risk, domain model change, API contract change, data model change, UI copy/flow change or AI/agent behavior change.
  2. Start with business intent: user/stakeholder, problem, expected outcome, value signal, scope and non-goals.
  3. Assign a requirement ID and owner for any behavior-changing work. Owner can be product, domain expert, technical owner or explicitly marked accepted gap.
  4. Capture constraints early: compliance, privacy, security, operational, performance, platform, accessibility, data retention, localization, cost and rollout.
  5. Write acceptance scenarios before implementation. Minimum trace is requirement -> scenario -> check -> evidence owner.
  6. Prefer concrete examples over abstract prose. Each rule should have at least one happy path and at least one edge/negative path when risk justifies it.
  7. Use Gherkin only when it improves collaboration or executable specification. Equivalent behavior tables are acceptable when easier for the team.
  8. Keep scenarios declarative. Hide UI selectors, database internals, implementation function names and test harness setup outside the behavior statement.
  9. For each user story, record acceptance criteria, business rules, open questions, deferred slices and non-goals. A story title alone is not ready.
  10. Use Example Mapping when a story is large, unclear or disputed. Stop when rules, examples and questions are explicit enough for development or when open questions block the slice.
  11. Use EventStorming or Domain Storytelling when the team lacks shared process/language understanding, especially before event-driven, workflow-heavy or cross-silo changes.
  12. Apply DDD only when domain complexity justifies it. For simple CRUD/MVP, record domain_model_not_required with owner and reason instead of creating ceremonial models.
  13. When DDD applies, define bounded contexts, key aggregates/entities/value objects, domain services, invariants, domain events and integration relationships.
  14. Every bounded context must map to an architecture boundary, team/agent ownership boundary or explicit accepted gap.
  15. Build ubiquitous language as traceability, not a static glossary. Map important terms to requirement, API/event/schema, UI label, code module/test and owner.
  16. Record unresolved term conflicts as decisions or open questions. Do not let one term silently mean different things across API, UI, code and data.
  17. Trace domain events to contracts. If an event crosses a boundary, document meaning, producer, consumers, schema, idempotency/ordering assumptions and privacy classification.
  18. Trace requirements downstream before completion: tests/evals, API contract, database changes, UI states/copy, documentation and release/rollback notes.
  19. When a requirement changes after planning, run change impact review and update affected scenarios, contracts, data model, UI states, tests/evals, docs and rollout plan.
  20. Require domain expert or owner review for business rules, compliance-sensitive claims, financial/legal meaning, AI-generated domain interpretations and accepted gaps.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Implementation starts from file/folder structure without confirmed business behavior.
  • A user story title is treated as complete requirements.
  • Acceptance criteria describe implementation tasks instead of observable outcomes.
  • Gherkin files duplicate test code and become unreadable to domain experts.
  • Example Mapping creates questions but no owner or next action.
  • DDD is forced on simple CRUD and slows delivery without reducing risk.
  • DDD is skipped for complex workflows because no one wants to own the model.
  • Bounded contexts are named but do not map to architecture, teams, APIs or data ownership.
  • Glossary terms are written once but code, API, UI and documentation drift into different vocabulary.
  • Domain events are named as technical messages with no business meaning, producer/consumer contract or privacy classification.
  • AI-generated domain assumptions are accepted without source or domain owner review.
  • Requirement changes do not update tests, contracts, data model, UI, docs, evals or release notes.

docs.title: Open questions for future research
docs.text:
• Should Product-Agent OS ship a generic requirements-traceability-matrix.md template or derive traceability from REQUIREMENTS.md, TEST.md, EVALS.md and contract docs?

  • Should EventStorming and Domain Storytelling become separate optional artifact templates or remain discovery guidance inside domain-modeling.md?
  • How should requirements-domain gates integrate with AI/RAG eval datasets where acceptance criteria are probabilistic or judge-based?

docs.title: Security, Privacy & Compliance Methodology Research
docs.text:
Source status: official + legal/regulatory reference + vendor documentation + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Target methodology page: ../../methodologies/security-privacy-compliance.md

Target Product-Agent OS behavior: detect security-sensitive work early, keep the workflow planning-first and approval-bound, require threat surface and data classification before implementation, prevent secrets/private data from entering artifacts, and block readiness claims without security/privacy evidence, owner review, rollback and residual-risk record.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers secure SDLC, threat modeling, authentication, authorization, permissions, secrets, PII and sensitive data handling, privacy-by-design, audit logging, abuse controls, rate limits, secure API and web verification, AI/LLM security, supply chain security, SBOM/provenance, CI permissions, compliance overlays, vulnerability response and approval boundaries.

It does not provide legal advice, replace security engineering review, replace privacy counsel, mandate one compliance framework for all projects or imply that a checklist proves compliance. Compliance overlays must be selected by jurisdiction, product domain, customer contract and owner/legal review.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• NIST SSDF SP 800-218 defines a secure software development framework with high-level practices that can be integrated into SDLC implementations and used as a common vocabulary across producers, purchasers and consumers.
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 is current NIST cybersecurity risk management guidance and adds governance as an explicit function around cybersecurity risk strategy, expectations and policy.
  • NIST Privacy Framework 1.1 usage guidance supports profiles, accountability, privacy program improvement, SDLC alignment and data processing ecosystem roles.
  • OWASP SAMM is a software assurance maturity model for analyzing and improving an organization's software security posture.
  • OWASP ASVS provides a basis for testing web application technical security controls with versioned verification requirements.
  • OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document for critical web application security risks, with OWASP's page listing Top 10 2025 as the most current released version as of this research date.
  • OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 is an API-specific risk catalog and should complement, not replace, API contract tests and authorization tests.
  • OWASP Cheat Sheet Series provides developer-focused guidance across application security topics, including secrets management and logging.
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 documents AI application security risks and is relevant when prompts, tools, RAG, agents or model outputs affect product behavior.
  • OpenAI Codex agent approvals and security guidance defines sandboxing, approvals and network controls for Codex work.
  • OpenAI API data controls guidance documents platform data controls; OpenAI safety and production best practices cover moderation, human oversight, adversarial testing, monitoring, rate limits, latency and operational safeguards.
  • GitHub Actions secure use guidance and GITHUB_TOKEN guidance support least-privilege CI design; GitHub secret scanning detects secret leaks and supports push protection workflows where enabled.
  • SLSA v1.1 defines supply chain levels and provenance concepts for build integrity.
  • OpenSSF Scorecard checks repository security practices such as branch protection, dangerous workflows, pinned dependencies, token permissions, vulnerabilities and security policy.
  • SPDX and CycloneDX are SBOM standards/specifications. SPDX 3.0 is listed as current by SPDX, and CycloneDX 1.7 is listed as current by CycloneDX as of this research date.
  • GDPR and CCPA are legal/regulatory sources for privacy obligations; engineering docs should map product/data behaviors to legal review, not claim compliance without qualified owner evidence.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• Product-Agent OS should use NIST SSDF as lifecycle vocabulary, OWASP ASVS/API/Top 10/LLM Top 10 as application risk vocabulary, NIST Privacy Framework as privacy program vocabulary, and SLSA/OpenSSF/SBOM sources as supply-chain vocabulary.
  • For most projects, a lightweight security risk review is more useful than a broad compliance checklist. Regulated projects can add overlays later.
  • Security scans and Codex Security workflows should be explicit opt-in. A security-sensitive workflow alone is not evidence that a full security scan was run.
  • Documentation should store classifications and evidence, not raw secrets, raw PII, payment data, access tokens or private customer data.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "Using OWASP Top 10 means the app is secure." OWASP Top 10 is awareness/risk guidance, not a full verification standard.
  • "ASVS mapping proves compliance." ASVS helps verification, but compliance depends on scope, evidence and review.
  • "No secrets in code means no secrets risk." Secrets can leak through prompts, logs, traces, screenshots, fixtures, CI config and generated docs.
  • "SBOM alone proves supply-chain security." SBOM improves transparency but needs vulnerability, provenance, signing and update workflows.
  • "Agent approvals are optional UX." For privileged tools, external writes, customer data or payment/billing behavior, approvals are security controls.
  • "Privacy compliance is universal." Privacy obligations vary by jurisdiction, user type, domain and data processing purpose.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify the slice before implementation. Mark as security-sensitive when it touches authn, authz, permissions, payment, billing, secrets, PII, sensitive data, abuse controls, rate limits, audit logs, CI permissions, package release, external writes or agent tool permissions.
  2. Keep security-sensitive work read-only until threat surface, data classification, approval boundary, rollback and verification plan are explicit.
  3. Identify actors, assets, entry points, trust boundaries, privileged operations, data exposed, external systems and abuse cases.
  4. Classify data before examples, fixtures, evals, logs, traces, screenshots or docs are created.
  5. Do not store raw secrets, credentials, private keys, raw PII, payment data, raw private chats, access tokens or private customer data in docs, prompts, memory, fixtures, examples or templates.
  6. For auth/authz changes, document allowed and forbidden behavior, role/scope matrix, object ownership checks and negative tests.
  7. For API/security scheme changes, update OpenAPI or equivalent contract and include security scheme, scopes, error behavior and negative examples.
  8. For web app technical controls, map checks to versioned ASVS requirements when ASVS applies.
  9. For public APIs, webhooks or integrations, add OWASP API Security risks to threat review and require object/function-level authorization checks where relevant.
  10. For AI/RAG/agent workflows, include OWASP LLM Top 10 risks and OpenAI safety/data-control boundaries where OpenAI services are used.
  11. For Codex App, CLI, IDE extension, subagents, skills, MCP or automations, treat sandbox, approvals, external writes and network access as security controls.
  12. For CI, GitHub Actions or release workflows, document least-privilege permissions, secret use, artifact exposure, external action pinning and approval boundary.
  13. For dependencies and releases, document vulnerability status, update path, SBOM/provenance status and release integrity evidence where applicable.
  14. For privacy-impacting work, document purpose, data minimization, retention, deletion/export expectations, access, sharing and legal/regulatory owner.
  15. For compliance-sensitive work, create an applicability matrix. Do not claim GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI, SOC 2 or enterprise compliance from engineering inspection alone.
  16. Require security tests or explicit test gaps for touched authn, authz, permission, secret handling, PII handling, abuse control, rate limit, audit logging and external write behavior.
  17. Require owner review for security-sensitive changes and explicit approval for external systems, production data, payment/billing, secret rotation and policy changes.
  18. Record rollback and mitigation: feature flag, kill switch, permission rollback, secret rollback, payment disable path, data access rollback or release revert.
  19. Record residual risk in RUNLOG.md, risk review or release packet before completion.
  20. Use Codex Security scan workflows only when explicitly requested and evidenced; do not imply that a scan ran from a methodology page alone.

docs.text:
• Security-sensitive scope is classified before implementation.

  • API security changes include contract security schemes and negative examples.

  • Supply chain review includes dependency/vulnerability status, SBOM/provenance status and release integrity notes where applicable.
  • CI workflow changes include least-privilege permissions and staged external-write policy.
  • AI/agent security review covers prompt injection, data leakage, tool misuse, excessive agency and red-team/eval path.
  • Compliance claims cite applicable legal/regulatory/contract source and qualified owner evidence.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Security review happens as a checklist after implementation.
  • Threat model omits actors, trust boundaries or abuse cases.
  • Authorization tests cover happy path only.
  • API docs list auth scheme but omit scopes, error behavior or negative examples.
  • Secrets are excluded from source but leak through prompts, logs, traces, screenshots, fixtures or generated docs.
  • Privacy review records data fields but omits purpose, retention, deletion/export or sharing.
  • Compliance claim is made without applicability matrix and qualified owner evidence.
  • SBOM is generated once but not tied to release, vulnerability triage or provenance.
  • CI workflow uses broad permissions or unpinned actions without review.
  • AI/agent workflow ignores prompt injection, tool misuse, data leakage or excessive agency.
  • Codex Security scan is implied but not explicitly requested or evidenced.
  • External security systems, production policy, customer data, payment/billing or secret rotation are changed without approval.

docs.title: Solution Architecture Methodology Research
docs.text:
Source status: official + verified methodology + local implementation evidence + tool-assisted

Research date: 2026-05-24

Target methodology page: ../../methodologies/solution-architecture.md

Target Product-Agent OS behavior: make architecture a reviewable, source-backed and verifiable artifact that maps requirements, domain boundaries, quality attributes, public contracts, data ownership, security boundaries, runtime topology, decisions, risks and rollback before implementation changes system structure.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This dossier covers solution architecture for large software projects: system context, containers/services, components, code-level detail when useful, quality attributes, tradeoffs, architecture decisions, contracts, data ownership, trust boundaries, runtime/deployment topology, observability, migration and architecture governance.

It does not mandate enterprise architecture frameworks, a specific cloud provider, UML, C4, Structurizr, Mermaid, arc42, microservices, DDD or ADRs for every change. These practices are conditional and should scale with system complexity, public contract risk, data/security impact, team count, deployment risk and long-lived maintainability needs.

docs.title: Supported facts
docs.text:
• The C4 model defines hierarchical abstractions for software architecture: software systems, containers, components and code. It also defines hierarchical diagrams: system context, container, component and code, plus supporting system landscape, dynamic and deployment diagrams.
  • The C4 model is notation independent and tooling independent. This supports Mermaid, Structurizr DSL, PlantUML or other project-appropriate tools as long as the architecture view is understandable and maintained.
  • C4 can be combined with arc42: system context aligns with Context and Scope, container with Building Block View level 1, component with level 2 and code with level 3.
  • arc42 provides an open-source, pragmatic template for documenting and communicating software and system architectures. It is process-agnostic, technology-agnostic and suited to lean/agile approaches.
  • ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 specifies requirements for the structure and expression of architecture descriptions. It distinguishes architecture from the architecture description that expresses it, covers frameworks/languages/viewpoints/model kinds, and does not prescribe a specific creation process, notation, tool or recording format.
  • SEI's Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) is a structured technique for understanding tradeoffs in software-intensive system architectures. It evaluates architecture fitness against competing quality attributes such as modifiability, security, performance and availability.
  • SEI ATAM guidance explicitly notes that quality attributes interact and improving one can worsen another, so architecture decisions need tradeoff analysis rather than one-dimensional optimization.
  • MADR defines an Architectural Decision as a justified software design choice that addresses an architecturally significant functional or non-functional requirement, and an ADR as the record that documents the decision and rationale.
  • Structurizr DSL is a text-based domain-specific language for defining software architecture models based on the C4 model. The Structurizr documentation includes Markdown/AsciiDoc documentation and ADR support.
  • Mermaid provides text-based diagram syntax for many diagram types and can live inside Markdown documentation. Its own documentation warns that syntax issues can break diagrams, so render/build checks are part of evidence.
  • Thoughtworks describes architecture fitness functions as objective tests or metrics that measure whether architecture is aligned with architectural goals and can provide continuous feedback against architectural drift.
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework defines six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. It also states that architecture tradeoffs are made based on business context.
  • Azure Well-Architected Framework is a set of quality-driven tenets, architectural decision points and review tools for workloads, with pillars including reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence and performance efficiency.
  • OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral observability framework for generating, collecting and exporting telemetry data such as traces, metrics and logs; this is useful as runtime evidence for architecture claims.
  • The local Product-Agent OS implementation already has architecture-overview.md, adr.md, architecture_boundary, bounded_context_architecture_boundary_trace, docs-as-code routing and readiness statuses for architecture-related gates.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• Solution architecture should be a decision and verification surface, not a decorative diagram pack.
  • For large projects, the minimum useful architecture artifact is an architecture-overview.md that names system purpose, users, external systems, trust boundaries, containers/services, data stores, quality attributes, risks, owners and verification route.
  • Context and container views are usually the default minimum for complex systems. Component and code views should be added only where they reduce delivery or review risk.
  • Every implementation slice should name the architecture boundary it touches and what remains out of scope.
  • Architecture decisions should be captured only when they are significant: public contract, boundary, data ownership, security model, runtime topology, migration, technology choice, quality attribute or rollback impact.
  • Quality attributes should be expressed as scenarios or measurable expectations, not vague "scalable/secure/fast" labels.
  • Architecture-as-code should be preferred when diagrams must survive review, diff, build and CI, but teams can record an accepted gap for docs-light or early prototype work.
  • Cloud well-architected frameworks are useful quality checklists, not vendor-neutral architecture law. Use them conditionally when the target workload is cloud-hosted or when the pillars help structure review.
  • AI-generated architecture should remain present_unverified until checked against repository evidence, primary sources and owner review.

docs.title: Unsupported claims not adopted
docs.text:
• "Solution architecture is a role title." Product-Agent OS treats it as a reviewable artifact and decision workflow.
  • "One diagram is enough for a large system." Large systems need views selected by stakeholder concerns and risk.
  • "C4 code-level diagrams are always required." Code views are optional and only useful when they add value beyond source navigation.
  • "arc42 is a process." arc42 is documentation and communication structure, not a required delivery process.
  • "ADR for every small decision." ADRs should capture architecturally significant decisions, not noise.
  • "A rendered diagram proves architecture correctness." Render proves syntax/display only; correctness needs source evidence, owner review, tests, contracts or runtime evidence.
  • "Well-Architected pillars mean a cloud vendor must be adopted." Pillars are review heuristics and should not imply provider lock-in.
  • "Architecture can be inferred from directory names." Directory structure is a clue, not verified architecture compliance.
  • "Architecture fitness functions replace review." Fitness functions provide continuous signals; tradeoff review and owner judgment still matter.

docs.title: Project application instructions
docs.text:
1. Classify architecture impact before implementation: new boundary, service split, public API/event, data ownership, runtime topology, security model, integration, dependency rule, migration, platform choice, AI/agent route or quality attribute.
  2. Start with stakeholders and concerns: users, product owner, domain owner, service owner, security/privacy, operations, support, data owner and release owner.
  3. Define the architecture question. Avoid generic diagrams; name the decision or risk the view must answer.
  4. Write or update architecture-overview.md for complex systems, public contracts, data/security sensitive work, multi-service work, multi-team work or unclear ownership.
  5. Start with C4 System Context: users, external systems, external APIs, trust boundaries and major data flows.
  6. Add C4 Container view for deployable/runtime boundaries: UI, services, workers, queues, storage, integration adapters and AI/LLM components.
  7. Add Component view only for containers whose internals are risky, non-obvious or owned by multiple agents/teams.
  8. Add Code view only when source navigation is insufficient and the diagram helps review a hard design decision.
  9. For every boundary, record responsibility, owner, public contract, data ownership, runtime evidence and mapped bounded context where applicable.
  10. For every slice, name architecture boundary, files in scope, files out of scope, contract impact, data impact, runtime impact and rollback path.
  11. Use ADR/MADR when a decision affects architecture boundary, public contract, persistent data, security/privacy, quality attributes, runtime topology, migration or irreversible cost.
  12. For each ADR, record considered options and consequences. A decision without alternatives is usually an assertion, not architecture reasoning.
  13. Convert vague quality attributes into scenarios or measurable targets: latency, throughput, availability, recovery, durability, consistency, security, privacy, accessibility, maintainability, observability and cost.
  14. When quality attributes conflict, record the tradeoff. Do not hide cost/reliability/performance/security compromises in implementation details.
  15. Use architecture-as-code where the diagram must be reviewed, diffed or built. Mermaid is enough for lightweight Markdown docs; Structurizr DSL is better when a single model must produce multiple C4 views.
  16. Validate diagram syntax or explicitly record the missing render check. A stale diagram is worse than an absent one.
  17. Map public contracts to architecture: OpenAPI operations, AsyncAPI channels, SDK interfaces, generated clients, event schemas and consumer/versioning impact.
  18. Map data ownership to architecture: source of truth, read replicas, derived data, analytics, retention, deletion, migration/backfill and privacy classification.
  19. Map runtime topology to evidence: environments, deployment units, config/secrets, health checks, observability, dashboards, alerts, rollback and runbook links.
  20. Use architecture fitness functions for repeated conformance risks: dependency direction, forbidden imports, public contract drift, missing observability, security gates, cost budgets, docs freshness or eval thresholds.
  21. Record accepted gaps explicitly with owner, reason, residual risk, review date and follow-up condition.
  22. Treat AI-generated architecture as draft. Verify against repository files, source-backed standards, runtime evidence and owner review before using it for implementation.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Architecture documentation describes the system after the fact and does not influence decisions.
  • Diagrams are decorative and not tied to requirements, decisions, owners, contracts or verification.
  • Context view omits external systems, trust boundaries or data flows.
  • Container view hides queues, workers, storage, batch jobs or AI/LLM components.
  • Component/code diagrams are overused and become stale faster than source navigation.
  • ADRs record the chosen option but omit alternatives, consequences, verification and rollback.
  • Quality attributes remain slogans: scalable, secure, reliable, maintainable.
  • Architecture decisions optimize one quality attribute while silently damaging another.
  • Public contracts, generated clients or event schemas change without architecture trace.
  • Data ownership and privacy classification stay implicit until migration/release time.
  • Runtime topology omits config/secrets, health checks, observability, rollback or runbook links.
  • Architecture-as-code exists but render/validate checks are never run.
  • AI-generated architecture is accepted without checking repository evidence and owner review.

  • Should solution architecture gates be hard for all public-contract/data/security changes, or conditional warnings until Track 8 readiness hardening is finished?
  • How should agent-team ownership use architecture boundaries when boundaries overlap with domain contexts and frontend feature slices?

  • Acceptance criteria: Contract version and enums have one mutable source; unknown fields, required fields, ranges, malformed arrays, timeout/no-op and normalization rules are executable; the observed red precedes production implementation; focused tests and seeded-corruption checks pass after the minimal fix; invalid pairs cannot reach reviewer or promotion logic; independent read-only review and claim-gate review report no blocking finding.

  • Complexity: high
  • Estimated execution time: 45-90 minutes
  • Agents: architect freezes the contract read-only; tester owns tests and fixtures; plugin-runtime-builder alone owns production files; reviewer and completion-skeptic are read-only; docs-maintainer owns post-gate evidence synchronization.
  • Skills: implementation-planner; agent-team-designer; python-design-patterns; python-code-style; tdd; project-local control-plane sync and docs maintenance.
  • Output artifacts: plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/promotion_contract.py; plugins/product-agent-os/scripts/codex_runtime_runner/model_output.py; tests/product_agent_os/test_codex_runtime_runner_promotion_contract.py; tests/fixtures/product_agent_os/batch45/promotion-contract/; this plan; required current-evidence control-plane and registry updates.
